#5658. Sjogren's Disease Brings a Lot More Misery Beyond Dryness

— Brain fog, fatigue, infections, death explored in new studies

Oral and ocular dryness are the hallmark features of Sjögren's disease, but understanding the full symptom burden is still an active area of investigation, with recent studies reported at the American College of Rheumatology's annual meeting shedding light on some of the condition's lesser-known aspects.

For example, one new study found that oral disease serious enough to cause tooth loss helps drive serious infections such as sepsis in Sjögren's patients, a risk that is worsened further with immunomodulators typically used to control the disease.

Another found that nonphysical symptoms including "brain fog" and fatigue are nearly as common as dryness in Sjögren's disease, and a third confirmed that patients face a significant risk for early mortality.

All in all, this research puts Sjögren's disease alongside conditions more famous for their broadly burdensome symptom spectrum, such as rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus, and systemic sclerosis.

An analysis of U.S. commercial and Medicaid insurance claims led by Thomas Grader-Beck, MD, of Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore, looked at associations between oral disease indicators and infection rates among some 60,000 people with Sjögren's disease.

Those suffering tooth loss, typically the result of periodontal disease, were significantly more likely to also experience systemic infections -- modestly when five or fewer teeth were lost (OR 1.18, 95% CI 1.13-1.24), or more strongly with more extensive extractions (OR 1.69, 95% CI 1.36-2.11). Absolute risks were substantial too: whereas systemic infections were recorded for 36% of those with no tooth loss (itself an indicator of risk associated with Sjögren's disease), the percentage reached 43% in patients with up to five lost teeth and 54% among those with six or more lost.

Dental visits, too, tracked with systemic infection risk in a "dose-response" relationship. Odds ratios for infections rose with each additional visit in the previous year: 1.11 with one visit, 1.32 with two, 1.41 with three, and 1.60 for four or more (all P<0.001 relative to no dental visits).

Moreover, the researchers reported, use of immunomodulator therapy -- a category that spans virtually every drug used for Sjögren's disease including corticosteroids, antimalarials, biologics, and conventional immunosuppressants -- by itself raised the risk for infections by 49%.

Oral disease and immunosuppression are "independent, additive risk factors for systemic infection," the group concluded.

Lane Destro, PhD, and colleagues at the Sjögren's Foundation in Reston, Virginia, had the Harris Poll organization survey people with the condition last year, with a total of 6,360 responses. It found that so-called brain fog -- a feeling of mental sluggishness and inability to focus -- and fatigue were almost as common as salivary and ocular dryness (prevalences of 77% and 90%, respectively, versus 93% and 95%), and also in the same range as joint pain (81%).

Other nonphysical symptoms were common too, if less so than brain fog and fatigue. Some 73% of respondents complained of insomnia, 64% reported eye fatigue specifically, 56% said they suffered headaches, and 56% indicated feeling dizzy or faint.

Patients also complained of additional burdens. Close to 60% said Sjögren's disease had affected relations with their spouses or partners and two-thirds reported impacts on other family relationships. A large majority agreed that Sjögren's "adds an emotional burden to my life," while half said the disease made them feel lonely. Not surprisingly, most also reported difficulties with work and employment stemming from the diagnosis.

Furthermore, the problems arising from fatigue and brain fog were disproportionately burdensome for these quality-of-life (QoL) issues. Having relatively severe dry eyes and mouth, for example, raised the likelihood of experiencing negative QoL effects by factors of roughly 1.5 to 2; a high fatigue burden, on the other hand, raised the risk by factors of 4 to 10, and the negative impact of brain fog was nearly as great.

French researchers confirmed that patients with Sjögren's disease face increased mortality risk, in the same way as patients with other autoimmune inflammatory conditions such as lupus.

Led by Elodie Portier, MD, of Hôpital Bicêtre in Paris, the group examined vital statistics for a 395-member cohort of Sjögren's disease patients in France and compared them with the general national population. Followed from 2007 to 2025, the cohort saw 77 deaths. The rate was 41% higher than among similar-age French people (95% CI 11-76). The gap was even greater for a Sjögren's subgroup marked by high symptom burden (54%, 95% CI 10-110).

The researchers also identified several risk factors for early mortality in the Sjögren's cohort. In multivariate analysis, each year of older age added 13% to the risk, while being male nearly tripled the likelihood of death (HR 2.66, 95% CI 1.04-6.77).

Having more than mild disease was also a mortality risk. Multivariate analysis comparing patients with EULAR Sjögren's Syndrome Activity Index (ESSDAI) scores of 6 or more to those with ESSDAI 5 or less yielded a hazard ratio of 2.16 (95% CI 1.29-3.60). Each ESSDAI point conferred a 15% extra risk for mortality.

Patient-reported overall symptom burden showed a similar pattern, the researchers noted, but it fell just short of statistical significance.

#5657. Over 70,000 km by Plane a Year: Travel Influencers Are Blowing Their Carbon Budgets and encouraging Europeans to Do the Same

Travel influencers have a disproportionate climate footprint, generating an average of 10.0t of CO₂e emissions each just from flights in 2025, according to a new report by T3 Transportation Think Tank, commissioned by T&E. This is 16.7 times higher than the average European’s four leisure round trips and around 0.6 t CO₂e per tourist each year across all modes of transport for the 95% of their trips taking place in the EU. This does not yet include the travel emissions of the people they influenced.

The study tracks 25 primarily European and US travel influencers representing millions of followers, and examines their role in the advertising strategy of airlines. Influencers took an average of 16 flights per year, visiting four times as many destinations as a standard European.

The study shows that influencers predominantly take long-haul flights (49%) over medium (24%) and short-haul (27%) journeys. Long-haul flying is the most polluting form of transport: an economy long-haul flight generates roughly three to four times more emissions than a short-haul flight.

In total, these influencers flew a total distance of 1.8 million kilometers in 2025, equivalent to approximately 45 trips around the globe. Individually, each influencer flew an average of 72,244 km, equivalent to 34 return holiday flights between Paris and Athens.

Travel influencers are frequent flyers, with a disproportionate climate footprint. They regularly post about luxury, comfort and aspirational destinations. Influencers play a significant role in shaping where people choose to travel, thereby driving demand for high polluting flying. Through travel influencers, frequent air travel is normalised and encouraged.

The study shows that European and Middle Eastern airlines are ranked among the top 30 carriers that advertise on social media and websites. These include easyJet, Emirates and KLM. Even though airlines are not currently obliged to disclose their advertising budgets, the analysis reveals that social media, including influencer marketing, likely accounts for the largest marketing expenditure, around one third, with the UK seeing the highest spend (€50.2 million).

The list is dominated by airlines headquartered in the respective country and those that hold the most slots at the major international airports in each country. For example Air France spends more on social media advertisements in France (€2 million) compared to Spain (€29,000). Other carriers spending a lot on social media are easyJet and Aer Lingus, spending almost €26 million and around €7 million respectively. EasyJet spends more than twice on social media and online advertising than the following airlines.

“Airlines have found a ridiculously cheap way of promoting climate intensive behaviour. They pay influencers to make very frequent and polluting long distance flights look normal and desirable. The average of 72,244 km shouldn’t be something to brag about… that would take an average European nearly 23 years to match” said Aiza Rodrigues Akhtar, T&E Aviation Campaigner. “The EU must enforce disclosure of airline-funded influencer promotions of harmful high-emission flights and enforce accountability of both parties.”

For airlines, partnering with travel influencers is remarkably cost-effective: it can cost just a few thousand euros¹ or just a free seat upgrade, yet it leads to significant results. Compared to traditional channels such as TV broadcasts or billboard displays, social media ads have a higher return on investment: posts that are liked, shared or reposted remain in the digital space for longer, significantly boosting visibility.

Yet, both influencers and airlines are not fully transparent when it comes to advertising. Influencers do not always clearly label their promotional content, and airlines do not publicly disclose how much they spend on digital advertising. Consumer organisations underline that any commercial promotion on social media should be clearly labelled so that consumers know what they are being marketed to and when. The EU Digital Fairness Act, currently under development, is key to tackling misleading influencer marketing and closing transparency loopholes. As travel influencers promote high-emission flights, any paid promotions must be clearly labelled as such.

“Transparency is a first step, but it is not enough to prevent the damage caused by influencer ads for flying”, says Rémi ter Haar, legal campaigner at Fossil Free Advertising. “Calling for more truthful advertising in the aviation sector is like playing a game of ‘whack-a-mole’. We must get ahead in the game and ban their advertising, for the sake of the climate and public health. We cannot expect people to behave more sustainably, only to then manipulate them through advertising into doing exactly the opposite.”

The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) recognises that regulating advertising is key to changing the behaviours needed to limit global warming to 1.5°C. Marketing portrays luxury goods as necessities, and the IPCC cites long-distance holiday ads as an example of how the industry creates and normalises carbon-intensive desires. While the EU Audiovisual Media Services Directive prohibits promotions that encourage behavior harmful to the environment, this rule is often interpreted too narrowly. Airline advertising, which promotes carbon-intensive behaviour, should be included in its definition.

¹ Influencers get paid between €269 to €2,692 for their travel content by airlines depending on the format: a 24-hour post (story), a static post or a short video (reel). Read more.

Transport & Environment’s (T&E) vision is a zero-emission mobility system that is affordable and has minimal impacts on our health, climate and environment. Created over 30 years ago, we have shaped some of Europe’s most important environmental laws.

#5655. High-Flying Influencers

This briefing is based on the T3 Transportation Think Tank study commissioned by T&E. This study examines the environmental footprint of travel influencers, and the role they and social media play in the advertising strategy of airlines. The first part analyses travel influencers’ associated emissions, travel frequencies and routes. The second part focuses on airline digital advertising investments in five European markets: France, Germany, Netherlands, Spain and the United Kingdom.

Travel influencers are digital opinion leaders that travel frequently and who shape the destination’s image, attitudes and behavioural intentions of their audiences through personal narratives. Most often, air travel is their main mode of transportation and they cover large distances by taking long-haul journeys. They post content all year-round, meaning they travel a lot and generate a substantial climate footprint. Through their posts, they display luxury, comfort and aspirational locations.

This constant posting of glamorised photogenic locations shapes their audiences’ destination preferences and can incite them to fly long-distance, fuelling air travel demand and contributing to overtourism and crowding of tourism hotspots. However, influencers are confronted with transparency issues: research suggests that too much sponsored content can undermine an influencer’s credibility, and at the same time identifies a lack of hashtags, used to explicitly disclose sponsored content (#ad or #sponsored), in such content.

Airlines’ advertisements promote carbon-intensive behaviours through frequent and long-distance flying. Although airlines don’t publicly disclose their digital advertising expenditure, social media forms one of the largest portions of their digital budgets. Social media is a powerful driver for travel inspiration, destination promotion and direct bookings. It exerts a high level of influence on consumer choices. Partnering with travel influencers offers airlines high returns on investment. Likes, shares and reposts ensure airlines secure continuous, long-term exposure and significant quantifiable marketing value.

Currently, regulatory standards specifically targeting influencer content and brand collaborations remain underdeveloped. There is also no regulation asking airlines to disclose their advertisement budget spend. In addition, the EU lacks a unified and robust regulatory framework that taxes, restricts or prohibits advertising for carbon-intensive advertisements, such as airline ads. Finally, aviation taxation and carbon pricing, needed to curb excessive emissions such as those from long-haul flights, are weak. To effectively fill these gaps, existing policy mechanisms as well as those currently being developed must be strengthened and expanded.

Travel influencers often disregard the significant carbon footprint of their long-distance trips, and encourage environmentally damaging lifestyles and excessive travel among their audiences. Airlines publicly commit to sustainability while actively funding social media campaigns and influencer promotions that encourage frequent, long-haul flying.

Together they drive carbon-intensive behaviours and air travel demand, which also contributes to overtourism. Regulatory measures need to be robust, strengthened and unified across the EU to enforce accountability of both parties:

By Aiza Rodrigues Akhtar, Aviation Campaign Officer, T&E

#5654. How Certain Foods in Adolescence Are Linked to IBD Risk

— Study finds associations with fruit, fish, and salty snacks, but not always in the same direction

Eating certain foods during childhood and adolescence was associated with higher or lower risks of later inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), prospective data suggested.

In pooled analyses of three cohorts in Norway, Denmark, and Sweden, high versus low intake of fruit in childhood was associated with a reduced risk of Crohn's disease (CD; adjusted HR 0.66, 95% CI 0.47-0.94), as was high versus low intake of fish (aHR 0.65, 95% CI 0.44-0.97), reported Annie Guo, PhD, of the University of Gothenburg Institute of Medicine in Sweden, and colleagues in Gut.

On the other hand, high versus low fruit intake in childhood was associated with an increased risk of ulcerative colitis (UC; aHR 1.54, 95% CI 1.07-2.20).

During adolescence, high versus low fruit intake was associated with a reduced risk of CD (aHR 0.57, 95% CI 0.36-0.88), but no significant associations were observed between fruit consumption and UC.

Meanwhile, high versus low intake of salty snacks during adolescence was initially associated with an increased risk of IBD (HR 1.43, 95% CI 1.11-1.86), but after multivariable adjustment, the risk was attenuated (aHR 1.32, 95% CI 0.99-1.77). The adjusted HR for UC with a high versus low intake of salty snacks in adolescence was 1.51 (95% CI 0.97-2.37).

"To our knowledge, this is the first prospective study to examine associations between food-group intake during both childhood and adolescence and the subsequent risk of IBD, CD, and UC," Guo and team wrote. "If our findings are confirmed in other cohorts and by other study designs, promoting healthy dietary habits could be a potential strategy for IBD prevention."

As to what explains the associations between fruit intake and reduced CD risk, the authors noted that the "dietary fiber content of fruit may partly contribute to the observed inverse association between fruit intake and CD risk by promoting a favorable gut microbial environment."

Conversely, they suggested that the association with an increased risk of UC "could potentially be explained by differences in the etiology between the subtypes, since CD has been suggested to be more related to dysbiosis and UC to mucosal immune dysregulation."

As for the link between higher intake of salty snacks and an increased risk of IBD, they pointed out that the salty snack food group across the three cohorts was mostly composed of items high in saturated fats, and saturated fatty acids "have been shown to promote proinflammatory immune responses."

For this study, Guo and colleagues pooled data from three prospective population-based birth cohorts in Norway, Denmark, and Sweden encompassing 111,999 participants born in 1996 through 2009, contributing a total of 1,541,247 person-years of follow-up.

Information on dietary intake in childhood (7-8 years) and adolescence (11-15 years) was obtained from food frequency questionnaires, and included intake of fruit, vegetables, dairy products, meat, fish, sugar-sweetened drinks, and sweet snacks. Questions on dietary intake of salty snacks, such as potato chips and popcorn, were only asked during the teen years.

Diagnoses of any IBD were captured in national patient registries by 2024.

During the observation period, 653 incident cases of IBD were identified, with country-specific incidence rates of 45, 39, and 62 per 100,000 person-years in Norway, Denmark, and Sweden, respectively.

Following dietary assessment in childhood, the median ages at diagnosis were 15.6 years, 18.3 years, and 25.7 years in Norway, Denmark, and Sweden, respectively.

While the authors observed associations between fruit, fish, and salty snack intake and IBD risk, there were no associations with other food groups such as vegetables and meats.

Guo and colleagues acknowledged that their study had limitations, particularly since it was observational, and thus unmeasured and residual confounding could not be excluded.

#5653. 1965 Plymouth Belvedere 1 Shows 81,000 Miles, Conceals 588 Cubic-Inch Hemi Routed Through Stout Torqueflite Automatic

Like a lot of cars on Bring a Trailer, this 1965 Plymouth Belvedere I has been for sale on the site before. It's up for bid on Bring a Trailer again, but back in 2020 it was bid up to $26,500 without meeting its reserve. According to the present listing, the car was sold privately in 2023. It was modified before 2010 to have a bored 588-cubic-inch Hemi with dual four-barrel Holley carbs.

That engine swap is said to be in tribute to what this car is not — an original A990 Belvedere. Those were limited-run, extra-lightweight stock racer factory builds designed for the capability of a drag car, but legal for the street. According to Hagerty, although the A990s had street-legal accoutrements such as turn signals and mufflers, they also came with a warning label inside their glove compartments that read: "This model is intended for use in supervised acceleration trials and is not intended for highway or general passenger car use."

The thing is, the Bring a Trailer car may be special, but the 9.6-liter V8 stuffed beneath its fiberglass hood isn't what the A990s ran, even paired with a period-correct Torqueflite three-speed automatic. Coronet and Plymouth Belvedere A990 sedans had 426-cubic-inch Hemi engines. They also got aluminum heads and higher compression. At least the dual four-barrel Holleys on the BaT car emulate what the A990s got. Still, this hat-tip-to-history Belvedere is unique, thanks to a litany of mods we'll partially tabulate here.

The Belvedere didn't make our cut of nine classic Plymouth models and what they're worth today. Nor is it as fully formed a creation as the later GTX, which we called a "gentleman's muscle car" that expertly combined luxury and performance. Probably, if you want this Belvedere, you don't care about any of that. You're here for the vibes and the output.

Which is dandy, because according to the listing, a former NASCAR engine builder both bored and stroked the engine using an Indy cylinder-head stroker kit to achieve the larger displacement. So they started with the right 426 block (even if it's not original to this car), then modified it. And you probably wouldn't want the original motor, since it was a pretty pedestrian 225-cubic-inch Slant Six. These were ubiquitous, if not special, oddly tilted engines that refused to die. Anyway, boring the 426 to 588 cubic inches is an historically honest process of chasing power and less weird than, say, adding a turbo.

If you study the 2020 Bring a Trailer listing and compare it to the present one, you can see that the current owner has tried to push the Belvedere in a slightly more historically accurate direction. For instance, they swapped American Racing Torq Thrust D wheels with BFGoodrich Radial T/A tires for body-color 15-inch steel wheels. The latter are shod with Firestone Deluxe Champion front tires and 255/70 piecrust rear slicks. (If they'd made a meaningful performance upgrade, it might have been to swap the manual front disc and rear drum brakes, but these remain.)

Actual A990 cars saw not only up to 425 horsepower, but significant efforts by the factory to reduce weight. Chyrsler cut fat from the body, using only thin-gauge steel, and the cabin had no rear seat, with only a pair of buckets up front (without headrests). This BaT Belvedere, paying proper homage, doesn't have a radio or a heater, as was the case for A990s.

If you're considering a purchase, know that the listing states that the odometer no longer works. Even though this six-decade-old Belvedere has supposedly logged 81,000 miles, that's probably incorrect. The listing also notes oil leaks, and you can see in the photos that the car was partially but not entirely repainted, with the roof and driver-side quarter panel getting stripping and retouching. Photos of that process look like the shop that did this work was thorough, but ideally you'd see the entire car get that treatment. This isn't the car's original hue, either; it was born wearing dark turquoise metallic paint with a tan-painted cabin.

The current owner made some mechanical upgrades worth mentioning, too, replacing the fuel pump, switching to a factory-style fuel tank behind the rear axle, and moving the battery to the trunk. Does any of that matter if you lust after this monster? Probably not. Just note that original A990s have sold for as high as $200,000, which is extraordinary when you consider the inflation-adjusted sticker price of $4,500 should amount to maybe $50,000. But this isn't an actual A990. Which is probably a good thing, since you can think of it as a car. Not an investment. And burn rubber, as nature, and Plymouth, intended.

#5652. The European Parliament Brings the EU One Step Closer to a Sound Investment Policy

Being locked-in a race for technological leadership with China and the US, the EU lacks focus, coordination and financial firepower to transform its industry, ensure long-term prosperity while reaching its climate objectives.

This could soon change thanks to the forthcoming European Competitiveness Fund that will become active from 2028. Yesterday, the European Parliament cemented its support to a robust fund. Today, EU leaders meet and need to secure an adequate budget for the ECF to deliver.

Since the launch of the US Inflation Reduction Act in 2022, Europe has developed several strategies, masterplans and policy initiatives to build a compelling industrial policy. Still, they largely failed to deliver on focus, coordination and financial firepower.

With the European Competitiveness Fund (ECF), the Commission proposed a new instrument to support Europe’s industry and deliver on its Clean Industrial Deal. Yesterday, the European Parliament voted on rules that would make the proposal even stronger.

MEPs raised the ECF’s overall budget by €30 billion to €264 billion. Crucially, they boosted the envelope for clean energy and industrial decarbonisation to €40 billion, with €4 billion earmarked specifically for clean-tech manufacturing.

MEPs backed a budget of €40 billion for InvestEU, including €15 billion specifically for clean energy and industrial decarbonisation. Through budgetary guarantees, debt and equity, InvestEU aims to collect private capital for higher-risk domestic manufacturing projects that would otherwise fail to reach a final investment decision. This extra €29 billion in additional guarantees compared to the Commission’s proposal could unlock over €300 billion in total mobilised investment.

The Parliament also earmarks €10 billion for the Critical Raw Materials Centre (CRM Centre). The Centre is poised to secure resilient and sustainable critical raw material supply chains for Europe by investing in strategic projects. Securing budgetary resources via the ECF is a crucial step for success.

Over the years, the EU has developed a broad range of funding instruments, but they still largely focus on supporting research and developments. Yet, every year the EU falls further behind China in terms of manufacturing of key technologies, such as batteries. This is because the existing funding programmes neglect the critical and capital intensive scale-up period. Many new market entrants do not survive due to technological risk, insufficient access to risk capital and foreign competition.

Europe does spend substantial money to support industry, both via European funds and at the national level under slow-moving state aid schemes. However, many of the support schemes are spread out widely across technologies without enough focus and clear priorities.

This makes sense for funding early research to steer innovation. For scaling this is different. Today, we know which technologies we need to produce in the next 5 to 10 years to cut emissions and retain leadership, starting with clean transport: the battery value chain, zero-emission vehicles, clean aviation and maritime technologies and e-fuels.

To deliver on the green transition, European funding must be decisively redirected toward the development of strategic clean industries and essential technology value chains. T&E estimates that manufacturing of clean transport technologies alone requires at least €39 billion public funding per year by 2030. Broader decarbonisation needs — industrial heat, buildings, and cleantech deployment — require significantly more.

European cleantech innovators too often stall in the “valley of death” between R&D and commercial production. The Parliament’s text tackles this directly by mandating “ramp up” support for projects that strengthen critical value chains and reduce foreign dependencies — backed by a dedicated €4 billion envelope for clean technologies like battery cell manufacturing. Finally, the EU will be able to deploy production aid — a model that has proven impactful in other jurisdictions like the US.

The Parliament has set out a far bolder industrial vision than EU governments who so far largely stuck to the Commission’s narrower draft.

One immediate test will decide whether the ECF will make a difference in the future. EU heads of states and governments who meet today for a special summit must reverse the heavy cuts inflicted on the ECF in recent Council negotiating drafts. They should listen to more than 75 businesses that also highlighted the importance of a well-resourced European Competitiveness Fund in the next EU budget.

Designing a smart new industrial investment tool means little if leaders starve it of cash. They must back a Competitiveness Fund with the budget to match its ambition.

Article from T&E. By Till Eichler, Public Investment Policy Manager, T&E and Nina Betz, Public Investment Policy Intern, T&E.

#5651. CDC Director Draws Doubts From Employees and Ire From Legislators

— "She has a tough job, at a tough time, and a tough boss," one expert says

Three months into her tenure as head of the CDC, Erica Schwartz, MD, MPH, is being investigated by House Democrats, facing a call to resign, and drawing ire from both within and outside the agency.

What's been happening at the nation's top public health agency has alarmed outside health professionals. It also has alienated staff, leaving morale as bad as ever, employees say.

Schwartz, 54, took the helm of the CDC at a very challenging time: the worst U.S. measles epidemic in more than three decades, a large dengue fever outbreak in Florida, and the fastest-growing overseas Ebola outbreak in history.

She reports to Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who is a longtime critic of vaccines and federal public health policy and who played a role in decimating CDC staffing last year.

"She has a tough job, at a tough time, and a tough boss," said Noel Brewer, PhD, a public health professor at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill.

In an interview with the Associated Press on Tuesday, Schwartz defended her work, saying she's trying to restore trust in the CDC -- including by changing how measles-associated deaths are being reported. She said some of the criticisms are based on misperceptions and argued she is making progress on her goals.

"I do understand why people have concerns," Schwartz told the AP from her home in Naples, Florida. "Have I made mistakes? Certainly. But I'm here to work on the behalf of the American people."

Some experts say she has made the situation worse. And critics are seizing on the Pan American Health Organization's declaration last week that measles is continuously spreading here, marking the re-establishment of a public health threat that was eliminated in the last century.

"I have no confidence that she will do what it takes to course-correct at the CDC, and she should resign immediately," said Sen. Michael Bennet (D-Colo.).

When President Donald Trump nominated Schwartz to be the next CDC director in April, he called her "a STAR!" on social media.

She holds both medical and law degrees. She was chief medical officer for the U.S. Coast Guard, where she oversaw 41 clinics and 150 sick bays. She served as deputy surgeon general in the U.S. Public Health Service, helping to lead uniformed medical and health professionals posted at the CDC and government health agencies.

Many public health leaders were cautiously optimistic, noting the CDC badly needed steady leadership after enduring more than a year of turmoil and months of being led by interim directors.

Schwartz was the third Trump nominee for CDC director in less than 18 months. The first was a former Florida congressman whose nomination was pulled an hour before a Senate confirmation hearing. The second was Susan Monarez, PhD, who won Senate approval but then was ousted less than a month into the job when Trump administration officials said she was not aligned with the president's agenda.

Under Kennedy, the agency has seen around 30% of its staff leave, mostly through layoffs, resignations, and retirements.

At her nomination hearing, Schwartz pledged "radical transparency" to rebuild public trust in the agency, which she noted declined during the COVID-19 pandemic and which has eroded further under Kennedy.

"I will always stand on science and speak the truth, even in difficult moments," she testified.

Meanwhile, public misperceptions about vaccines have persisted. A recent Annenberg Public Policy Center survey found that about one in six Americans said they believed that "vaccines given to children for diseases like measles, mumps, and rubella cause autism" -- even though dozens of studies have determined there's no causal link. Roughly another one in five said they didn't know whether it was true.

Schwartz started at the Atlanta-based agency in mid-August. A week later, she held her first "all hands" staff meeting, during which she promised to advocate for the agency and said she wouldn't hesitate to disagree with Kennedy -- but only privately.

Some say that's when their optimism for Schwartz began to fade.

"I don't have a clear sense of what is important to her, what are her red lines," one CDC health scientist told the AP. "If we're talking about radical transparency," it is appropriate to know on what issues and what messaging she will not compromise, the scientist added. The employee spoke on condition of anonymity for fear of retribution.

Asked about that assessment, Schwartz said: "I would never do anything unethical or illegal. ... That is a red line."

Despite that transparency pledge, CDC and HHS officials for months would not release Schwartz's salary -- even though it is public information. Schwartz is paid about $375,000 a year, CDC officials finally told the AP this week, above the typical range for previous CDC directors.

So far she also has been less visible than some predecessors. She has not held any news conferences, and has not used her bully pulpit to try to persuade more Americans to get vaccinations -- including for measles, the flu, and COVID-19.

Schwartz told the AP that, concerning measles, she doesn't believe a federal health official on TV will sway most of the unvaccinated.

But with the nation experiencing its worst measles epidemic in decades, many public health and medical leaders say Schwartz should be strongly urging Americans to get vaccinated.

"I hope to see her display independence from the vaccine rhetoric and challenges that have been part of this administration," said Wendy Armstrong, MD, president of the Infectious Diseases Society of America. "I don't think we have seen that yet."

Congressional Democrats Are Launching Investigations

Some Democratic legislators accuse Schwartz and Kennedy of downplaying measles.

Kennedy has challenged health officials' accounts of measles deaths. And the CDC has stopped quickly relaying state reports of measles deaths. It adopted a new policy requiring the review of death certificates, which has resulted in CDC counting only about half the measles-associated deaths that states are reporting.

Schwartz said that was her decision, and stemmed from her desire to have a uniform definition of what counts as a measles death.

Democrats on the House Energy & Commerce Committee have questioned why CDC changed the policy.

"As the crisis worsens, we are concerned that you continue to direct an effort at CDC to downplay the outbreak and artificially reduce the number of deaths that CDC reports," said Reps. Frank Pallone Jr. of New Jersey, Diana DeGette of Colorado, and Yvette Clarke of New York in a statement.

"We are expanding our investigation to examine the threats your actions pose to Americans' health and whether changes to your statutory authority are required," they added.

The statement followed a briefing at which Schwartz was supposed to answer congressional staffers' questions about the measles data. The committee leaders described Schwartz as unresponsive and, at times, misleading.

Schwartz argued that she was "fully transparent. And I am really concerned that they think there is more to the story. There isn't."

CDC Employees See Little Sign of Progress

The AP interviewed eight current CDC workers about Schwartz's tenure. They all spoke on condition of anonymity, saying they feared retribution for speaking frankly about what's going on within the agency.

Some said they never had high expectations. Others said they initially were hopeful but lost confidence, some of them blaming her handling of the measles death count. One said it's still too early to judge her.

Several said they had hoped for more improvements and stability. Announcements about leadership appointees coming, going, and changing titles have continued in a blur, the employees told the AP.

Some mentioned Caroline DeBerry, a former vice president at a conservative think tank and author of independently published novels including one titled "Esther: The Woman Who Didn't Know Her Place."

DeBerry got a job as acting director of communications, starting in August. Employees said she gained notoriety within the agency when all CDC website updates ground to a halt while awaiting her approval.

Asked about it, Schwartz said: "There was a bit of clunkiness that happened one day." She also said DeBerry is on "terminal leave" and her last day will be in December, but did not immediately offer additional detail.

None of the agency veterans interviewed by the AP said they have spoken with Schwartz. But some said they had seen her around the CDC campus accompanied by a group of security guards.

Security has been a sensitive topic at CDC, especially since an August 2025 shooting outside the entrance of CDC's main campus. A Georgia man who had blamed the COVID-19 vaccine for making him depressed and suicidal opened fire, killing a police officer and spraying bullets into 150 windows.

(The slain officer, David Rose, is widely held up as a hero by CDC employees, and some expressed irritation that Schwartz referred to him as "Officer Stone" during a recent health summit appearance.)

Tom Frieden, MD, MPH, who served as CDC director in the Obama administration, said he occasionally had an escort outside the CDC campus after he received death threats. But Schwartz moves with a large security team inside CDC, and agency staffers said they don't recall seeing that before.

"It feels like they're afraid of us," one health scientist said.

Schwartz acknowledged that early in her time at CDC, she walked the halls accompanied by about a half dozen guards at the recommendation of security leadership. The security details have been reduced to one plainclothes guard, she said.

Confusion Over the Publication of Scientific Reports

A directive about research publications shows just how far apart CDC staff feel from the political leadership.

Two CDC scientists told the AP that they were directed in a recent meeting to stop submitting their research to journals run by organizations that have sued Kennedy. The prohibition would cover Pediatrics, one of the most-cited journals for doctors who specialize in children's medical care, and Clinical Infectious Diseases, a highly regarded publication for doctors focused on germs.

The scientists said the directive was clearly stated but not written down in a memo or email.

HHS and CDC officials are adamant that neither Kennedy nor any other HHS or CDC official ever issued such a directive.

At the health summit, Schwartz acknowledged that CDC employees have lost trust in the political appointees who have been put in charge of the agency, "and I'm trying to earn that trust every day."

She talked about work going on to stabilize the agency's leadership and develop a "strategic hiring plan" for 2027.

CDC employees look around and see burned-out colleagues.

"I think everyone is just exhausted," one health scientist said. "There's just a sense that we can't go on like this anymore."

#5650. Graph of the Day: The World Now Makes 7 Solar Panels for Every TV

In 2015, the world made six solar panels a second. In 2026, it’s on track to make ten times as many.

At an Australian clean-energy conference in 2015 hosted by Renew Economy Disruption and the Energy Industry conference, I posed a simple test for the solar boom. If the world was still making more panels that consumed electricity — TVs — than panels that generated it, I reckoned we hadn’t quite seen the real boom yet.

On the updated chart (Figure 1), solar overtook televisions in 2016.

By May 2018, when I spoke at Power Philippines in Manila, the crossover had become a line in journalist Lala Rimando’s live coverage of my talk: more solar panels were now being made than TV sets.

We are now making more solar panels than TV sets. Check out this slide by @ProfRayWills .#powerph18#solarph18https://t.co/UGjfZke4IM pic.twitter.com/Kkf6R41RHx

— Lala Rimando (@lalarimando) May 23, 2018

Passing televisions was an important milestone, but it’s really the least interesting part of the story.

In 2021, the world made an estimated 360 million solar panels. A year later, it made about 790 million. By 2025, annual production had reached about 1.4 billion panels, against just over 200 million televisions. The gap opened not because the world stopped making TVs, but because it started making solar panels on a much bigger scale.

Put another way, the world went from making about six solar panels a second in 2015 to about 45 in 2025, averaged across every second of the year. My full-year estimate for 2026 puts the rate at about 62 panels a second — nearly two billion panels in a year (Figure 2).

And the panel count tells only part of the story. The average module rating I used to estimate those counts rose from 150 watts in 2008 to 475 watts in 2025. At that 2025 rating, 1.4 billion panels represent roughly 665 gigawatts of rated generating capacity coming out of factories in a single year.

Televisions offered me a familiar yardstick for what mass production for a consumer market looked like. A decade later, the question isn’t whether solar can match that scale. It’s how quickly we can put all those panels to work. After all, it is the fastest shift in energy in human history.

Ray Willis is a Perth-based energy futurist and director of Future Smart Strategies, and Adjunct Professor at The University of Western Australia, who writes on renewables, electrification, and the energy transition.

#5649. Ford Returns To The 24 Hours Of Le Mans With The 2027 GT41

Ford has a relatively short but lauded history with the 24 Hours of Le Mans. In the 1960s it won four years in a row with the GT40, and pop culture fell in love with the GT40 via the film "Le Mans," and then again decades later with "Ford V Ferrari." The Big Blue Oval returned to Le Mans in 2016 with the Ford GT, which came first in its class, and it continued to race through 2019. Now Ford is headed back to Le Mans in 2027 with its latest hypercar effort, the GT41. Its new FIA Endurance Championship racer was revealed Thanksgiving day on Ford Field, while a different heated rivalry plays out: the Detroit Lions vs. Chicago Bears game.

The LMDh car sports a livery featuring footballs, bald eagles, the Ford name, and the Spirit of Detroit, a statue that has sat downtown since 1958. The Ford family owns the Detroit Lions, as well as a controlling share in the auto manufacturer that bears their name. This is the kind of synergy newer oligarchs wish they could achieve.

Powering the new GT41 is a naturally aspirated 5.4-liter V8 that's based on the same Coyote engine any old Ford-head can get in Mustangs and F-150s. The Coyote in the GT41 has been, of course, lovingly and painstakingly modified and rebuilt over and over again to drill down to peak Ford performance. The company then worked hard to destroy these delicately crafted pieces of machinery to ensure longevity during 24 hours of continuous driving. Ford is doing all of the development and testing in-house to make sure this new racer is the manufacturer's most ambitious program yet, born out of lessons learned during F1 Red Bull racing development.

It was 60 years ago when Ford swept the race in 1966, taking positions 1, 2 and 3. The manufacturer's program ended in 1967, but the GT40 went on to three more consecutive races, just with other operators, until 1969. That car was called GT40 because it stood 40 inches from the ground to the air intake; the new GT41 has grown by a single inch.

There is a direct line from the sport of kings to the global dominance of the car, and Ford had its hand in both. It was developing and racing his own automobiles 125 years ago that got Henry Ford interested in cars in the first place. Racing awards turned into seed money for manufacturing, and the rest is history.

The Ford GT41 already has a full suite of drivers, so sorry if you were planning on putting your name into the hat. Taking the wheel will be Logan Sargeant, Tom Blomqvist, Matt Campbell, Sebastian Priaulx, Mike Rockenfeller and Nick Yelloly, plus Tom Dillmann, who was recently announced as reserve driver. Running a car for 24 hours is a lot to ask of a single driver, after all. To really cement things, Ford has a new ad campaign using Carroll Shelby's motto "Go Like Hell," with voiceover work from "Ford V Ferrari' actor Matt Damon, who portrayed Shelby in the film.

This time it's not just Ferrari that Ford is looking to beat, though Ferrari did win in 2023, 2024 and 2025, so Ford should definitely be looking over its shoulder. 2027 is proving to be a crowed year for the WEC, with 12 different factory prototypes going head-to-head at Le Mans, including this year's new kid on the block, Genesis. Next year's 24 Hours of Le Mans will be a race worth remembering, no matter who comes out on top.

#5648. As GLP-1 Use Grows, Patients and Doctors Rethink Thanksgiving Dinner

— Navigating the holiday while taking weight-loss drugs

For many people, Thanksgiving can feel like a competitive eating event. But for Kim Dillard Davis, one of millions of American adults who take prescribed GLP-1 receptor agonists, it is a day like any other.

The 54-year-old Raleigh, North Carolina-based digital creator and wellness coach has lost around 80 pounds since 2023 using GLP-1 drugs. Thanksgiving on a GLP-1 means she doesn't participate in the part of the holiday associated with indulgence.

"I can't sit down and eat the amount of calories that I once could. I'll still be able to sample everything, but I just can't overdo it," said Dillard Davis, who said she plans to be on the drug for life so long as her insurance is covering it.

More and more Americans are using GLP-1 agonists, and as the medications become more popular, they could be changing some Americans' approach to food-centric holidays like Thanksgiving, altering how they eat, what they enjoy about food, and scrambling some social interactions surrounding food.

The jump in popularity comes as President Donald Trump's second administration has made expanding access to GLP-1 drugs part of its health policy, arguing that the drugs, if made more affordable, could help combat rising obesity rates and other related chronic illnesses, eventually lowering broader healthcare costs.

While GLP-1 drugs will likely cause major shifts in ways that are hard to predict, Ashley Gearhardt, PhD, a psychology professor at the University of Michigan in Ann Arbor, suggests the overindulgence associated with Thanksgiving could diminish over time.

"I anticipate that flavors and tastes that have been culturally linked with Thanksgiving will continue to be important. There just may be fewer turkey comas at the end of the day," she said.

Navigating the Holiday While Taking GLP-1 Agonists

Some people who use GLP-1 drugs feel full faster and stay full longer, meaning they tend to eat smaller portions. The drugs have been reported to change how people think about food, reducing cravings and emotional eating but also diminishing the sensory pleasure people get from food. Some users also avoid eating rich or heavy foods, because the drugs can cause nausea or bloating.

Doctors say people who are just starting their weight-loss journey this year with the drugs should be particularly mindful of potential side effects.

"Thanksgiving doesn't have to be off-limits," said John Horlander, MD, a gastroenterologist in Louisville, Kentucky. "The key is moderation, smaller portions, avoiding excessive fatty foods, staying hydrated, and recognizing warning signs."

"A little prevention can go a long way toward keeping someone out of the emergency room over the holiday," he added.

The Trump administration has framed its steps toward increasing access to and bringing down costs for GLP-1 drugs as "a historic opportunity to reverse the obesity epidemic." More than 100 million American adults have obesity, according to the latest CDC data.

In 2025, Trump, a Republican, signed a deal with drugmakers Eli Lilly and Novo Nordisk to expand coverage and reduce prices for the popular weight-loss drugs tirzepatide (Zepbound) and semaglutide (Wegovy).

And coverage of the drugs for obesity was expanded to Medicare patients this year when the federal government began offering a selection of the brand-name medications to certain Medicare and Medicare Advantage beneficiaries for $50 a month through a new trial called Medicare GLP-1 Bridge. The program is scheduled to sunset after Dec. 31, 2027.

A June analysis by healthcare research nonprofit KFF found that 3.8 million Medicare beneficiaries could be eligible for the Medicare GLP-1 Bridge, based on claims data from 2023. The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services does not provide projections of how many people will start taking GLP-1 agonists as a result of the Trump administration's actions. The agency wants to expand access to these treatments, said a spokesperson, who was not authorized to speak publicly and talked to the Associated Press on the condition of anonymity.

Those policy changes come as the share of people on GLP-1 medications for weight loss has risen in the past few years -- 11% of U.S. adults said they currently take the drugs for weight-loss purposes, according to a Gallup poll conducted in May and June. The poll found that 15% of Americans report having used the medicine for weight loss, an increase of 9 percentage points from 2 years ago.

That means Americans, even if they aren't taking the drugs, could find more people on the medication who are sitting across from them at the Thanksgiving table. That could change how people talk about eating.

Gearhardt said that dinner guests should be mindful about not pushing loved ones to eat or commenting on appearances.

"We all have a tendency to kind of monitor and police each other's eating behavior," said Gearhardt, who studies food marketing and how addictive processes shape eating behaviors and mental health.

Commenting on how little or how much someone is eating "usually isn't a great relationship strengthener," she said. GLP-1 users might be especially sensitive, she said, because Thanksgiving can evoke feelings of grief over losing the intense reward sensation of highly processed foods.

Dillard Davis advised family members not to ask, "Is that all you're going to eat?"

"Leave that phrase off the table. We've spent our whole lives overeating. Let us eat small portions and be happy," she said.

Babak Orandi, MD, PhD, an obesity medicine specialist at NYU Langone Health in New York City, said, "There's a social aspect of eating, especially around the holidays. We don't want to lose that."

Patients, Orandi said, should focus "a little bit less on weight loss and a little bit more on weight loss maintenance" during the holidays, so as to not lose the enjoyment of eating.

For Dillard Davis, Thanksgiving has changed in other ways. Because of the reduced appetite brought on by the medication and to avoid large quantities of leftovers at home, her family has spent the last 4 years celebrating Thanksgiving at restaurants.

But as someone who has been on a weight-loss journey since she was 8 years old, she has learned to accept the changes.

"We still have to eat," she said. "Just don't worry about it so much."

#5646. The Proof Is In The Lettuce: Perovskite Makes Things Grow Better

Last year’s sharp U-turn in energy policy came with catastrophic consequences for farmers who were counting on federal assistance for solar power on their land. Still, the pace of innovation in the solar industry never stopped, and farmers may ultimately benefit whenever the policy winds blow in a more positive direction. In one particularly interesting development, the US startup UbiQD has assembled more evidence that its “UbiGro” perovskite-enhanced glass can help hothouse farmers improve their yields while saving water, too.

For those of you new to the topic, perovskite refers to a new class of relatively inexpensive, easy-to-fabricate solar materials, characterized by a crystalline structure based on the naturally occurring mineral perovskite (see lots more background here).

Raw perovskite is too unstable to function as a solar material on its own, but it can be combined with more durable materials in a solar cell, or in a solar module. Silicon-perovskite combinations are already emerging in the market, for example.

UbiQD developed its UbiGro glass to incorporate sub-microscopic particles of perovskite. Particles of that size are known as “artificial atoms” or quantum dots, as capably explained by scientists at Los Alamos National Laboratory:

Quantum dots are ultra-small bits of semiconductor matter that can be synthesized with nearly atomic precision via modern methods of colloidal chemistry. Their emission color can be tuned by simply varying their dimensions. Color tunability is combined with high emission efficiencies approaching 100%.

As Los Alamos indicates, quantum dots initially appeared in the LED field of the lighting industry before moving into solar energy applications as a means of ramping up the efficiency of solar cells. By 2016 researchers were experimenting with quantum dots in a perovskite solar cell. The pioneering startup Blue Dot was among those pursuing the perovskite connection.

Activity began to accelerate in 2025 when UbiQD acquired BlueDot. In the meantime, UbiQD had previously hooked up with the US thin film solar manufacturer First Solar to develop quantum dots for solar panels. That project also ramped up in 2025 when UbiQD closed on a $20 million round of Series B funding. According to UbiQD, its enhancements could double the solar conversion efficiency of First Solar’s bifacial solar panels.

In 2025, UbiQD also announced the findings from a study of its UbiGro greenhouse glass. The glass is treated with quantum dots as a means of fine-tuning sunlight to improve crop yields. The study was published by researchers at the University of California – Davis in the journal Materials Today Sustainability under the title, “Spectrally selective quantum dot laminated glass for photonic modulation and climate regulation in greenhouses.”

— Fresh biomass increased by 37.8%. Plants were nearly 40% heavier, indicating significantly more edible yield.

— Leaf area was increased by 38.0%. Larger leaf area means higher photosynthetic surface.

— Root length increased by 38.0%. Deeper roots improve water and nutrient uptake, resilience, and shelf life.

— Light-use efficiency was increased by 41.0%. The plants used sunlight more effectively, with more biomass per photon.

— Nutrient concentrations (N, P, K, Mg, Zn, Cu) were significantly elevated. The crops were more nutritious, with higher levels of essential nutrients.

— Spectral red:blue ratio increased by 61.0%, with no significant PAR losses. More red light was delivered without sacrificing total usable light levels.

“The findings highlight a promising pathway toward climate-smart greenhouse envelopes that integrate photonics with sustainable food and energy strategies,” the research team concluded.

In a series of followup trials last Spring, UC-Davis focused on the impact of UbiGro on water consumption by greenhouse-grown lettuce. The results were similarly encouraging.

“Water use efficiency improved by approximately 9%. Lettuce grown under QD glass produced 101 grams of fresh biomass per liter of water compared 93 grams per liter under conventional glass,” UbiQD noted.

“Unlike technologies that require additional energy inputs or changes to irrigation infrastructure, UbiGro glass works passively by optimizing the sunlight already entering the greenhouse while optimizing water use efficiency,” UbiD emphasized in a press statement.

UbiQD’s VP of Sales and Marketing, Eric Moody, also chipped in his two cents. “It’s an important new area of validation for UbiGro as we continue exploring how our technology can help growers get more from the resources they already use,”said Moody.

Want more details? Check out the study, “Crop Water Use and Evapotranspiration Estimation in Deep Water Culture Hydroponic System under Quantum Dot Glazed Greenhouse,” presented by UC-Davis Ph.D. candidate Mala Parvin at the 2026 American Society of Agricultural and Biological Engineers Annual International Meeting in Indianapolis last July.

First Solar has also been making some moves of its own. The iconic US firm is of particular interest for its focus on CdTe (cadmium-telluride) solar film instead of the silicon formula commonly used around the world. Here in the US, the Department of Energy has been promoting CdTe since the early 1990’s as a domestically sourced alternative to silicon, and it has become particularly popular in utility-scale applications.

First Solar has been embroiled in patent disputes of late, but the dust appeared to be settling last month when the company announced a non-exclusive patent licensing agreement with the US firm CubicPV Inc.

Among other, undisclosed terms of the agreement, First Solar will have access to CubicPV patents covering perovskite solar technology in the US. “The license further clears the path for First Solar to continue its development of photovoltaic (PV) devices built with a perovskite semiconductor for the US utility-scale, commercial and industrial, and residential markets, and applies to sales and distribution of those products domestically,” First Solar explains.

Somewhat ironically, if US President Donald Trump were to lend his full support to the domestic solar industry, First Solar would be a feather in his cap. First Solar bills itself as the largest producer of thin film solar in the world, and the largest solar manufacturer of any kind in the Western Hemisphere.

First Solar is also among the solar stakeholders contributing to the President’s oft-stated ambition of bringing more manufacturing back to the US during his time in office. “The Company’s investments include a new perovskite development line at its Perrysburg, Ohio, campus that produces small form-factor modules featuring a perovskite semiconductor, allowing First Solar to meet key internal milestones in its perovskite development program, including initial-stage efficiency, stability, and manufacturability objectives,” First Solar notes.

That’s just for starters. By the middle of next year, First Solar expects to have a pilot line up and running at a facility in Ohio, which will apply the technology to its existing Series 6 solar modules.

In addition, last month First Solar announced the start of Phase I of operations at its sixth facility in the US. Located in Gaffney, South Carolina, the new factory represents another step in First Solar’s onshoring plan for Series 6 production.

“The second phase is forecast to be completed by mid-2027, at which time the approximately $330 million facility is expected to double its annual nameplate capacity to 3.4 gigawatts (GW) and produce the Company’s CuRe technology, while supporting nearly 700 jobs. Approximately 500 of those jobs have already been filled,” First Solar explains.

For the record, the Gaffney facility expands First Solar’s existing footprint in South Carolina. The company also operates in Alabama, Louisiana, and Ohio. All together, First Solar anticipates to have a total of 17 gigawatts’ worth of domestic solar module manufacturing under its belt by the end of this year, which is just around the corner.

Photo: Greenhouse lettuce thrives under natural sunlight filtered through specialized glass from the perovskite solar startup UbiQD, while conserving water resources, too (cropped, courtesy of UbiQD).

#5645. Antibiotic Paste Approved to Prevent Surgical Site Infections

— Bacfenssi becomes the first approved product for local application following colorectal surgery

The FDA approved doxycycline hyclate (Bacfenssi) to reduce the risk of surgical site infections (SSIs) in adults and kids undergoing colorectal surgery, the agency announced on Tuesday.

Sold as a powder to be reconstituted into an extended-release paste, the tetracycline product is indicated specifically for surgeries involving incisions larger than 20 cm, as efficacy for smaller incisions was not established in trials. Pediatric patients must weigh at least 45 kg, according to the agency.

It marks the first approved option for preventing SSIs that is applied locally, the FDA said. Before closing the incision, the paste is applied directly to the fascia and tissues of the abdominal wall along the incision.

Support for the approval came primarily from SHIELD II, a multinational double-blind phase III trial, which showed that adding the doxycycline hyclate paste to standard of care reduced the risk for SSIs, mortality, or surgical reintervention by 40% over the month after surgery. In the investigational arm, that composite outcome occurred in 10.9% of patients compared with 18.1% in the control arm (P=0.004).

When looking at SSIs specifically, a key secondary endpoint, the product reduced the risk by 60%, with infections recorded in 3.8% of the doxycycline hyclate arm and 9.5% of controls (P=0.001).

Commonly occurring following colorectal surgeries, SSIs "can lead to prolonged hospital stays, reoperation, and significant patient morbidity, including wound breakdown and systemic infection," the FDA noted. "Despite the administration of systemic antibacterial drugs prior to colorectal surgery to reduce SSIs, the infection rate remains substantial, underscoring the need for additional preventive strategies."

Adverse events observed in trials of doxycycline hyclate were mostly mild and included incision site reactions, procedural pain, anemia, and wound dehiscence.

Labeling for the antibiotic paste includes potential risks for tooth discoloration and inhibition of bone growth if used in pregnancy and in children, Clostridioides difficile infection, potential for microbial overgrowth, along with known class effects of tetracyclines -- photosensitivity, fixed drug eruption, pseudotumor cerebri, and anti-anabolic actions. Drug interactions are possible with concomitant use of anticoagulants.

Doxycycline hyclate can cause fetal harm, the FDA noted, and "breastfeeding is not recommended for 40 days after administration."

Launch of the product is expected in early 2027.

#5644. Musk Space Based Data Center Idea Is A Betrayal Of Humanity

Despite copious evidence that Elon Musk is little more than a snake oil salesman and carnival barker like P. T. Barnum, the world continues to believe the man is somehow smarter than the rest of us. Few seem to realize his empire is built on nothing more than wildly inflated boasts and  OPM — other people’s money.

Take away the billions Tesla received over the years from other automakers by selling emissions credits and the company likely would have failed early on. Musk recognized the opportunity those emissions credits offered and seized it with both hands. The existence of SpaceX depends almost entirely on the contracts it has secured from the US government.

People (including some here at CleanTechnica) get all weak in the knees when Musk makes his outlandish claims about robotaxis and Cybercabs, but the truth is that, after a decade, we are still waiting for that Model S to leave California, drive across the country, and park itself in a garage in Manhattan without a human driver ever touching the wheel.

Tesla, the car company, has shrunk its model lineup rather than expanding it. The Model S, Model X, and Cybertruck are now out of production, with no replacements in sight. The Roadster 2.0 is a party trick with a very limited potential market. The $25,000 Tesla is completely off the table.

Are the Model Y and Model 3 pretty good cars? Yes, they are. Yet the competition is bringing dozens of new models to market every month and introducing electric cars to world markets where their lack of exhaust emissions and lower operating costs can be a real benefit to the local population. The fact that Tesla ignores those markets is proof the company is little more than a niche player in the global automotive marketplace.

Musk’s penchant for issuing pie in the sky predictions and boldly going where no one has gone before is now fully underway in the AI madness. In a recent report by the New York Times by Grace Kay and Ryan Mac, the pair detail the same Muskian passion for making bold claims and then bullying his employees to make them a reality.

Musk has used his connections to the White House to construct a sprawling (and rapidly expanding) data center — which Musk, with his usual modesty, calls Colossus — in a predominantly minority neighborhood in Memphis, Tennessee. That enterprise has now spread to nearby Mississippi. The local utilities could not possible supply all the electrical power those enormous facilities consume, and so Musk is powering them with portable methane fired generators that spew far more emissions into the air than a modern combined cycle generating station would.

Musk cannot wait for environmental reviews and other government restrictions, so he has blanketed the neighborhoods around his data centers with effluvia from those portable generators and used his political clout to suppress opposition to  his plans. AI is too important to be delayed by such trivial concerns as people’s health or a massive influx of carbon emissions.

Colossus is home — assuming their is such a thing — to Grok, Musk’s AI invention that features the ability to undress virtually anyone for the amusement of pre-pubescent boys. We hear a lot today about Claude, the AI wizard from Anthropic, and ChatGPT from OpenAI, but Grok is hardly ever mentioned in the same breath as those AI tools.

That has placed Musk in a familiar bind. His dreams are far removed from reality, and so he has been forced to rent out computing power (now known simple as “compute”) to his competitors in order to pay the bills. The Times report says he has told employees that “SpaceX is falling behind in AI development, making it more lucrative to rent the company’s computing power out to rivals than use it to improve its own products,” three people told the Times reporters.

In August, Musk temporarily changed the group chat name for his AI team to “Sell compute because we can’t compete,” the Times was told. Then he did what Musk does so well — he tried motivating his people by threatening them. “Anyone wasting GPUs on bullshit while we are failing to compete will be asked to leave immediately, as this constitutes a betrayal of your team.” This type of bullying is typical of Musk, whose motto seems to be, “The beatings will continue until morale improves.”

Part of the problem is that SpaceX — the nominal owner of Musk’s AI ambitions — is now a public company, after its blockbuster IPO earlier this year. Before, it was a private company with no need to disclose its finances to the outside world. Now, it must justify is lofty valuation with real world results, and the pressure on Musk to justify his bet on AI is intense.

“SpaceX makes way more money right now renting out compute than from Grok,” said Nicolas Owens, an analyst who covers SpaceX for Morningstar Research, told the New York Times. “Grok is not the premier model in town, so I think it’s more doubtful that they would be able to tip the scale to where serving up A.I. off of their own servers is more lucrative than branching it out to Anthropic.”

Musk told his engineers in August, “At the end of the day, the only thing that matters for competitiveness is revenue per GPU, not benchmarks. If you can’t pay for your GPUs, then you either go bankrupt or you become a computer rental company. Move the needle on revenue.”

And yet, despite such blandishments, the company has shifted resources away from internal AI projects. The Times reports that Mike Nicolls, the president of the AI unit, disbanded the 60 member team behind Grok Imagine, an image and video generation tool that was once a top priority. He told the workers involved the cuts would “better align our structure and resources with critical business priorities.”

Those priorities now appear to be focused on renting out as much “compute” as possible to competitors such as OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and anyone else who needs extra computing power to drive the AI revolution forward.

In another attempt to distract the world of finance away from SpaceX’s financial struggles here on Earth, Musk now says he has received permission from the Federal Communications Commission to place up to one million data centers into sun-synchronous orbit around the Earth. That means they will be powered by sunlight nearly 24 hours a day, and their cooling needs will be minimized by the low temperatures in space.

SpaceX will build the 98 foot (30 m) long satellites at its Gigasat Factory in Bastrop, Texas, using AI chips manufactured at the 100 million square foot (ten times the size of the Texas Gigafactory) Terafab manufacturing facility in Grimes County, Texas.

On its website, Terafab modestly announces, “We aspire to be a galactic civilization.” To make that happen, first it intends to “Harness all the energy on a planet,” then “Harness all the energy from a star,” and finally “Harness all of the energy in a galaxy.” Some readers may find all this hype and hysteria reminds them of a phrase made popular during Barry Goldwater’s presidential campaign: “In your heart, you know he’s nuts.”

In a press release, the FCC said it had approved the request to place one million satellites in orbit subject to certain conditions. According to Reuters, SpaceX must begin deployment no ​later than November 2033, deploy 10 percent of the maximum number no later ⁠than November of 2035, and deploy 50 percent by November 2038. Approving the application ​will permit SpaceX “to pioneer emergent technology that advances American leadership in space and artificial intelligence,” the ​FCC said.

The enormity of this plan is illustrated by the fact that, at present, there are only a total of 17,000 satellites orbiting the Earth (not counting the moon). SpaceX originally asked for permission to launch 42,000 Starlink satellites, yet today only 11,000 have been deployed.

The satellites will be placed in Earth orbit by Starship, a reusable rocket developed by SpaceX. Those rockets are powered by methane, which has led environmental advocates to question the wisdom of the entire data centers in space project. But Elon has demonstrated by his actions with Colossus in Memphis and Mississippi he doesn’t care a flying fig leaf about the harm burning methane can do.

“Drastically expanding satellites in space has a direct impact on people’s everyday lives as well as the future of our planet,” said Jan Hasselman, senior attorney at Earthjustice. “Agencies that authorize companies looking to space as the next frontier still must operate within the law, and the law requires the FCC to consider all the risks and impacts of these proposals. It is dismaying that the FCC has ignored the law so blatantly and tried to mask the fact with a holiday filing.”

The approval by the FCC seems to be in violation of the National Environmental Protection Act (NEPA). Sharp eyed readers will notice that NEPA will be gutted by the proposed Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) that may slip through a lame duck Congress before the end of this year.

“This approval to deploy a million data centers in space without any thought to the impacts on Earth is just a glimpse of what we’ll see during the next two years of Trump,” said Sam Sankar, senior vice president at Earthjustice. “This is great example of why Congress should not pass a flawed bill like BAAJA that would lock in terrible projects like this one. Donald Trump is going to do a lot more dirty and lawless deals over the next years, and BAAJA prevents future presidents from reconsidering them.”

Does human civilization need Musk’s Starmind? It seems clear Musk is hellbent on exporting humanity to the moon, Mars, and beyond because he knows for dead solid certain that he and his tech bro cronies will make the Earth uninhabitable in the not too distant future. If you think about what Musk did to Ukraine recently when he unilaterally restricted its access to Starlink, the prospect of him running the world, if not the entire galaxy, should fill you with dread.

A certifiable lunatic with the power to play God? Be afraid; be very afraid.

#5643. At $17,000, Is This LS-Swapped 2001 BMW M3 A Black Friday Bargain?

Today's Nice Price or No Dice M3 has a built LS V8 under the hood and a driver's seat that shows the wear and tear of someone having enjoyed the car for its intended purpose. Let's see if it's priced to spread that joy.

Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade has been a New York City tradition for over 100 years, an unofficial kickoff to the holiday season. This year, for the first time in the event's history, the parade has been postponed from Thanksgiving Day to tomorrow, Saturday, because the forecast called for heavy rain and wind. That storm could turn the record 100 inflatable cartoon characters into ballistic balloons, potentially endangering parade-goers who already braved the inclement weather.

We had no such qualms about the weather in bringing you a slice of Thanksgiving cheer yesterday in the form of a tidy little classic 1973 Chevy Vega notchback. And it had a V8 under its hood! It also had a not-insubstantial $17,000 asking price, which didn't sit well with most of you. That price quickly racked up a massive 91% 'No Dice' loss in the voting.

Okay, I have to apologize to you all. We started this week with a BMW E46 M3, and now, here we are finishing it off with... a BMW E46 M3. Here's the thing, though: this car dovetails nicely, not only with Monday's near-stock coupe but also with yesterday's Chevy Vega, since both this 2001 BMW M3 convertible and the Vega have been recipients of a Chevy V8 engine swap and carry the exact same asking price. With its LS under the hood and a few other issues, this E46 is also over 20% cheaper than the Monday car.

Say what you will about engine swaps and sullying the purity of so excellent a car as an E46 M3, the reasons behind this particular car's heart transplant may actually make sense. After all, being a drop top, it's much less desirable as a track toy. Plus, it probably could be converted back to S54 status without much trouble should the LS prove too mortifying for the next owner.

For the moment, however, it has a 5.3-liter LS V8, an engine that likely started life in a pickup or SUV before finding a new home here in this black-over-gray leather M3. It's not an unusual conversion, and the LS fits in the BMW's engine bay without much fuss. According to the ad, the engine drives the original BMW power steering pump, but an A/C compressor wasn't in the cards. That might make the BMW climate controls a bit wonky and make the open top a welcome feature for airflow.

The ad notes numerous internal and external engine updates, including an aggressive cam, aluminum heads, hardened internals, and a DOD/AFM delete. It runs a special ECU tuned by PCM of Mooresville, North Carolina, a company that specializes in GM engine tweaking.

Other conversion updates include a new high-performance clutch ahead of a ZF five-speed manual gearbox and strengthened rear subframe mounts. It all appears tidy and well put together, but the ad lacks details on how the car runs and rides, or even whether the original instruments function.

As for the car's looks, there are some plusses and minuses. Overall, it looks to be in solid shape with no body damage evident, a seemingly intact top, and the same Style 163M Cross Spoke alloys as we saw on Monday's car. Looking a bit more closely, as you would when considering buying something like this, a few issues stand out. Notably, the clear coat on the top of the rear bumper cap is fading significantly, and the leather on the driver's seat is also starting to give up the ghost. The rest of the upholstery appears to be in decent shape, with only minor scuffing on the passenger seat. The rear seats look like they've never been used at all.

Other things to note: the center console now houses a pair of add-on gauges, canted toward the driver. Those monitor engine coolant temperature and oil pressure. Above that sits a big screen infotainment unit that, hysterically, still has its protective plastic film intact. Per the ad, the car comes with a clean title. It also notes the mileage at 460, but doesn't explain when that count began.

This being Black Friday, one might expect to find a total door-buster bargain on tap for our consideration and judgment. The thing is, the way this all works is that you decide what's a bargain or not. You're in control. You're the final arbitrator of value. Use this power wisely.

With that in mind, let's now consider this LS-equipped M3's $17,000 asking price. See? That is exactly the same as yesterday's also V8-powered Vega. Which car would you rather have instead of $17K in your bank account? And yes, "neither" is an acceptable answer. For anyone with a wild hair about this Bimmer, though, would $17,000 be a fair price to pay for the car as it's presented in its ad? Or do the demerits (and lack of originality) make this a Black Friday deal you would pass up?
