However, even while I'm looking at the crowd of kooks around me, I can't help but notice the absolutely fantastic deals some stores are offering up. It's not uncommon to see things marked down 10%, 20%, 30% or maybe even 40% from their original price, and that's what has led me to today's question.

I want to know what new car you'd buy with a 40% off Black Friday deal. Yes, I know some automakers will run promotional events on Black Friday and through the holiday season, but the deals never come close to a 40% off doorbuster. That's why today we're daring to dream, daring to imagine, daring to bask in the light of American consumerism and the hunt for a good deal.

For me, the choice is a simple one. If I can have any new car for 40% off its MSRP, I'm heading to my local Acura dealership, waking up the salesperson and leaving with a new Integra Type S. With an MSRP of $55,295 including destination, the Integra Type S already isn't a bad deal. I know some people will say it's too expensive, but they don't know what the hell they're talking about and clearly haven't driven it or looked at the rest of the automotive landscape.

In any case, lopping 40% off of that brings the car's price to just $33,177, and I genuinely cannot fathom a better deal in the entire automotive world than spending 33 grand on an ITS. Santa, if you're real, this is what I want this year. I don't want a free one, that's too greedy, but I want one I could theoretically afford. Pretty please.

That's enough out of me, though. How about you all drop on down below and let your fellow Jalops know what car you'd buy with a 40% Black Friday discount?

#5641. Loblaw’s Hydrogen Truck Crossed the Rockies. Another Truck Brought Its Fuel.

Loblaw’s Hyundai XCIENT hydrogen fuel-cell truck crossed the Canadian Rockies from Vancouver to Calgary on November 18. The 1,046 km journey attracted enthusiastic coverage as a Canadian heavy-freight milestone. It also illustrated an infrastructure problem that gets much less attention than a successful crossing: the hydrogen had to be brought to the truck.

The Edmonton Region Hydrogen Hub announcement describes three fuelling occasions. The truck started with a fill at HTEC’s Vancouver hydrogen station, then refuelled at Sicamous and Golden from a mobile tube trailer supplied by Powertech. Other project partners arranged the trailer’s transportation and logistics. The tractor hauling the mobile fuel was almost certainly diesel-powered. The public account did not include that support truck’s fuel consumption, emissions or cost.

The hydrogen truck completed the trip, and the project partners demonstrated that a mobile hydrogen supply operation could support a freight vehicle across the mountains. Those are achievements, albeit not novel ones. A fleet operator considering hydrogen needs a more demanding result: dependable places to refuel on repeated journeys, delivered hydrogen prices, vehicle availability, maintenance requirements and the complete cost of the support system. Moving a fuel trailer between planned stops is not the same thing as operating a commercial refuelling corridor.

The three fills also complicate the familiar argument that hydrogen offers heavy trucks a decisive range advantage. Hyundai’s fuel-cell truck has marketed range specifications, but the crossing did not establish that range advantage against battery-electric heavy trucks. Battery trucks had completed demanding Alpine journeys years earlier, and commercial electric freight operations have progressed since then. The comparative distances, energy stops and subsequent operating evidence are important when evaluating what this latest event contributed.

There is a second question about what happened after the official announcement. In the TFIE Strategy Briefing assessment, I reviewed a bounded sample of news reports and social posts from the week after the journey. The press generally included the mobile refills. The promotional accounts circulating on social media were much more likely to celebrate the distance and mountains while leaving out the operation that supplied the fuel.

That difference matters. A photograph of a truck crossing a mountain pass makes an effective announcement. Refuelling arrangements, energy costs and repeatability are harder to compress into a congratulatory post. As the story travels, a demonstration can start to resemble a commercially proven transport system even when the fundamental business questions remain unanswered.

Loblaw also operates battery-electric freight vehicles. Those trucks are making commercial deliveries and accumulating service kilometres rather than appearing in a single supported trial. Comparing the deployment record within the same company with the attention lavished on its hydrogen journey is a useful way to test how publicity can distort perceptions of technological maturity.

The earlier TFIE analysis, Hydrogen Has Narrative Density. Electrification Has Deployment Density, identified that mismatch across several energy and transport markets. The Loblaw event shows the mechanism: an attractive milestone generates attention while the surrounding operating system receives less attention, and routine electric deployment barely enters the story.

The project partners have said operational results will follow. The decisive questions concern delivered fuel, support logistics and recurring freight service, rather than whether a fuel-cell truck can make one successful trip with dedicated logistical support. Fleet investment requires operating evidence, not publicity counts.

The full TFIE Strategy Briefing quantifies the media-versus-social disclosure gap, compares the driving legs with an earlier battery-electric mountain crossing, and sets the demonstration against Loblaw’s existing electric-fleet deployment. A free subscription opens the complete assessment and its two analytical graphics.

The broader narrative-density assessment traces the same gap between announcements and deployments across energy sectors.

#5640. Novel ADC Could Be New Option in Recurrent Ovarian Cancer

— A phase III trial will test sofetabart mipitecan in platinum-sensitive and -resistant disease

Promising data from a phase I study presented at the European Society for Medical Oncology congress suggested encouraging activity with the investigational antibody-drug conjugate (ADC) sofetabart mipitecan (Sofe-M) combined with bevacizumab in patients with recurrent platinum-sensitive ovarian cancer.

In this exclusive MedPage Today video, Roisin O'Cearbhaill, MD, of Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center in New York City, discusses the early findings and how the three-part FRAmework-01 study could expand treatment options for patients with platinum-sensitive and platinum-resistant ovarian cancer.

Following is a transcript of her remarks:

It was a very exciting phase I study. It was looking at a folate-targeting antibody-drug conjugate, and they were looking at the platinum-sensitive population, patients whose cancer had recurred more than 6 months after prior platinum-based therapy. The majority of patients had measurable disease and they treated the patients with Sofe-M plus bevacizumab. So it was phenomenal to see the waterfall plots with such great response rates, objective response rates, in the vast majority of patients and disease control rates in 100% of the patients.

Not only the efficacy data, but also the toxicity data was very exciting in terms of the thing that we always worry about with antibody-drug conjugates or eye toxicity or pneumonitis. So it was great to see that those really weren't a concern with this novel ADC.

And so based on this and other clinical data, we're actually participating in a global phase III study. There are three different subprotocols in that.

In part A, we're looking at the platinum-resistant population, and that is going to be looking at standard-of-care, single-agent chemotherapy versus the Sofe-M. And then in the other two cohorts, they're for patients who have platinum-sensitive disease. In part B, patients have received a prior PARP inhibitor. And in part C, patients have not received a prior PARP inhibitor. In both part B and C, patients are randomized to the standard of care, which would be carboplatin plus another chemotherapy agent with bevacizumab. And then the investigational arm is looking at Sofe-M in combination with bevacizumab.

I hope that we'll have a new treatment option for our patients with recurrent platinum-resistant and platinum-sensitive disease. It would be really great if we could move away from empiric platinum-based chemotherapy and have other options to offer our patients in the platinum-sensitive setting. And for the platinum-resistant, it would be great to have yet another effective treatment option.

#5639. GRIDSERVE Secures £420 Million Financing to Strengthen Leadership Position in EV Charging & Support Next Phase of Growth

London, UK — GRIDSERVE, the UK’s most-used electric vehicle (EV) charging network, has secured a £420 million financing package, marking a significant milestone in the company’s financial development and providing a strengthened funding platform for its next phase of growth.

One of the largest financing packages of its kind in the EV charging sector, the deal comprises a £240 million loan to refinance existing debt, a £165 million capital expenditure facility to fund future investment in the network and a £15 million revolving credit facility to support working capital and liquidity.

Structured as green senior debt under GRIDSERVE’s Green Finance Framework, the financing was anchored by the National Wealth Fund, Crédit Agricole CIB, NatWest and Rabobank as cornerstone lenders, each acting as Mandated Lead Arranger alongside MUFG, with MUFG also acting as Sole Financial Advisor. The package strengthens the company’s long-term funding position, providing greater financial flexibility and dedicated capital to support its ongoing investment in critical UK EV charging infrastructure.

The refinancing also reflects the significant financial progress GRIDSERVE has made under CEO Daniel Kunkel. In 2025, the company reported positive EBITDA for the first time in its history, following a renewed focus on disciplined investment, utilisation-led growth and capital efficiency. The new financing structure builds on this progress, providing a robust foundation for sustainable growth and continued investment in the business.

Since opening its first EV charging station in Braintree in 2020, GRIDSERVE has established itself as a leading force in the transition to electric mobility. Its nationwide network now supports an average of 350,000 charging sessions every month across more than 200 locations. GRIDSERVE also remains the only UK charging operator to have invested in a dedicated interoperability testing facility, helping to underpin its 99% availability record and ensure that new electric vehicle models, regardless of manufacturer, can charge seamlessly across its network.

Alongside continued investment in its existing network, the new capital expenditure facility will support GRIDSERVE’s next phase of expansion, including the development of ultra-rapid EV charging provision beyond the motorway network.

Daniel Kunkel, CEO of GRIDSERVE, said: “Securing this refinancing package is a significant milestone for GRIDSERVE and reflects the progress we have made over the last year. We have demonstrated that our network can grow sustainably, supported by a disciplined approach to investment, utilisation and capital efficiency.

“The strength of this financing package, and the confidence shown in us by our lending partners, puts GRIDSERVE in a strong position for the future. It reinforces our long-term commitment to the UK and gives us the funding platform to continue investing in the infrastructure needed to decarbonise road transport. We look forward to building on this momentum as we enter the next phase of our growth.”

Oliver Holbourn, National Wealth Fund CEO, said: “Drivers need confidence that reliable charging will be available where they need it before making the switch to electric. By lending alongside commercial banks, the National Wealth Fund is supporting GRIDSERVE’s continued investment in its network, including plans to expand ultra-rapid charging beyond motorways. This is about backing the infrastructure that makes cleaner transport a practical choice for more people.”

Priya Veerapen, Managing Director, Infracapital, said, “GRIDSERVE has made significant progress since our investment in 2022, and this £420 million refinancing marks an important next step in its growth. Alongside TPG, we have invested more than £300 million in the business, reflecting our conviction in the long-term need for high-quality EV charging infrastructure and the important role GRIDSERVE can play in delivering it across the UK.”

Jamie Gilbert, Business Unit Partner at TPG Rise Climate, said: “The strength of this refinancing reflects the quality of GRIDSERVE’s business and the progress the company has made in establishing itself as a leader in UK EV charging. It also underscores the importance of continued investment in the infrastructure needed to support the UK’s transition to electric mobility.”

#5638. 2020 Shelby GT500KR With 21,000 Miles Is Ready To Terrify With 900-HP Supercharged 5.2-Liter Predator V8

When we first drove the Mustang Shelby GT500KR back in 2020, we called it a preposterous 760-horsepower daily drivable monster. The funny thing is, this currently listed monster on Bring a Trailer has been modified to produce an even more preposterous 900 horsepower.

Shelby American produced a limited-run of factory-made special-edition GT500KRs as part of Shelby American's 60th-anniversary celebration. Those cars got a 60th-anniversary badge and were dubbed King of the Road. — hence the KR tacked on to the model name.

The GT500KR received a number of modifications to differentiate it from the standard GT500, including the supercharger and intercooler, upgraded adjustable springs and revised sway bars, and big Brembo brakes – specifically, six- and four-piston (front and rear, respectively) stoppers with ventilated rotors. Shelby offers the body kit and tuning to owners of 2020-22 GT500KRs for $54,495. But it was only open to 60 cars for the 2020 model year (a total of 225 over a three-year period), making this a very rare Mustang indeed.

We don't know what this GT500KR will cost when the gavel finally drops on this auction, but the original pricer was $127,895 for the direct-from-Shelby version. So the final price likely won't be cheap — especially for a Mustang.

Thinking about this another way, though, it's a deeply modified, 900-horsepower machine that can likely keep up with expensive supercars from the likes of Porsche or Ferrari. And Shelby American didn't just bolt on parts. They claim that they worked closely with Whipple to develop a 3.8-liter capacity supercharger with a larger throttle body, cold air intake, and a revised pulley system, as well as a multi-core intercooler. Shelby also made certain the car would pass emissions across the U.S.

Shelby American also worked directly with Ford on the carbon fiber hood – the side vents suck heat from the exhaust manifold to prevent heat soak from robbing the V8 of power. Forged 6061-T6 aluminum wheels were specifically developed for this version of the Shelby GT500KR, too, and buyers could get them in either brushed silver or gloss black. The black looks sweet, but I think this car would look equally special with silver rims. As befits a street racer, this Mustang gets Recaro front buckets in red-and-black leather, with grippy Alcantara side bolsters.

There aren't very many comps for the GT500KR, so setting expectations for the price is a bit tough. A few older models from the 1968 run have sold for well over $200,000, as have a few low-mileage versions of the most modern KR. A 592-mile example of the 2022 KR was bid recently to $153,000, but it didn't sell. Maybe the KR's sibling, the Code Red, could lend a bit of perspective.

In 2022, Shelby also brought back the twin-turbo Code Red with 1,300 horsepower and made just 30 examples. That car cost $209,995 when it was new, and it wasn't street legal, so you'd need a very big wallet and track access to enjoy it. To make that much power, Shelby swapped the supercharger for twin turbochargers. It also gave the car a unique, dual-fuel feed so it can run on racing octane as well as E85. A Code Red was also up for auction on Bring a Trailer recently, and it was bid up to $282,500 — but that didn't meet the seller's reserve.

You want a 2020 GT500KR with 900 horsepower to drive, though, not to be parked in a collection like that 226-mile Code Red most likely has been. And you can't street drive the Code Red. This car hits the sweet spot for insane power that's still usable, and no matter what price it goes for, this GT500KR should be driven. With 21,000 miles already on the clock, that's the sort of treatment it deserves.

Google Ads Quality Score is essentially a measurement of the quality and relevance of both your keywords and PPC ads. It is a dynamic metric, assigned on a scale of 1 to 10, with 10 being the best possible score. It is used by Google to determine your cost per click (CPC) and your ad rank in the ad auction process.

Quality Score is calculated based on three primary components: click-through rate (CTR), ad relevance, and landing page experience.

For any industry, including real estate, a good Quality Score is generally around 7 or above. However, in the competitive world of real estate, striving for an even higher Quality Score could give you an advantage. So, for realtors, a great Quality Score might be considered 8 or above.

That said, keep in mind that a high-Quality Score is not an end in itself. It's a sign that your ads are relevant, and your landing pages provide a good user experience, but it's still just one factor in the overall success of your Google Ads campaigns.

#5636. New Biologics May Be Able to Change the Course of Sjogren's Disease

— Experts discuss promising dazodalibep and ianalumab data presented at ACR

In this exclusive roundtable video from MedPage Today, three rheumatology experts discuss promising new treatments for Sjögren's disease, highlighting emerging data presented at the American College of Rheumatology (ACR) annual meeting.

Moderator Hanna Zembrzuska, MD, of the University of Iowa in Iowa City, is joined by Nancy Carteron, MD, of the University of California Berkeley, and Thomas Grader-Beck, MD, of Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore. In this first of four episodes, they examine phase III OASIZ-301 results for dazodalibep and long-term NEPTUNUS extension findings for ianalumab, including whether improvements in salivary flow could signal the potential to preserve salivary gland function.

Following is a transcript of their remarks:

Zembrzuska: Hello, and welcome to MedPage Today Roundtable on the most recent American College of Rheumatology meeting. My name is Hanna Zembrzuska. I'm an adult rheumatologist in Iowa City, Iowa, and I'm joined by some colleagues here who I will have them introduce themselves. Go ahead.

Grader-Beck: Hi, my name is Thomas Grader-Beck. I'm an associate professor at Johns Hopkins Rheumatology. I'm a member of the interdisciplinary Sjögren's center and I'm very excited to be here.

Carteron: Hi, I'm Nancy Carteron. I'm a professor at University of California at Berkeley and UCSF [University of California San Francisco], and I'm based at a Sjögren's center in Berkeley, and I'm happy to be here.

Zembrzuska: Yeah, I'm so happy to be here with Dr. Carteron and Dr. Grader-Beck, and we are going to do a virtual roundtable covering Sjögren's news from the most recent ACR meeting.

This is the most promising era in the history of Sjögren's disease research. For decades, care was limited to managing symptoms like eye drops and saliva substitutes with zero FDA-approved targeted therapies. But over the past year, multiple late-stage clinical trials have succeeded, bringing the first disease-modifying drugs to the brink of approval. So very exciting.

At the recent American College of Rheumatology annual meeting, there was a late-breaking oral abstract session that discussed dazodalibep, which is a CD40 ligand antagonist, and the results from its phase III OASIZ-301 trial. What were your main takeaways from this trial?

Carteron: I'll jump in. I think seeing yet another product meet the endpoints in Sjögren's historically was terrific. I think the fact that it also targets an additional pathway in the disease pathogenesis is promising.

Grader-Beck: I will say one other thing, maybe. I think the side effect profile overall was good. There was a little bit of a signal of hypertension and there wasn't much additional information about that, but maybe that's something to just keep in the back of the mind to see if that is something to really be concerned about. But otherwise, I thought it looked great.

Carteron: I would also add that in their study, they included a pretty significant number of patients that also had another coexistent autoimmune disease. So both lupus and rheumatoid arthritis plus Sjögren's patients were allowed in the study. And I think it was maybe even up to 20%.

I don't think there was any data presented separating that out, but I think that will begin to give us a little more information about real-world use of this particular kind of product. And I think the other point really is it's not a monoclonal antibody, so it's a different technology of inhibition. So it's actually a fusion protein that's very targeted.

But to get to Thomas's point about safety profile, it really does look like the newer technologies have figured out a workaround against some of the thrombotic effects that we saw early on when that particular pathway was inhibited. But intriguing the point that he's making about the hypertension, so stay vigilant.

Zembrzuska: So at ACR, long-term results from the NEPTUNUS extension study for ianalumab were also presented. This study had high retention rates and it reported data on stimulated salivary flow with improvements maintained through week 96. What does this mean exactly? Does this mean that sustained stimulated salivary flow indicates gland preservation or is that too strong of a statement? What do we think this means?

Grader-Beck: Yeah, I mean, it's very, very interesting and it's exciting to see that we see a consistent longer-term signal. So in the extension study, of course, everyone is on the drug and then you have some patients from placebo switching over to drug and you can start to see similar effects in the placebo group in terms of improvement of disease activity. And then also there was a little bit of a signal of the salivary flow.

I think it's too early, it's too early to say. We really need some more dedicated studies to tease that out. But if you look at the more mechanistic studies -- and there was data also presented at ACR this year, and last year actually too -- where you measure, for example, the vascularity in the glands before and after treatment. And you can clearly see a decrease of inflammation if you measure it by vascularity, you can see improvement of infiltrates, you can see actually improvement of salivary flow, but those were not placebo controlled. These are mechanistic studies.

So certainly that all points towards a possible effect. And the way it looks like, it would be patients that are actually earlier in the disease course that have more residual saliva may be the ones that may benefit more.

Carteron: I think we have data showing a decrease in glandular infiltrates of lymphocytes, but predominantly B cells, with deep B-cell depletion from a number of different products looking at it when they have. And so I think the overwhelming evidence is that there can be improvement, and I think even a small amount of improvement in salivary function may translate into a significantly meaningful outcome for patients. Whether it then translates into decreased dental damage or other things, clearly we need more.

But I think that for quality of life, not even well established, but even early on for patients, I find it particularly exciting. And also anecdotally for patients that were within the study that elected to continue and go into the long-term extension study because of a number of factors, but one of them also was increased oral comfort.

#5635. Monta Joins ChargeHub’s Passport Hub, North America’s Leading EV Roaming Platform

Monta joins Passport Hub, bringing nearly 4,500 charging ports from networks like EnviroSpark and FLASH to dozens of automakers, charging apps and fleets.

“Every time a world-class CSMS like Monta joins Passport Hub, the whole ecosystem levels up” —Simon Ouellette, CEO of ChargeHub

Monta, the global EV charging software platform, and ChargeHub, operator of Passport Hub, North America’s leading EV roaming platform, today announced a partnership that connects Monta’s charging station management system (CSMS) to Passport Hub. Through this single integration, charge point operators (CPOs) running on Monta’s software, including established U.S. networks such as EnviroSpark, FLASH, and Get Charged, will become discoverable and payable for drivers across dozens of automakers, charging apps, fleets, and other eMSPs already connected to Passport Hub.

The partnership is expected to bring close to 4,500 additional charging ports into the Passport Hub roaming ecosystem, according to Monta, as of November 2026. Monta’s CPO customers will be connected to Passport Hub automatically, at no additional cost. As the integration rolls out, operators will gain real-time visibility of their stations’ location, availability and pricing across the Passport Hub network. Drivers will also be able to activate stations remotely from partner apps, including the ChargeHub app, used by more than 1 million drivers annually.

Monta opened its U.S. headquarters in Miami in 2024 after achieving a leading position in the European charging software space. The agreement will accelerate its North American growth by giving its customers access to the continent’s roaming demand, without having to negotiate and maintain dozens of bilateral OCPI connections. For Passport Hub partners, a fast-growing pool of public chargers will become available through a connection they already have.

“In Europe, roaming is simply expected in every market: drivers plug in wherever they are, and it works. That’s the standard we aim to bring to the North American market,” said Casper Rasmussen, CEO of Monta. “Connecting to Passport Hub lets every North American operator on Monta reach the continent’s major driver apps and automakers through one integration, with the roaming revenue deposited immediately in their operator wallet, so they can focus on running excellent—and busy—charging networks.”

“Every time a world-class CSMS like Monta joins Passport Hub, the whole ecosystem levels up,” said Simon Ouellette, CEO of ChargeHub. “Monta brings deep operational know-how from some of the most mature charging markets in the world, and with one connection, entire networks open up to roaming. Operators get more sessions, eMSPs and automakers get more coverage, and drivers get one less reason to worry about where they’ll charge. Everyone wins.”

#5633. 1998 Family Sedans Get Pushed To Their Limits On Track In The Latest 'Best Motoring' Episode

We've been raving about the ridiculously entertaining on-track comparison tests performed by the Japanese video series Best Motoring for over a decade now, but I stumbled into a gaping rabbit hole over the weekend and binged as many episodes as possible, so it's fresh on my mind. If you're unfamiliar with the work of Best Motoring, it was a Japanese car magazine and video series that ran for 24 years between 1987 and 2011, most famous for its hardcore on-track comparison tests. These tests put professional racing drivers into a lineup of several different competing road cars and set them on a five-lap battle, consistently coming within millimeters of disaster while pushing the limits in cars that often would never otherwise be used on a track.

It's always great fun to watch, and the latest upload is no exception. It pits six 1998 midsize sporty family sedans against each other: the JDM Honda Accord SiR, Nissan Primera Camino Te-V, Mazda Capella Zi-R, Volkswagen Passat 1.8T, Audi A6 2.8 Quattro, and Mercedes-Benz E320. None of these cars are the first names that come to mind when it comes to track day heroes, but that doesn't stop the Best Motoring team from driving the snot out of them.

The domestic Japanese cars included in this test didn't directly compete with the Mercedes E-Class and Audi A6, but they were included as performance benchmarks. The JDM Honda Accord SiR only had a 2.0-liter four-cylinder engine with VTEC, and it sent its 177 horsepower to the front wheels through a five-speed automatic transmission.

The JDM Nissan Primera actually made its way to the United States in the form of the Infiniti G20, and it also only packed a naturally aspirated 2.0-liter four-cylinder engine that sent about 140 horsepower to the front wheels through a CVT automatic. The Mazda Capella also made its way to the United States in the form of the Mazda 626, and in this test the former is fitted with a 168 horsepower 2.0-liter four-cylinder that sends power to the front wheels through a four-speed automatic.

As far as imports go, the Passat competed closely with the JDM cars, but the A6 and E-Class were from a class above. I don't want to spoil the results, though, so you'll have to watch and see for yourself how things shake out. If you're looking for a way to fill your long weekend, the Best Motoring official YouTube channel has over 830 videos to binge, with new uploads on a pretty regular basis.

Cigna will allot $10.5 million to each of the three focus areas under the initiative, per the announcement. In that partnership, Cigna has helped build out trauma-informed care services to 90% of clubs, reaching 11,000 employees. The company said that these efforts have supported 1,600 youths, and that its workforce has contributed more than 2,000 hours to local clubs.

Eligible organizations can apply for two-year, $250,000 grants to support programs in the three categories. The funds will be available to groups in Arizona, Connecticut, Florida, Georgia, Illinois, Missouri, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, Tennessee and Texas, per the announcement.

#5631. Why European Households Are Rushing to Buy Solar Panels Ahead of a Dark, Cold Winter

Changes to solar incentives and long installation processes mean European homeowners could benefit from planning now.

Winter is cold, dark, and grey. Yet for many Europeans, it’s a great time to switch to solar power.

While many are focused on the holiday season, industry experts are urging homeowners considering a switch to solar to contact suppliers before Christmas — although not to take advantage of the winter sun.

Several European countries are making changes to solar energy subsidies and tax breaks in 2027, meaning homeowners might want to fast-track their plans to enjoy the financial benefits.

But even without changes to government incentives, there are good reasons to get ahead of the spring sunshine.

Although a typical rooftop solar installation takes just one or two days, getting building permits and, in some cases, approval to connect to electricity grids can take weeks. Sometimes months.

Last year, an OECD report citing earlier research found that permit times for rooftop solar projects ranged from six weeks in Malta to as many as 10 months in Bulgaria.

The country has since made it easier for homeowners, scrapping permit requirements for solar systems up to 20 kilowatts intended for personal use, but delays are still common across Europe.

In Germany, a consumer watchdog warned last year that homeowners in Saxony were waiting months to have their solar panels connected to the grid — and, in extreme cases, more than a year.

And Edward Gurney, the founding director of the UK-based Solar and Battery Company, says getting approval from electricity providers can take four to five weeks even under normal circumstances.

“A lot of solar equipment is manufactured in China, and getting replacement stock delivered can take around six weeks,” he says.

Winter weather can also disrupt installation schedules, as icy roofs make working conditions unsafe.

“When you’ve already got a busy installation schedule, losing even a few days to bad weather can push subsequent installations back,” Gurney says.

Waiting until the weather warms up could mean missing out on a prime period for solar production, too.

Solar power generated less than five per cent of the EU’s electricity in January last year, but by May, it was supplying more than 20 percent, according to the European Environment Agency.

In Germany alone, 74 per cent of the solar electricity fed into the grid last year was generated between April and September.

The sooner homeowners have their panels installed, the sooner they can start benefitting from this springtime bump.

In the meantime, Gurney recommends using winter to assess how much electricity you might use and compare quotations from different installers.

“The number of panels, battery capacity and how much electricity your household uses will all affect the long-term value of the installation,” he says.

Homeowners in several European countries could face changes to the cost of installing solar panels in 2027. Since April 2022, homeowners in England, Scotland and Wales have been able to have solar panels installed without paying value-added tax. From 1 April 2027, the tax rate will return to five per cent.

In Germany, people who install solar panels from January onward could miss out on government support unless new energy laws are approved before the end of the year, the German Solar Industry Association warns.

Although German lawmakers have tentatively agreed to continue paying homeowners for surplus electricity they sell to the grid from solar systems up to 25 kilowatts, they have yet to strike a final deal.

And in Austria, the government plans to stop offering grants for solar panels in 2027 and instead help homeowners buy batteries to store the electricity they generate.

Source: Euronews via EIN PRESSWIRE. By Craig Sauers

#5630. Hepatitis B Shot at Birth Dips Among Babies of Infected Moms

— "Birth dose vaccination serves as a critical safety net," researchers say

Fewer newborns are receiving the birth dose of the hepatitis B virus (HBV) vaccine, including those born to infected mothers, according to a national retrospective review.

For over 1.3 million U.S. infants born between January 2018 and June 2026, vaccination rates were 76.4% in 2018 and 79.8% in 2022 before beginning to fall in mid-2023, landing at 65.6% in June of this year, reported Nina Masters, PhD, MPH, of Truveta in Bellevue, Washington, and colleagues in NEJM Evidence.

From 2018 through 2025, a positive maternal HBV test led to vaccination in 97%-98% of newborns born to those mothers -- but that percentage dropped to 93.9% during January through June 2026.

Overall, as newborn HBV vaccination rates fell, maternal HBV screening rates rose. Over the study period, 90.5% of mothers had evidence of an HBV test, with 0.18% testing positive for the virus. The proportion of moms who had no recorded HBV test during pregnancy dropped from 15.6% in 2018 to 7.6% in 2026.

"Hepatitis B birth dose vaccination serves as a critical safety net against gaps in protection against perinatal HBV infection," Masters and team wrote.

"Applying the 90% screening rate found in this study to the approximately 3.6 million births per year, mothers without evidence of HBV screening during pregnancy may give birth to an estimated 360,000 infants per year," they noted. "Applying the 0.18% ... positivity rate in this study could translate to more than 640 infants a year born to mothers with HBV infection who are untested."

Universal HBV vaccination of newborns at birth has been shown to be safe and effective. However, the CDC's revamped Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices last December abandoned more than three decades of U.S. vaccine policy and voted to stop recommending a universal birth dose.

The panel recommended instead a shared clinical decision-making process for babies born to mothers who test negative for HBV. Under that approach, parents and clinicians would decide "when or if" to administer the vaccine. For families that opt to not give the birth dose, the panel suggested delaying the first dose until a child is 2 months old. The CDC's proposed childhood immunization schedule would move HBV vaccination to shared clinical decision-making except in high-risk groups.

The steady declines in newborn HBV vaccination rates across all maternal groups "potentially indicate distrust of medical interventions even beyond recommendations," Masters and team cautioned. "These results reinforce previous reports, likely reflecting continuing vaccine hesitancy and confusion among parents after recent changes in recommendations for newborn HBV guidelines."

The trends seen in this study could lead to more chronic HBV infections in the years ahead, according to a recent modeling study. That research predicted that moving from a universal birth dose to deferred vaccination or a shared decision-making approach could increase chronic HBV infections by 19% with delayed vaccination and 83% with shared decision-making. Other research has suggested that unvaccinated infants may face unexpected HBV household exposure risks even when moms test negative.

For this study, Masters and colleagues reviewed electronic health records from the nationwide Truveta Data database. The analysis included 1,338,961 infants born to 1,075,767 mothers who were ages 15-49 years at delivery.

Over the study period, 75.9% of newborns received HBV vaccination within 1 day of birth.

Vaccination rates were highest among babies born to moms who tested positive for HBV, at 96.9%. Vaccination rates were 75.9% among those with mothers who tested negative, 76.8% among those with moms with unknown infection status, and 75.4% among those with moms who had no evidence of a test in the database.

Among the 2,231 mothers who tested positive for HBV infection during pregnancy, 92.8% received both hepatitis B immunoglobulin and HBV vaccination.

#5629. HLTH 2026: Elsevier upgrades ClinicalKey AI with full patient EHR context

HLTH 2026: Elsevier upgrades ClinicalKey AI with full patient EHR context" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Elsevier unveiled this week a major upgrade to ClinicalKey AI, enabling the AI-powered clinical decision support tool to access a patient’s full electronic health record and evaluate treatment plans against the company’s evidence-based medical library.

As AI advances, Elsevier has strategically shifted from a traditional academic publisher—it’s one of the world's largest publishers of scientific, technical and medical content—to an AI-driven analytics information company, incorporating generative and agentic AI into its healthcare and academic research.

ClinicalKey AI is a HIPAA-ready point-of-care decision support tool that draws answers from articles sourced from approximately 1,000 world-leading journals. Elsevier’s upgraded ClinicalKey AI is already deployed at more than 1,200 hospitals, and the company says the solution integrates with all EHR providers. Elsevier recently struck a content agreement with the JAMA Network that brings full-text content and visuals from the JAMA Network Family of Journals to ClinicalKey AI.

ClinicalKey AI was originally co-developed through a strategic partnership between Elsevier and OpenEvidence. An Elsevier spokesperson said the company's collaboration with OpenEvidence on ClinicalKey AI has concluded.

The company has rapidly expanded its AI capabilities and features, including ClinicalKey Nursing AI, an AI-powered tool built specifically for nurses and nursing workflows. Elsevier has also developed specialized AI assistants, such as LeapSpace, an AI-assisted workspace for researchers that’s built on 15+ million peer-reviewed articles and book content and 100 million Scopus records, according to the company.

Three months ago, the company rolled out its "Ask AI" feature across more than 1,500 U.S. hospital sites using its flagship ClinicalKey platform. With the generative AI feature, clinicians can ask conversational clinical questions and receive direct, cited answers drawn from evidence-based sources, including premium journals and content from leading medical organizations, the company said. Unlike general-purpose chatbots, Ask AI does not pull from the open web and does not store, process or retain patient-identifiable information, according to the company.

In a move to develop context-aware AI, the company acquired Wellsheet in June. The health technology company aggregates and synthesizes patient chart data—including notes, labs, imaging and medication orders—from EHRs to provide relevant clinical intelligence at the bedside.

“The problem we’re trying to solve here is that physicians are challenged by so many things when they’re taking care of patients; top among them is patient complexity. Patients have more and more conditions, and they’re taking more and more medications. It can be hard to really understand the full picture and determine how to proceed,” Dr. Claudine Lott, physician executive for clinical solutions at Elsevier, told Fierce Healthcare during the HLTH conference this week.

“Our original ClinicalKey AI tool has been a place where the clinician can go, and they can ask a question, and it searches this curated database of evidence-based content we’ve given it and gives them an answer. But there was a bit of a missing piece in that it wasn’t capturing that patient context. If you wanted to get an answer, that’s really tailored to a patient, it was limited to what you can type in,” she said.

She added, “Wellsheet has 10 years of experience with looking at the entirety of the patient chart and helping to surface that to the clinician.”

There is a growing market for AI-powered clinical decision support products, but Elsevier contends its advantage lies in its depth of patient context and its large, curated content base, with a wholly owned, large proprietary library of peer-reviewed STM literature, including content from millions of articles, journals and books.

San Juan Regional Medical Center in Farmington, New Mexico, is using ClinicalKey AI’s new patient context functionality to provide quality care with fewer resources. With smaller clinical and quality teams than large academic health systems, and in a state where nearly 40% of residents rely on Medicaid, the medical center, which serves the Four Corners area, has found this support especially valuable, according to Carlo Hallak, M.D., physician executive, information services, at San Juan Regional Medical Center.

A non-profit, community-owned acute care hospital and Level III trauma center, San Juan Regional Medical Center operates outpatient and specialty clinics alongside its main hospital campus, San Juan Regional Rehabilitation Hospital and San Juan Health Partners clinics.

Hallak emphasized that Elsevier is a primary source of medical knowledge rather than a “wrapper” for other AI platforms, and that was a key distinction for the organization, he said. And ClinicalKey AI is designed for the entire care team. “The hospital is run by nurses, mid-level providers, other caregiver teams,” he told Fierce Healthcare at the HLTH conference.

The medical center aims to move clinicians to enterprise LLMs integrated with the electronic health record that can provide the full patient context, Hallak said.

"We're already seeing how ClinicalKey AI can be instrumental at the bedside and help improve care for our patients. As a rural healthcare center, we are proud to say that by using ClinicalKey AI to check each patient’s care against the same evidence base that major health systems rely on, we’re able to deliver the standard of care patients expect in any major city or leading academic center," Hallak said.

He added, "ClinicalKey AI reads the whole chart, checks it against the evidence and shows exactly where each finding comes from. That support is invaluable for a hospital like ours, and we’re already seeing strong adoption of ClinicalKey AI among our clinicians."

Hallak cited an example of a physician who used ClinicalKey AI to correctly identify viral meningitis, preventing an aggressive and unnecessary treatment course for bacterial meningitis.

ClinicalKey AI supports the physician’s judgment rather than replacing it, helping the clinician get to relevant evidence faster, he said, noting that, in the case of the viral meningitis patient, the physician’s clinical judgment was critical in recognizing that something was unusual and then consulting colleagues. The AI tool then helped accelerate the next step by quickly surfacing information the clinician otherwise would have found by searching the medical literature.

Physicians also use the tool during weekly complex case discussions to quickly review trending medications, images and test results in one summarized sheet, he noted.

“It’s going to expedite a lot of the work they do when it comes to these complex cases,” he said.

The AI solution can quickly summarize a complex patient history at the point of care, and this can help care teams in the emergency department understand a frequent ED patient, Hallak said.

One patient has visited their emergency department 95 times in less than a year, in addition to making numerous visits to neighboring health systems, Hallak said. When that patient arrives, clinicians who aren't familiar with him would traditionally have to dig through the chart to understand his history. With Elsevier's ClinicalKey AI tool, they can ask for a summary of the patient's recent visits and care and get that information within seconds, he noted.

Because patients who frequently visit hospital EDs typically receive care at multiple organizations, San Juan Regional Medical Center is also working with other local health systems on interoperability efforts so clinicians can get a more complete picture of what happened during the patient's visits across different facilities.

As a rural hospital with staffing constraints, technology is essential to filling workforce gaps and supporting care delivery, Hallak contends.

"We don't have enough physicians, enough nurses, enough transporters, enough caregivers. We will never be able to have enough of those," he said.

Hallak envisions ClinicalKey AI will be particularly valuable for discharging patients from the hospital faster.

Generative AI tools can help speed up patient discharges by identifying barriers, assessing patients’ care needs and providing relevant information from both structured and unstructured data. Because the platform is designed for the broader care team, case managers and physicians can access the same information, while push notifications can alert clinicians when test results are available so they can act quickly, Hallak said.

"From an operational perspective, it allows for this care team coordination of care, and also from a physician perspective, it provides the context whenever there's something hanging and they're trying to understand more what's happening with the patient['s] discharge. You could be a hospitalist, and you've been off shift for like seven days, and then you come to the hospital and now the patient is on their tenth day, but you inherit that discharge. Going through, reading every progress note for every single day, reading every consult for every subspecialty that looked at this patient usually would take two to three days to actually get the patient out of the building safely," he said.

Rather than manually compiling information for a discharge summary, clinicians can use ClinicalKey AI to aggregate relevant information from across the patient’s record, trace it back to its source and review the AI-generated summary before signing off on the discharge, according to Hallak.

"It is a game changer, in my opinion. One of our hospitals said it used to take me three days to discharge a patient; now it takes me less than three hours," he said.

Going forward, the system expects to measure operational outcomes such as length of stay, safe discharge and multidisciplinary-rounds use, according to Hallak. The medical center also plans to evaluate clinicians' use of the tool and how it changes care decisions.

The medical center has also deployed other AI tools such as Oracle Health's clinical AI agent for ambient documentation.

"These things are crucial. We're hoping to bring in a clinical AI agent for nurses as well to help the whole care team be able to eliminate the noise, the friction that typically EHRs or IT would bring to the conversation," Hallak said.

The medical center is taking a risk-based approach to AI governance, using source verification and peer review for AI-generated summaries while applying greater scrutiny to tools that are predictive or suggestive, Hallak noted. That oversight involves clinical experts as well as compliance, legal and cybersecurity teams along with traditional vendor security and product-vetting requirements.

AI governance should become stricter as the technology moves from summarizing information to recommending or taking actions, he said.

Elsevier designed ClinicalKey AI with security and trust in mind, including HIPAA compliance, citations that show where information comes from and safeguards that keep the tool from prescribing what clinicians should do. Instead, it surfaces relevant information to help clinicians make their own decisions, Lott said.

"Health systems tell us two things stand in the way of adopting AI: tools that don’t work with their existing EHR partners, and concerns about security, compliance and responsible use," Omry Bigger, president of Clinical Solutions at Elsevier, said. "ClinicalKey AI was designed to address both. As an EHR-supported and HIPAA-compliant ready solution, ClinicalKey AI integrates seamlessly across health systems to provide clinicians with trusted evidence and patient context that gives them tailored clinical insights for each patient at the point of care."

#5626. Consumers believe AI will be key in making healthcare simpler: survey

Consumers believe AI will be key in making healthcare simpler: survey" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Americans want a healthcare experience that's simpler and easier to understand, and artificial intelligence may be the key to getting there, a new survey shows.

The poll, conducted by the Harris Poll and commissioned by Elevance Health, found that 82% of American patients view at least some part of healthcare information as a "foreign language," and close to half (45%) said they made a healthcare decision they later regretted due to a lack of understanding.

The survey was conducted among 2,0001 adults in mid-July, and 74% said they have encountered a key barrier, such as understanding their health insurance or a medical bill. And only a quarter (27%) said they completely understand their own health coverage.

That said, most (79%) of those surveyed said they believe AI can help to improve the healthcare experience overall.

Ratnakar Lavu, chief digital information officer at Elevance Health, told Fierce in an email that because the tech has the ability to quickly surface and parse key data about a member or health need, it can serve as a central piece of the puzzle in making a more personalized experience.

"AI-enabled tools give us the ability to create a unique member context," he said. "Because of this digital technology, we can now truly 'know the person' and proactively work with them to help them manage their healthcare needs."

For example, 82% of those surveyed said they would like to receive answers about healthcare as quickly as they can use an app to order a food delivery, and 83% would like to easily access recommendations that pull from their health coverage, individual health needs and financial situation.

Seventy-two percent said they would trust AI for accuracy on at least one type of information, such as an explanation of benefits, cost estimates or details on medication.

However, while many Americans believe AI can play a leading role in driving a better health experience, just 20% said they currently use the tech regularly as a source of information. And while 72% said they trusted the tech to surface key health information, 33% said they would trust an AI platform to translate their insurance benefits, and 30% said they trust the tech to estimate care costs.

Just 13% said they would trust AI to make diagnoses.

Lavu said that healthcare organizations looking to roll out new tools need to avoid simply embedding AI into programs for the sake of it, and be transparent about both the use case as well as the role of the human in the loop.

The study also found that women were less likely than men to trust AI, and younger generations were more likely to use it as a source of healthcare information than older groups.

"We have to implement AI at the speed of trust, which means being thoughtful about where AI adds value, not just delivering technology for technology’s sake," he said. "Trust is also earned when AI-enabled programs truly make things easier for the consumer. "

For example, Elevance Health has deployed an AI-powered program to support utilization management reviews and help drive faster approvals where possible, though AI is not used to make claims denials. It is also leaning on AI for more proactive member engagement initiatives through its digital channels, identifying individuals that would benefit from extra support or who may face gaps in care.

"We start by listening to members and identifying where healthcare is creating the most confusion or friction," Lavu said. "From there, we determine the right solution, which may or may not involve AI. When AI is the right tool, it should fit naturally into familiar interactions and make it easier for members to get an answer or take the next step."

The National Association of Benefits and Insurance Professionals and Health Agents for America both sued over the regulation. NABIP argued that the moratorium would have a significant impact on licensed professionals operating in accordance with the law.

Per the document, that stay will remain in place until CMS publishes its withdrawal notice. Once that has been put forth, the plaintiffs will dismiss their complaints as moot. CMS also agreed not to take further action against agents and brokers during the current open enrollment period.

The moratorium, finalized in September, was a part the agency's broader efforts to root out fraud, waste and abuse on the Affordable Care Act's exchanges.

A federal court has granted a preliminary injunction to two key groups representing insurance brokers over the Trump administration's moratorium on new broker enrollments.

The District Court of Maryland issued the injunction after determining that the National Association of Benefits and Insurance Professionals and Health Agents for America "have shown that they are likely to succeed on the merits of their claims under the Administrative Procedure Act."

The court also said that the organizations made clear they would likely suffer significant harm if the moratorium stays in place.

NABIP said that the ruling means that it will restart training for new brokers beginning on Nov. 6.

"Today’s ruling is a significant victory for licensed agents and brokers and the consumers who rely on their expertise," said NABIP President Mychal Walker in an announcement (PDF). "With Open Enrollment already underway, every day matters."

"Lifting the moratorium immediately and beginning training tomorrow will help affected professionals get to work assisting individuals and families in finding coverage that fits their needs and budgets," said Walker.

NABIP initially sued on Oct. 15 to challenge the moratorium. The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services instituted the moratorium in late September as part of its broader push to combat fraud on the Affordable Care Act's exchanges.

The National Association of Benefits and Insurance Professionals is suing the Trump administration over its moratorium on new brokers entering the Affordable Care Act marketplaces.

The organization, the leading trade group for insurance brokers and agents, said the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services' moratorium impacts close to 19,000 brokers and agents who will be barred from registering ahead of open enrollment.

CMS unveiled the moratorium in late September as part of its ongoing push to root out fraud, waste and abuse. In addition, the agency said it would terminate more than 200 agents and brokers that failed to comply with marketplace standards.

The agency said new brokers and agents were disproportionately responsible for submitting inappropriate enrollments and engaging in behaviors at high risk for fraud.

In an announcement (PDF), NABIP says that it supports the broader effort to combat fraud, but that CMS' moratorium "threatens the livelihoods of thousands of legitimate, licensed professionals who have not been accused of fraud and limits consumers’ access to professional assistance as they navigate Open Enrollment."

The organization argues in the lawsuit that the rule instituting the moratorium violates both the Administrative Procedure Act and the Affordable Care Act. The regulation is unlawful as it is "arbitrary, capricious, and unsupported by sufficient evidence," NABIP said.

The 19,000 agents who would be barred from participating under the rule are part of a critical network of professionals who help consumers find coverage that meets their needs, the organization said.

NABIP President Mychal Walker said that CMS should look elsewhere in its fraud efforts.

"The existence of fraud is not in dispute. NABIP has raised these concerns with CMS repeatedly and has offered concrete solutions to address them," Walker said in the announcement. "What is in dispute is whether the appropriate response is to exclude thousands of legitimate agents based solely on whether they registered last year, without any individualized evidence about them."

"There is a better approach: target fraud where it occurs, strengthen the system’s security and hold bad actors accountable while preserving consumers’ access to trusted professionals," Walker continued.

CMS has taken steps to crack down on brokers as the agency views improper ACA enrollments as a key target in its fight against fraud. CMS officials have repeatedly raised concerns that people are enrolled in ACA plans without their knowledge, or despite being deceased.

Earlier this week, the agency revealed it will purge 189,000 enrollees who are currently listed as enrolled in both ACA plans and other coverage, such as Medicaid or Medicare.

#5623. Vitamin B12 may hold the key to treating a rare genetic disorder

A surprising discovery involving vitamin B12 could open new possibilities for understanding and potentially treating rare genetic disorders. Researchers found that the vitamin can correct developmental problems in tiny worms carrying a genetic mutation associated with Verheij syndrome, a rare human condition that causes developmental delays, impaired growth, and short stature.

The findings center on a cellular process called RNA splicing, which helps prepare the genetic instructions cells use to produce proteins. During splicing, unnecessary portions of messenger RNA are removed, and the remaining sections are joined together in the correct order. When this process goes wrong, it can disrupt essential cellular functions and contribute to serious developmental disorders.

Mutations in genes responsible for splicing can cause conditions such as Verheij syndrome. To better understand the effects of these genetic changes, scientists investigated how a related mutation affects growth and metabolism in a laboratory model.

Vitamin B12 Reverses Developmental Defects in Worms

The discovery emerged from experiments involving C. elegans, a tiny roundworm commonly used in biological research. The researchers were initially searching for previously unknown genes that influence lifespan when they began examining a mutation in a gene involved in RNA splicing. The same gene is associated with Verheij syndrome in humans.

Worms carrying the mutation developed problems resembling important features of the human disorder. Their growth slowed considerably, and they remained smaller than normal.

To investigate why this happened, the scientists conducted genetic screens and analyzed the worms' metabolism. They discovered that the mutation disrupted specific metabolic pathways that depend on vitamin B12 and are essential for healthy growth and normal cellular activity.

The researchers then tested whether providing additional vitamin B12 could counteract these changes. Remarkably, the treatment restored the affected metabolic processes to normal and corrected the developmental abnormalities associated with the mutation.

"We were surprised to find that a change in a fundamental process of RNA processing had such a targeted effect on vitamin B12-dependent metabolism," says Jonathan Kölschbach, first author of the study. "Even more exciting was that we were able to largely correct the consequences of this change in the worm model using vitamin B12."

Could Vitamin B12 Help Treat a Rare Genetic Disorder?

To explore whether their findings might also apply to people, the researchers examined publicly available datasets from human cells. They also worked with Hormos Dafsari, a neuropediatrician at the University Hospital Cologne, to collect blood samples from patients diagnosed with Verheij syndrome.

These investigations uncovered evidence of similar metabolic changes in humans, suggesting that the vitamin B12-related pathways affected in the worms may also play a role in the human disorder.

Although the results are promising, researchers have not yet established whether vitamin B12 supplementation can improve symptoms in people with Verheij syndrome. Additional studies will be necessary to determine whether the benefits observed in worms can be translated into a treatment for patients.

The discovery also raises a broader possibility. Metabolic disruptions may contribute more substantially to diseases caused by faulty RNA splicing than scientists previously recognized. Understanding these connections could help researchers identify new therapeutic strategies, potentially extending beyond Verheij syndrome to other rare genetic conditions.

"Our study is a good example of how basic research on model organisms can provide new insights into human diseases," says Adam Antebi, Director at the Max Planck Institute for Biology of Ageing and lead author of the study. "A fundamental biological question can thus give rise to a new approach that could also become medically relevant in the long term."

#5622. UnitedHealth the latest insurer to sue over the 2027 Medicare Advantage star ratings

UnitedHealth the latest insurer to sue over the 2027 Medicare Advantage star ratings" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

UnitedHealth Group is joining the ranks of insurers that are suing the feds over the 2027 Medicare Advantage star ratings calculations.

Much like other recent lawsuits, the healthcare giant argues that the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services inappropriately used multiple measures in the calculations. Over the summer, a Georgia federal court sided with MA plan Clover Health, and tossed 20 measures that were used in its 2026 scores.

That legal ruling has been the basis of much of the current round of legal wrangling.

UnitedHealth said in its complaint that it is bringing the lawsuit to ensure "that their 2027 Star Ratings are calculated in accordance with CMS’s statutory authority and procedural obligations."

The star ratings are tied to quality bonus payments for Medicare Advantage plans and listed on the Medicare plan finder to help individuals identify high-quality coverage. When those payments are lower due to a decline in scores, the insurer may not be as nimble in lowering premiums or enhancing benefits.

"The Star Ratings carry real consequences," UnitedHealth wrote in the complaint. "A plan’s Star Rating thus directly affects the benefits and healthcare offerings that Medicare beneficiaries receive."

Elevance Health is the latest insurer to sue the feds over its performance in the latest round of star ratings for the Medicare Advantage program.

The company sued the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services in District of Columbia federal court on Friday, arguing that the 2027 star ratings calculations violated the Administrative Procedure Act in using 11 measures that it says were adopted unlawfully.

In the lawsuit, the company said that the harm from including these measures is "concrete and substantial." If they were excluded, it would increase the scores for 12 of its Medicare Advantage contracts and generate $516 million in additional quality bonus payments.

"Their inclusion therefore does more than violate statutory requirements in the abstract: it depresses Elevance Health’s ratings and reduces the funding available for the following payment year," per the lawsuit. "That funding could support broader supplemental benefits, lower premiums and cost-sharing, and improved care coordination."

"CMS’s unlawful methodology puts those resources out of reach," the company said.

In addition to the financial impacts, Elevance argues that the star ratings scores can also lead to reputational damage that makes it harder for them to compete in the MA market. It also provides prospective enrollees with inaccurate information, the company said.

"Beneficiaries cannot make informed coverage choices when the government’s own comparison tool conveys a distorted assessment of the plans available to them," Elevance said.

"An artificially depressed rating does not merely place Elevance Health at a competitive disadvantage; it undermines the very comparison the program is supposed to enable," the company continued. "A rating lowered by unlawful measures presents beneficiaries with a misleading signal of relative quality, rather than a lawful basis for distinguishing among competing plans."

CVS Heath's Aetna is joining the ranks of insurers suing over its results in the 2027 Medicare Advantage star ratings.

The insured filed suit Monday in Georgia's Southern District Court, and argues that 28 measures used by the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services to calculate its scores were "unlawfully adopted" and should have been excluded.

The court is the same venue that ruled in favor of Clover Health over the summer, and set aside 20 measures that were used to determine its 2026 scores. That decision, which the feds have appealed, kicked off a broad recalculation of 2026 scores that looked different for insurers outside of Clover, triggering a wave of litigation.

In its lawsuit, Aetna cites the Clover decision in finding that CMS extended beyond its statutory authority in deploying those 20 measures.

The company said that calculating its scores using the 28 measures in question will likely cost it $2 billion in 2028 quality bonus payments and rebate retention. Those are funds that the insurer could "apply toward expanding member benefits, reducing premiums and investing in quality improvement."

Aetna adds that in addition to the monetary loss, having lower scores negatively impacts the company's reputation and its ability to attract potential members.

"The harm to CVS Health is not exclusively financial; lower ratings carry meaningful reputational harm, which can in turn impact membership," per the lawsuit. "By incorporating unlawful measures into the 2027 Star Ratings calculation, CMS cast CVS Health’s ratings in a poorer light in the eyes of Medicare Advantage consumers relative to peer MAOs, undermining CVS Health’s ability to compete for Medicare beneficiaries through enhanced benefits and the like."

Aetna did not respond to a request for comment at the time of publication.

Based on an analysis from Stephens, 69% of Aetna's MA members are in plans with four or more stars for 2027, down from 81%. That threshold is the key to securing quality bonus payments.

Aetna's complaint follows others focused on the 2027 scores from Centene and Alignment Healthcare (see those stories below).

Centene has become the latest insurer to sue the federal government over its 2027 Medicare Advantage star ratings.

In a lawsuit filed Thursday in Georgia's Southern District Court, the company argues that the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services violated the Administrative Procedure Act in determining its latest scores. Centene says that CMS ran afoul of "core statutory safeguards" in deploying 17 measures.

The use of those measures ultimately caused "significant injury" to the company, according to the complaint. For 2027, 9% of Centene's members are enrolled in plans with at least four stars, which declined from 18% in the prior year.

"In implementing each of the individual Star measures that Centene challenges, CMS violated applicable law and thereby caused Centene to lose out on hundreds of millions of dollars in revenue that Centene could use to strengthen benefits, reduce premiums, and improve health outcomes," the company said in the lawsuit.

CMS argues that the court has already sided with a similar argument in its decision in favor of Clover Health earlier this year. In that case, which led to a broad recalculation in scores, the courts set aside 20 measures that were used in determining Clover's star ratings for 2026.

If the 17 measures in question had been excluded in calculating Centene's scores, the company estimates it would receive $448 million more in quality bonus payments for the 2028 plan year, funds it would deploy to expand benefits, lower premiums and enhance programs like care coordination.

In addition to the financial impact, a drop in star ratings also carries a reputational hit, Centene said.

"Beyond the financial impact to the company and its members, depressed ratings also inflict significant reputational damage and diminished membership," the company said in the complaint

Centene had not returned a request for comment at the time of publication.

Alignment Healthcare sued federal regulators, alleging that its 2027 Medicare Advantage star ratings were determined "in flagrant violation" of statute.

In the lawsuit filed Friday in District of Columbia federal court, the insurer says that the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services "has completely departed from Congress’s vision of leveraging predictable, valid measures developed with input from providers, plans, and the public" in establishing the methodology for the star ratings.

The company argues that rather than establish "consistent, stable specifications" for metrics through the traditional rule-making process, the agency instead detailed key measures through a series of "technical notes." This violates the Administrative Procedure Act, per the lawsuit.

The program's star ratings are the critical determinant in quality bonus payments to insurers as well as a tool that aims to make it easier for enrollees and brokers to identify benefits with the highest quality.

"Consistent application of the statutory requirements governing Star Ratings is therefore essential not only to plan payments and competition but also to ensuring that beneficiaries can rely on the Star Ratings as meaningful and comparable measures of plan quality," Alignment said in the lawsuit.

The company adds that multiple recent court decisions have set aside CMS' star ratings methodology, notably a ruling over the summer in favor of Clover Health that tossed 20 metrics used in the 2026 calculations. A Georgia federal judge determined that 10 measures utilized exceeded CMS' authority, while 10 other measures were promulgated inappropriately.

CMS recalculated the scores across the board following the ruling, but only set aside the 10 measures that the courts determined were outside the bounds of its regulatory authority. The agency maintained that approach in the 2027 calculations, Alignment argues.

"Congress created the Star Ratings program to allow Medicare Advantage beneficiaries to make informed decisions about plan enrollment based on clinically validated measures of plan quality that had been subjected to notice and comment," the company said. "CMS’s contrary approach fails to carry out the vision that Congress set forth by statute."

The Trump administration has appealed the Clover decision, so that legal case remains ongoing.

In addition, Alignment argues it suffered reputational and financial damage as a result of its 2027 scores, which plummeted compared to the prior year. Just 25% of its members are in plans with four or more stars for 2027, down from 100% in 2026.

Shares in the company tumbled following the release of the ratings, though stock prices have rebounded since.

Alignment sued the feds following the Clover decision to secure a recalculation for its scores that aligns with the court's decision, and in a statement to Fierce Healthcare, said that the lawsuit aligns with that perspective.

"Our lawsuit seeks to ensure that the Star Ratings program operates as Congress intended and that Alignment is properly compensated for the care we provide," Alignment said in the statement. "We respect the judicial process and will present our case in court. Because this matter involves pending litigation, we will not comment on the specific legal arguments beyond our filings."

"Our focus remains on delivering exceptional care, improving health outcomes and advocating for a stable, lawful regulatory framework that supports seniors and strengthens the Medicare Advantage program," the company said.

#5621. New Obesity Definition Flags More Adults at Dementia Risk

— Dementia risk shifts as obesity definition expands

A new definition of obesity identified more adults with an increased risk of dementia compared with defining obesity by body mass index (BMI) alone, pooled data from two cohorts showed.

Using the European Association for the Study of Obesity (EASO) definition, more than 80% of adults classified as overweight were reclassified as having obesity, according to Rui Zhou, PhD, of Guangdong Pharmaceutical University in Guangzhou, China, and co-authors.

Compared with people of normal weight without comorbidities, those with EASO-defined obesity had a significantly higher risk of dementia (pooled HR 1.93, 95% CI 1.50-2.48), Zhou and colleagues reported in Neurology.

Those with EASO-defined overweight, on the other hand, had a lower risk of dementia than those with normal weight (pooled HR 0.61, 95% CI 0.45-0.81).

The EASO framework incorporates BMI, body fat distribution (waist-to-height ratio), and medical, functional, or psychological comorbidities.

"These findings underscore the inadequacy of using BMI alone to define obesity," Zhou said in a statement. "The results support the integration of body fat distribution and other health conditions into classifying obesity."

Obesity is linked with dementia, with midlife obesity having an especially high risk. Evidence from both animal and human studies suggests that obesity negatively affects the brain through multiple mechanisms, including hypothalamic dysregulation and metabolic, inflammatory, and vascular disruptions that target the hippocampus and prefrontal cortex.

The BMI definition of obesity has drawn criticism in recent years, leading to alternative frameworks from groups like EASO and the Lancet Diabetes & Endocrinology global commission.

The implications of the new obesity definitions for dementia risk have been unclear, Zhou and co-authors noted. To help clarify this, they compared the prevalence of obesity under the EASO framework versus traditional BMI criteria and examined how obesity was associated with incident dementia and all-cause mortality.

The study used data from the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing (ELSA; 6,542 people) and the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (CHARLS; 12,402 people).

The researchers defined dementia using algorithmic criteria or self-reported physician diagnoses, and determined all-cause mortality from death registries, medical records, or interviews with relatives. They included 17,617 participants in the dementia analysis and 18,197 in the mortality analysis.

The mean baseline age in the ELSA group was 65.9 years and 54.3% were women. In CHARLS, the mean baseline age was 58.2 and 53.2% were women. The median follow-up was 11.5 years in ELSA and 8.2 years in CHARLS.

Under the EASO framework, 85.8% of ELSA participants and 80.2% of CHARLS participants who were previously classified as overweight by BMI shifted to the obesity category.

Overall, 37.7% of ELSA participants and 24.9% of CHARLS participants had obesity using the EASO definition. The most common comorbidities in the newly defined obesity group were high blood pressure (42.6%) and diabetes (35.1%).

Compared with people with normal weight and no comorbidities, people with EASO-defined obesity had higher dementia risk in both cohorts. They had higher mortality risk only in the CHARLS cohort, but the pooled mortality estimate was significant (pooled HR 1.30, 95% CI 1.01-1.68).

EASO-defined overweight was associated with lower dementia risk in both cohorts and with lower mortality (pooled HR 0.32, 95% CI 0.13-0.81).

The so-called "obesity paradox" seen in earlier studies may stem from failures to account for obesity-related comorbidities or to exclude unhealthy individuals from comparison groups, the researchers suggested.

When normal weight without morbidity was the reference in this study, both EASO-defined and BMI-defined obesity were consistently associated with increased dementia risk, they noted. "However, when all normal weight individuals (including those with comorbidities) were used as the reference, these harmful associations were masked," Zhou and colleagues pointed out.

Obesity was measured only at baseline, and changes over time were not captured, the researchers acknowledged. Despite adjusting for multiple variables, residual confounding cannot be excluded.
