#5577. Opinion: Washington and Beijing are building walls around biotechnology. That’s the wrong approach

We ranked the 25 most valuable publicly traded Chinese drugmakers

Kinch is a professor of pharmacology at Stony Brook University and the author of six books on pharmaceutical innovation.

For more than a decade, my colleagues and I at the Center for Research Innovation in Biotechnology have tracked every experimental medicine that enters human testing anywhere in the world. Last December, I wrote in STAT that China had reached parity with the United States in terms of the absolute number of new drugs introduced into clinical trials each year. Starting in 2018, the rate of U.S. contributions began to stagnate. Meanwhile, in 2013, Chinese organizations had introduced about 30 new experimental drugs. A decade later, the number topped 400. And there is no reason to expect the momentum in either country is changing.

Over the past month, both governments have seemingly been moving to wall themselves off. On Oct. 16, Beijing proposed barring foreign acquisition of its companies’ proprietary cell and gene platforms. Within a week, the U.S. Department of the Treasury proposed restrictions that would bar Americans from taking equity stakes, forming joint ventures, or making limited-partner investments in Chinese biotech companies and their equipment suppliers.

The proposals from Beijing and Washington do not impact licensing. American drugmakers can keep licensing Chinese molecules, and Chinese companies may develop new medicines to sell to the U.S. and European companies.

That open door matters more than either wall. Data show that the U.S.-China contest in biotechnology is not one race but several. Restricting investment will not help America win the races it is already losing. The bigger threat to U.S. leadership is not Chinese capital. It is the erosion, at home, of the research enterprise that built America’s lead.

The Center for Research Innovation in Biotechnology’s newest analysis, published in September in Drug Discovery Today, emphasizes the importance of these continued engagements. My colleagues and I evaluated the 17,000 new drugs that first entered human trials between 2000 and 2024, separating them into eight different modalities. These ranged from conventional pills to gene therapies. The convergence in the numbers of overall active ingredients that we reported last year turned out to be anything but uniform when looking at the details.

The growth by China was concentrated in a key subset of biologics. By the late 2010s, Chinese sponsors often had introduced more, and more novel, cell therapies annually than American sponsors. By the early 2020s, China had matched or exceeded the U.S. in the introduction of new monoclonal antibodies, a commercially important class of biologic drugs. China took a commanding lead in certain categories of monoclonals, such as multispecific antibodies and drug conjugates.

The U.S. still holds a larger share in two categories: nucleic acid drugs and gene therapy. Dominance in both technologies reflects tools built over decades of Western public and private investment. Examples include lipid nanoparticles that conveyed SARS-CoV2 vaccines, viral vectors, and CRISPR gene editing.

Those differences help explain why the two governments are building different walls. Beijing’s proposal shields cell and gene therapy from outside entities, areas where they have a demonstrated or aspirational determination to lead the world. Platforms must remain domiciled in China while individual products can be marketed abroad. That is a coherent industrial strategy, and it is paying off well. Chinese financial regulators report that foreign deals for Chinese biotech assets reached $120 billion through August 2026, up more than a third from the year before.

Washington’s proposal works differently. The Treasury Department proposal prevents American investors from punting on a piece of Chinese biotech and yet still allows American companies to pay for Chinese molecules. In areas where China now leads, the combined effect would seem at best to be a division of labor. As my co-author and I pointed out in our earlier STAT article, China increasingly invents and owns while American firms are more prone to take licenses, complete late stage development, and pay royalties.

Nonetheless, a decision to cut off scientific and/or economic engagement would seem detrimental to both nations.

Restriction is a defensive move. It does not put a single new medicine into the clinic. It treats “biotech” — which comprises drugs, devices, diagnostics, ag-tech, and many other areas — as one thing. Each of these competitive races is being run at different speeds and with entirely different players, outcomes, and pole positions.

The fundamental problem is the one described in our December 2025 article. American output of new experimental drugs has been flat since 2018. In our earlier study, China’s public sector, including universities and state-linked enterprises, contributed more than twice as many new drugs in 2024 as their American counterparts. All the while, the U.S. universities that built our lead in nucleic acids and gene therapy face shrinking federal research support as has been highlighted by STAT.

A competitor lacking fuel will lose the race even if regulators try to slow the opposition.

Three steps would accomplish more than walls ever can.

First, subject matter experts should take advantage of the public comment period the Treasury Department has opened through Dec. 7.

Those comments should press Treasury on several points. If it does impose restrictions, and it is not obvious that it should, they should be aimed narrowly at transfers of platforms and capabilities rather than at all investment. More clarity is also needed to address “NewCo” deals, in which a Chinese licensor takes a stake in a new U.S. company. Importantly, the regulator should set a date and objective criteria to review whether any new rules are working as intended.

Second, policymakers should prioritize and incentivize investment in areas where America leads or could lead. Nucleic acid and gene therapies depend on academic discovery and specialized manufacturing. Stable funding for proven models such as translational research by the National Institutes of Health, ARPA-H, and domestic manufacturing is the most obvious and reliable way to protect a declining margin. In cell therapy, policymakers should ask candidly why so many early trials now start in China (regulation, investment, technology, or combinations thereof), and how we might alleviate domestic hurdles.

Third, Washington should measure the race in a more nuanced way, such as by drug or disease type. The totals of new experimental drugs, such as those we have previously emphasized, can hide more meaningful long-term outcomes, such as FDA approvals as well as market and public health improvements. Federal agencies could start by tracking first-in-human trials by drug type and sponsor country. As this will take time, it should become a long-term indicator, ignoring annual variations. Policy aimed at the aggregate and/or based solely on short term measures will miss key details.

Walls are what you construct when you think you are under attack or are losing. In the technologies that will define the next generation of medicines, from RNA drugs to gene editing, American institutions still lead. The biggest threat does not come from abroad but from changes in domestic policy, such as cutting biomedical research. Our current lead in these fields was built with reliable investments by the public and private sectors, not barriers.

Michael S. Kinch is a professor of pharmacology at Stony Brook University and the author of six books on pharmaceutical innovation.

#5576. A study of 30,000 people reveals which antidepressants may work best

A new review has found some antidepressants may be more effective than others at helping people reduce the severity of their symptoms of depression over the long term.

The research, published in The Lancet Psychiatry, found people taking escitalopram (commonly sold as Lexapro), duloxetine (Cymbalta) and agomelatine (Valdoxan) were more likely to report improved symptoms over the long term than those taking fluoxetine (Prozac). For those taking Lexapro and Cymbalta, they were also more likely to stay on their medications.

But does that mean these are the best antidepressants?

Around one in seven Australians will experience depression during their lifetime.

Treatment can involve psychological therapies, social support and lifestyle changes, such as doing more exercise. For some people, these approaches may be enough to support recovery. For others, adding an antidepressant can be an important part of treatment.

In 2024-2025, 3.8 million Australians were dispensed a prescription for an antidepressant.

For adults with depression, clinical guidelines recommend continuing antidepressants for at least six months, and preferably 12 months, after an acceptable response to treatment is achieved.

If, after six to 12 months, the depressive episode has resolved, it may be appropriate to reduce, and eventually stop the antidepressant. But symptoms can occur when discontinuing antidepressants so it’s important this is done gradually, in consultation with a doctor.

Studies of real world antidepressant prescribing patterns in Australia suggest many people take antidepressants for longer than this. One 2022 study found nearly a quarter of those prescribed antidepressants were still receiving prescriptions for them two years later.

Another Australian study found people take antidepressants for an average of four years.

The new review set out to compare how well different antidepressants help people maintain improvements in depression. The researchers also compared how acceptable the medicines were to the people taking them. They measured this by looking at the proportion of people who stopped treatment for any reason during the study period.

The researchers identified and reviewed 115 randomized controlled trials, involving more than 30,000 people. The researchers classified long-term use as six months or more. Their main analysis combined the results of 35 trials that directly compared one antidepressant with another.

They found that three antidepressants – escitalopram, duloxetine and agomelatine – were associated with a greater likelihood of sustained response than fluoxetine.

People taking escitalopram or duloxetine were also less likely to drop out of the trials than those taking fluoxetine.

The findings are interesting as escitalopram (Lexapro) is the most commonly prescribed antidepressant in Australia. It ranked number 13 out of all PBS-dispensed prescriptions in 2024–25. Duloxetine was number 45, but agomelatine isn’t available on the PBS.

The findings suggest some antidepressants may be more effective than others at sustaining a response to treatment, but the results are far from definitive. More than half of the studies included in the main analysis were assessed as having a high risk of bias.

This means some of the differences between antidepressants may reflect limitations in the original studies rather than genuine differences between the medicines. Some medicines were also supported by very few studies, making comparisons less certain.

Another aspect to keep in mind when considering these results is what is meant by “long term.” The trials directly comparing antidepressants typically followed participants for around six months after they first started taking the medication. Only six followed people for longer than six months.

This means we still know relatively little about how the effectiveness of different antidepressants compares over longer periods. This is important given the average time people take them is much longer.

Importantly, these findings reflect average outcomes across groups of people. They can’t tell us which antidepressant will work best for any particular person.

People respond differently to antidepressants, and what makes a medicine acceptable to one person may not be acceptable to another. While the researchers used trial drop-out rates as a measure of acceptability, this doesn’t necessarily capture people’s experiences of taking these medicines.

For someone taking an antidepressant, acceptability might not be so binary. It may involve a trade-off between how the medication improves symptoms, its side effects, and how the medicine affects their everyday life.

Continuing to take an antidepressant doesn’t necessarily mean someone finds it acceptable. Some people experience withdrawal symptoms when trying to stop, which can make discontinuation difficult.

Ultimately, determining if an antidepressant is right for you, and which is the best fit, depends on many factors. These include your symptoms, other health conditions, previous experiences with medicines, potential side effects and what matters most to you.

If you’re taking an antidepressant that’s working well for you, the findings of this study aren’t a reason to switch.

And if you’re considering starting, changing or stopping an antidepressant, discuss your options with your doctor.

#5574. ‘DWTS’ Finalist Amber Glenn Reveals the Sweet Way She and Pasha Pashkov Bonded with Daniella Karagach and Ezra Frech at Home ‘From Day One’

All season long, the "Dancing with the Stars" judges recognized Amber Glenn's competitive nature, but now that the season has come to an end, the Olympic figure skater is proving that she has been a team player all along.

Glen came in second place in the competition dance series, with two-time Paralympian Ezra Frech taking home the coveted Len Goodman Mirrorball Trophy.

And while the contestants share a spot on Team USA—for which they've both brought home gold medals—they quickly bonded in the competition as their professional dance partners, Pasha Pashkov and Daniella Karagach, are married.

When asked how she felt about the results after the finale, Glenn told Extra she "couldn't ask for a better result," and described a "triumphant feeling" as she walked away from Season 35 having earned 10s across the board in all three of her final performances.

"From day one, we all met up, had a little dinner over at their house, and we said, 'We wanna go 1-2,'" she explained to the outlet. "And we didn't specify, like, whatever happens, happens, but the fact that we came in here and we both got those perfect scores. We both did everything we could and it was truly in the hands of the people at home. I'm really proud of what we did and I'm really, really happy that Team USA took it home."

The group—who have been unofficially dubbed "Team USA and the Pashkovs" by fans and even the official U.S. Olympic and Paralmypic team all season—have been close collaborators throughout the competition.

During the Nov. 10 episode, when teams were paired off and required to compete in two-on-two dance-offs, Glenn and Pashkov and Frech and Karagach put a friendly spin on the format by switching partners mid-choreography as they performed a Rumba to "The Boy Is Mine" by Brandy and Monica.

"It felt more like a team dance than anything else," Karagach told Us magazine. "We came together ,and we had the best time sharing the dance floor, and we couldn't also not end swapping partners because I've always wanted to dance with Amber, and Ezra and Pasha secretly wanted to dance with each other. So that was fun."

The competitors-turned-pals took to social media to share plenty of heartwarming behind-the-scenes moments throughout the experience, providing a glimpse at what their down time is like between rehearsals. In one Sept. 18 post, Pashkov wrote, "We're a tightly-knit fam now."

In a post-finale interview with Deadline, Glenn described the moment she had realized Frech would win. The Plano, TX native said, "I don't know if I felt as many emotions watching a performance as I did when watching Ezra and Dani. It was like, at first, it's excitement. I'm like, 'I love that Linkin Park [song].' And then horror, fear, and like, panic.'"

The moment Glenn was referring to was the malfunction in which Frech's prosthetic fell off mid-performance. Frech and Karagach quickly communicated while dancing, allowing him to secure it into place properly and complete the routine.

"I think I gasped so loud I threw my rib out again," Glenn continued. "So then, the physical pain and just like, fear, panic, and then just awe, inspiration, something you feel in your core. I know that's a saying, but like you feel it in your gut, and it takes your breath away, and that's what it was."

Glenn said that in that moment, she "was like, 'They won.'" She even added that she "would feel bad" if she had taken home the trophy after seeing Frech and Karagach pull off "such a perfect dance" after "working so hard for it all season."

#5572. Centralized platform for submitting, managing out-of-network billing disputes launches

Centralized platform for submitting, managing out-of-network billing disputes launches" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

The Trump administration has launched a new online portal for payers, providers and other stakeholders to manage and monitor disputes under the federal Independent Dispute Resolution process.

The IDR Gateway went online Nov. 13 and was officially unveiled Nov. 20. It replaces the web forms parties previously used to manage disputes, most of which will no longer be available outside of the centralized platform after Jan. 15, 2027, per a government fact sheet.

Payers will eventually be required to register on IDR Gateway so that it is easier for providers to identify the correct party, the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services said earlier this year when finalizing an overhaul of No Surprises Act protocols. That registration feature will be added “in the future on a rolling basis,” CMS said last week, with others like in-portal negotiation similarly rolling out over time “to improve accountability and reduce unnecessary filings,” the agency said last spring.

For now, the IDR Gateway allows parties and their representatives to initiate a dispute, respond to proposed selections of IDR entities and submit a payment offer. Its other tools allow users to view, search, set up notifications and broadly analyze open disputes for their organization; an IDR Gateway Dashboard, CMS said, offers a color-coded donut chart breaking down an organization’s different types of open disputes by phase, while another tool can generate detailed reports of dispute line items.

The administration also touted security measures inherent to the new portal. These include a new sign-up process that requires users to verify their identity with an approved credential service provider, and other protocols like a terms and conditions agreement that notes that unauthorized users could be subject to criminal prosecution.

The baseball-style IDR process enacted under the No Surprises Act, intended to handle out-of-network billing disputes away from the patient’s purview, has become a point of contention amid dispute volumes and payouts well beyond legislators’ expectations.

Arbitrators’ decisions have largely favored providers over payers (85% of decisions went toward providers last year), which alongside court decisions that tweaked CMS’ processes further toward provider preferences, has triggered outright condemnation from payers who have turned to lawsuits, restrictive policies and lobbying in a bit to reform the process. Recent analyses have pegged the IDR process’ impact for employer plans at $8.4 billion in 2025 and total costs associated with the process at $22 billion for that same year.

Lawmakers including the No Surprises Act’s chief authors have said they hope to pass new legislation to fix or fully replace the IDR process, with December’s must-pass budget bill now looking like a likely vehicle for such a change.

#5571. Why don't weight-loss drugs like Ozempic and Wegovy work for everyone?

Medications like Ozempic and Wegovy, which contain semaglutide — a GLP‑1 receptor agonist that helps regulate blood sugar, appetite and body weight — have become household names and important pillars in obesity management for the medical profession.

Research has shown GLP-1 medications reduce body weight by an average of 15 percent when used weekly for 68 weeks and combined with lifestyle interventions. This is because semaglutide acts on the brain to increase the feeling of fullness and to decrease appetite.

These medications don’t work the same way for everyone, however. Our multidisciplinary research team at the University of Alberta is working to improve obesity care for people of all ages and to understand why some people respond better to semaglutide than others, and how their weight loss can be maintained over time.

We are investigating the role of energy metabolism as a potentially important piece in a complex puzzle.

Research has shown semaglutide medications to improve quality of life, blood markers such as sugar or cholesterol, strength and overall health. Weight loss is only one measure of how well they work.

We are exploring whether people’s responses to these medications could lie in individual factors such as genetics, metabolism, body composition, lifestyle, microbiota, associated diseases, age and sex.

Energy metabolism may also be an important piece of this puzzle. This is a measure of the total calories consumed (in) and the total calories burned (out). We burn calories all the time: for vital processes like breathing and thinking, physical activities like going to the gym and the everyday act of digesting food.

When we lose weight, our bodies naturally need less energy. But sometimes, the body goes into an extra “energy-saving mode,” burning even fewer calories than we would expect. This is called metabolic adaptation, or adaptive thermogenesis.

Think of it like a light bulb that automatically dims to save electricity. This is one reason why losing weight can become more difficult over time, sometimes leading to a weight-loss plateau.

Changes in body weight and composition (the amount of fat and fat-free mass in our bodies) play an important role in energy metabolism. Both fat and fat-free mass use energy, even when we are resting. As we lose these tissues, our bodies naturally burn fewer calories.

Researchers are still trying to understand whether weight-loss medications influence these processes differently. If we can understand how our bodies use energy during and after weight loss, this could help us develop better strategies for maintaining weight loss over the long term.

We published a recent review of studies investigating the effects of GLP-1 therapies on energy utilization. We found a few studies exploring how semaglutide affects resting energy use, with findings that were neutral or inconclusive.

The question of how semaglutide impacts energy use is an emerging area of study, and remains an open question for exploration.

At the University of Alberta, we have a gold-standard method to measure energy utilization called a whole-room indirect calorimeter. This is a rare research facility and is similar to a hotel suite that can precisely measure each component of energy use. This room can isolate the effects of changes in someone’s calorie burning at rest, after eating and during exercise.

We are currently recruiting research participants with blood sugar regulation issues, such as insulin resistance or diabetes, who are about to start semaglutide treatment. We will follow their weight loss journey over six months to investigate changes in body weight and composition, and energy utilization using sophisticated approaches.

Understanding how semaglutide influences energy use and body composition, and how these changes interact, could be an important step toward explaining why individuals respond differently to weight-loss treatment.

This will allow us to contribute to more personalized approaches to obesity and Type 2 diabetes management in the future. Having a better understanding of how energy use changes with semaglutide-induced weight loss will also help us to better anticipate potential non-responders (people who do not lose weight) and offer alternative treatments sooner in their health journey.

Importantly, current evidence suggests that if you are taking semaglutide or considering starting treatment, you should make a few lifestyle changes.

#5569. Academic hospital heads petition Congress for 2-year delay to CMS' 340B cuts

Academic hospital heads petition Congress for 2-year delay to CMS' 340B cuts" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Dozens of academic health system and teaching hospital chief executives are turning to Congress in a bid to blunt a controversial subsidy cut coming to Medicare Part B in the new year.

Earlier this month, the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services locked in plans to reduce reimbursements for outpatient drugs dispensed by participants in the 340B Drug Pricing Program during the 2027 calendar year.

Specifically, the agency said it will move from the current rate of average sales price (ASP) plus 6% down to ASP minus 28%, with a corresponding 7.5% increase in non-drug outpatient payments to maintain budget neutrality. CMS said the change will reduce Original Medicare drug payments by an estimated $4.35 billion and drug payments from beneficiaries by $1.1 billion during the policy’s first year.

Hospital groups—particularly those that chiefly represent nonprofit or safety-net hospitals—have denounced the plan’s disproportionate effect on hospitals participating in the decades-old subsidy program, as well as a gift to for-profit hospitals that do not participate but will benefit from the budget-neutral offset.

With their formal opposition to the policy’s proposal set aside by CMS, 95 executives whose organizations are members of the Association of American Medical Colleges have now penned a letter to leaders of the House and the Senate pleading for a two-year delay to the rate cut’s implementation.

“This policy will exacerbate already negative Medicare margins at a time when teaching hospitals are already grappling with rising financial challenges resulting from inflation, workforce shortages, manufacturer-driven restrictions on the 340B program and an expected rise in uncompensated care costs,” they wrote.

The executives acknowledged that the final policy’s rate of ASP minus 28% is “slightly smaller” than CMS’ initial proposal of ASP minus 33.4%, but said the change was still a threat to the country’s healthcare safety net. They noted the cuts represent a nearly $5.5 billion reduction that would be disproportionately shouldered by AAMC-member teaching hospitals—who comprise 17% of all impacted hospitals—but will see almost $3 billion of that total.

Those funds are necessary to finance critical care services at academic hospitals including trauma care, inpatient behavioral care, transplant surgery and labor and delivery, the signatories warned lawmakers. They also noted that their institutions are major referral hubs that accept “the most complex transfer cases from lower acuity settings, such as rural and community hospitals,” in a way that for-profit hospitals and others who will benefit from the final rule do not.

“While we understand that Congress has an interest in improving the 340B program, and are broadly supportive of meaningful transparency and accountability for covered entities, we also strongly believe that cutting Medicare payment to 340B hospitals is not the appropriate policy mechanism to achieve these goals,” they wrote. “Therefore, we respectfully request that you support a two-year delay in the [Outpatient Prospective Payment System] rule’s payment cuts for 340B-acquired drugs.”

Among the letter’s 95 signatories were the heads of Cedars-Sinai, Stanford Health Care, Yale New Haven Health, Tampa General Hospital, Rush University System for Health, Mass General Brigham, Nebraska Medicine, RWJBarnabas Health, NewYork-Presbyterian, UNC Health and School of Medicine, OHSU, Jefferson Health, Penn Medicine, Vanderbilt Health and Froedtert ThedaCare.

The academic health systems and hospitals’ turn to lawmakers comes after their rebukes of CMS’ 340B policy have fallen on deaf ears. The agency and broader Trump administration have often sided with critics of the subsidy program on related initiatives like a pilot rebate program, citing 340B’s rapid growth and contribution to increased healthcare spending. A Health and Human Services Office of the Assistant Secretary for Planning and Evaluation policy brief defending the rate cut made those views crystal clear with claims that the program has incentivized provider consolidation while doing little to serve patients’ needs.

Meanwhile, Congress, spurred by public pressure to reduce healthcare costs, has proposed its own legislative fixes to 340B. Though each bill aims to preserve the program and subsidize safety-net care, some are more friendly to the hospital industry than others.

#5567. Powerful new weight-loss drug helps patients cut knee pain in half

For people living with painful knee osteoarthritis (OA), even simple activities like walking, climbing stairs, or getting out of a chair can become a struggle. Excess body weight can make these challenges even worse. Now, two major clinical trials suggest that a powerful experimental weight-loss drug could provide substantial relief.

The two phase 3 trials, led by Northwestern University, included more than 1,000 participants in total. People receiving the highest dose of retatrutide, an experimental injectable weight-loss medication, lost an average of about 25% of their body weight. When researchers combined the findings from both trials, they found that approximately two-thirds of participants treated with retatrutide reported a reduction in knee pain of at least 50%. By comparison, only 38% of those given a placebo experienced that level of relief.

The benefits extended beyond weight loss and improved knee pain. Participants also showed reductions in blood pressure, blood lipid levels, and inflammation throughout the body.

Findings from both studies were published on Nov. 8 in the New England Journal of Medicine.

"The findings are really saying for people who are overweight and have OA, if you lose a significant amount of weight with this treatment, there is a good chance that you're going to get a meaningful reduction in your knee pain," said corresponding author Dr. Thomas Schnitzer, professor of physical medicine and rehabilitation, anesthesiology and medicine (rheumatology) at Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine.

"A major factor is that you're loading your knees less and therefore, there's less pain and it allows you to increase your function."

Philip Conaghan, a study co-author and professor of musculoskeletal medicine at the University of Leeds in the United Kingdom, presented results from one of the trials, TRIUMPH-4, on Nov. 8 at the American College of Rheumatology annual meeting in Orlando, Florida. Findings from the second trial, TRIUMPH-1-OA, were scheduled for presentation during a separate poster session that same day.

A Potential New Treatment for Millions With Knee Osteoarthritis

Painful knee osteoarthritis affects approximately 5% of Americans (15 million people). Available treatments range from physical therapy and medications applied to the skin to oral anti-inflammatory drugs such as ibuprofen and Voltaren. Other options include opioids and corticosteroid injections, although the relief provided by steroid injections generally lasts only a short time.

Weight loss is another established way to ease symptoms. Previous studies have shown that losing 5% to 10% of body weight through changes in diet and exercise can improve knee osteoarthritis pain. However, Schnitzer explained that losing more than 10% through these approaches alone is often challenging. For people already struggling with painful knees, exercising enough to achieve substantial weight loss can be especially difficult.

Retatrutide could offer another approach. Developed by Eli Lilly, the experimental medication is administered as a once-weekly injection and works differently from existing GLP-1 medications such as semaglutide and tirzepatide.

While those drugs act on one or two hormone receptors and typically produce weight reductions of 10% to 20%, retatrutide activates receptors associated with three different naturally occurring hormones. In the clinical trials, participants lost approximately 20% to 25% of their body weight, depending on the dose. Eli Lilly scientists also contributed to the research as study co-authors.

"Participants had remarkable responses," Schnitzer said. "Many of the people in this study lost considerable amounts of weight, with a few losing up to a hundred pounds or more."

Despite the encouraging findings, Schnitzer emphasized that lifestyle changes should remain the starting point for people who are overweight and have painful knee osteoarthritis.

Improving eating habits, increasing physical activity, and making other sustainable lifestyle adjustments can help reduce symptoms without the expense of newer weight-loss medications. These strategies also avoid side effects associated with GLP-1 drugs, including gastrointestinal problems and muscle loss.

Maintaining muscle strength is particularly important for people with knee osteoarthritis because the muscles surrounding the joint help support and stabilize it. Losing too much muscle could therefore create additional challenges for patients who already have difficulty moving comfortably.

For individuals who cannot achieve sufficient weight loss through lifestyle changes and continue to experience significant knee pain, Schnitzer believes retatrutide could become a valuable option if it receives approval from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration.

Could the Drug Also Slow Knee Arthritis Progression?

Although the trials demonstrated substantial improvements in weight and pain, several important questions remain unanswered.

One of the biggest is whether retatrutide does more than relieve symptoms. Researchers still do not know if the drug can slow the underlying progression of knee osteoarthritis enough to reduce the likelihood that patients will eventually need knee replacement surgery. People who already required a knee replacement were excluded from the trials.

"That would be the goal here to say you can reduce people's pain, and you can stop the progression of their osteoarthritis," Schnitzer said.

Another unanswered question is whether retatrutide might benefit people with painful knee osteoarthritis who are not overweight. Because the trials did not include these patients, further studies will be needed to determine whether they could experience similar improvements.

Researchers are also interested in understanding how much of the pain relief comes directly from weight loss and how much might be related to the drug's effects on inflammation.

"These drugs are believed to have significant anti-inflammatory activity, but the mechanism is not entirely known," Schnitzer said. "Whether cutting down inflammation in the joint is also important in addition to reducing load needs more research, so this is still a first step, in my view. I've been working in the OA field for a long time, and I think this opens up opportunities to do a lot more studies to understand the condition better."

How Researchers Measured Knee Pain Relief

To evaluate changes in symptoms, the research teams used the Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Arthritis Index (WOMAC) Pain index, a standardized tool for assessing osteoarthritis pain.

During study visits, participants rated their pain on a scale from 0 to 10. They also used a mobile app to record their pain levels each day, allowing researchers to track how symptoms changed throughout treatment.

The study is titled, "Retatrutide Once Weekly in Adults with Knee Osteoarthritis Pain and Obesity."

#5566. The Home Audit That Could Save Homeowners Thousands—and Cost You Only $50

With housing costs skyrocketing, every little bit helps—and sometimes, there are options even longtime homeowners are unaware of.

For example, a homeowner recently turned to Reddit to vent about humidity and outdoor air entering their home. They received quotes for an energy audit ranging from $100 to $200 and asked if this service is actually worth it.

Someone from Connecticut replied saying they paid only $50 for the same type of audit, thanks to a subsidy from their electric company—and depending on your location, utility provider, and/or income, you could also qualify for a subsidized or even free energy audit.

While experts agree that a $50 assessment is less common, even paying a few hundred for one may save you thousands of dollars down the road. That's because it can uncover hidden air leaks that may contribute to higher utility bills and damaging moisture issues.

“When you seal air leaks, you may prevent water vapor inside your house from turning into liquid inside your walls. This eliminates the need for costly wood rot and mold issues that may lead to $5,000 or more in repairs and reduces wear and tear on your HVAC unit,” explains Andrew Pho, a home renovation and improvement expert at Mister Balustealing in Toronto.

Energy audits are designed to find what’s causing energy loss in your home, but they’re not all created equal.

Before booking one, confirm what it includes.

“At the very least, it should consist of a blower-door test (a blower fan is set up in a doorway to measure how much air is leaking in or out of the home), check the levels of insulation in your attic, walls, etc., and look at your HVAC system to make sure it’s running efficiently,” says Dennis Vong, founder and owner of Inland Power Wash in Orange County, CA.

Clear, written suggestions on how to improve the energy efficiency of your home are important as well.

“Additionally, you may want to ask if minor fixes like caulking and weatherstripping are included in the audit or available for an additional cost,” Vong explains.

Niki O'Brien, operations manager at Custom Exteriors in Loveland, CO, reinforces the importance of ensuring your home has proper insulation and ventilation in your attic.

“It can prevent dangerous freeze/thaw cycles that can trap moisture and lead to ice damming and interior leaks,” O’Brien says.

If your goal is to improve energy efficiency and reduce the risk of needing repairs, an energy audit is a good idea.

According to Energy Star, proper insulation and air sealing can cut your heating and cooling bills by as much as 15% on average.

“If you spend $200 a month on heating and cooling, that could mean savings of about $30 a month, or $360 a year,” Vong explains.

O’Brien has experienced the benefits of an energy audit firsthand.

“We have seen many cases, including a home we owned personally, that needed additional insulation and resulted in lower energy costs,” says O’Brien.

At the end of the day, the information you get from an energy audit will absolutely save you money in the long run.

“Whether that means getting new, energy-efficient products, adding additional weather proofing to existing systems, or repairing/replacing caulking, insulation, or creating effective ventilation, eventually it will surpass the cost of an audit,” O’Brien adds.

According to the Department of Energy, an energy audit will typically run you between $250 and $600. The good news is you may be able to get one at a subsidized rate.

“I recommend calling your gas and electric providers to see if they offer energy audits at a subsidized rate and what rebates may be available if you were to make any energy improvements to your home,” says Vong.

Aaron Christy, founder and owner of Indy Roof & Restoration in Indianapolis, says that in Indianapolis, for example, AES Indiana offers all of its customers a no-cost virtual assessment, and a free in-home assessment if you meet certain income limits.

Your state may also offer a no-cost assessment.

“In my state, Massachusetts, there’s the Mass Save Program, which provides free audits to qualifying homeowners, renters, and landlords,” explains Ted Dow, vice president of delivery at Power Home Remodeling in Boston.

While you’re waiting for an audit, you can perform your own DIY assessment.

Make sure the weatherstripping around your doors and windows isn’t falling apart, check for any dripping faucets or leaking pipes, and make sure your gutters are draining properly away from your foundation.

“Just remember that it’s best to leave the more specialized services to the pros,” adds Vong.

#5565. Voters expect lawmakers to address healthcare affordability, access: poll

Voters expect lawmakers to address healthcare affordability, access: poll" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Half of voters said they are paying more this year in premiums and out-of-pocket costs, according to a new national poll.

Lake Research Partners and Bellwether Research & Consulting surveyed 1,000 voters between Oct. 20 and Oct. 28 on behalf of the National Health Council, and 50% said their premiums and out-of-pocket costs are higher this year compared to last year. Among those with commercial insurance, 63% said their premiums have risen, and 60% said their out-of-pocket costs have grown year-over-year.

In addition, 25% of those surveyed said they had a claim for a prescription denied, and 24% said they waited more than two weeks for a prior authorization decision. Twenty-one percent said that they struggled to find a specialist.

Healthcare costs and the broader economy were major factors in Democrats' significant victories in the latest midterm election. And the NHC poll finds that voters expect Congress to act on addressing the costs that they face.

Most of the surveyed voters (78%) said they believe that the healthcare system warrants major changes or a complete overhaul, and 84% said they would support a candidate that would make it a priority to reform the healthcare insurance system.

However, 74% of those surveyed rated the effort from elected officials to address affordability and access as either fair or poor.

“Holding onto a plan isn’t the same as being protected by it. Patients are watching their costs rise and their coverage change, and they’re worried about what that means for their families down the road,” said Randall Rutta, CEO of the National Health Council, in an announcement. “The new Congress has a real opportunity to change that, and patients across the country will be watching.”

The survey highlights a number of potential policies that would have broad voter support. For example, 91% of those surveyed said they would support eliminating surprise medical bills and policies to require price transparency.

In addition, 90% said they would back efforts to reduce out-of-pocket costs, while 89% said they favor requiring health plans to cover treatments that were prescribed by doctors. Eighty-eight percent support efforts to increase screening and early detection for medical risks.

"Voters aren't asking lawmakers to talk about health care differently," said Christine Matthews, president of Bellwether Research and Consulting, in the release. "They want to see it work differently. Reform is a priority they expect the new Congress to deliver on."

#5564. Why Medicare’s 2027 physician pay changes worry some specialists

We ranked the 25 most valuable publicly traded Chinese drugmakers

Disability in Health Care Reporting Fellow

Rose covers disability and mental health, and she helps write STAT’s daily Morning Rounds newsletter. Confidential tips can be sent to Rose on Signal at rosebroderick.11.

Podiatrist Heather McGuire always wanted to serve in a clinic in her hometown of Ventura, Calif. Fifteen years after she opened her practice, she is realizing her dream in the community that raised her, treating suburbanites and agricultural workers with diabetes on Medicare.

But McGuire believes that dream may be ending.

The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services’ recent update to how Medicare pays physicians cut the payment rate for certain services provided on the same day by 20% when it’s provided by the same physician or practice. McGuire’s practice already operates on extremely thin margins, and she recently shelved a plan to hire another doctor to improve the practice’s exceedingly long wait times.

It could worsen Medicare recipients’ access to specialist care in Ventura, too. Last week, the podiatrist saw a new patient, a woman in her 80s, who waited two and a half months for an appointment to get her heel pain checked out. When the patient arrived, McGuire found that it wasn’t just heel pain. The woman had also developed an ulcer on her other foot during her long appointment wait. Left unchecked, an ulcer in someone with diabetes can lead to amputations.

“I would be paid 20% less for providing potentially lifesaving or limb-saving treatment care for that wound because she also had another complaint at the same visit,” McGuire said.

Podiatrists, dermatologists, and otolaryngologists are among the biggest losers with this change, according to an analysis by the American Medical Association, an advocacy group for physicians. Opponents of the policy, including the AMA, say it will force patients to return for separate appointments, raise out-of-pocket costs, and increase wait times, especially for patients in rural areas who have less access to specialists.

“If you’re running your own small group practice [accepting Medicare patients], can you still financially do that?” said Miranda Franco, a senior policy adviser at the law firm Holland & Knight. “Or are you going to start thinking about, you know, maybe consolidating into a hospital system or private equity to defray some of that financial loss?”

These billing code changes are an attempt to modernize Medicare and reduce administrative burden, a CMS spokesperson said. It is part of the agency’s broader shift away from specialist care and the fee-for-service model, and one of many reimbursement challenges that specialists are contending with.

Not everyone is against the change in payment rates for services rendered on the same day. The Medicare Payment Advisory Commission, a nonpartisan group that advises Congress on Medicare, supports it, saying it will remove redundancies and duplicative payments. The Justice Department has also found multiple instances of providers committing fraud through this billing code.

The cuts to payment rates for same-day services were slated to be 50% when first proposed in 2018, before backlash from physicians and patients softened the blow. Under the final rule, effective Jan. 1, 2027, Medicare will pay for the highest-valued same-day service at 100%, then reduce payment for each additional service rendered on the same day by 20% when physicians perform evaluations and other routine outpatient services. CMS argues the lowered rate is justified because providers use less resources — for patient registration, scheduling, and support, for example — when patients are seen and treated on the same day at the same practice.

Amy Hunsberger, a lawyer with Manatt, a legal advisory and consultancy, said the cuts are partly motivated by the statutory requirement that physician payments cannot increase without Congressional approval, forcing Medicare to cut back on expenses as the agency spends more on health care costs.

“You have a balloon that has so much air in it, and when you reduce payment in one area of services, you’re squeezing the balloon on one side, and it pushes payments out to the rest of the balloon,” said Hunsberger. “This balloon is not updated for inflation and relies on continual, almost annual congressional bailouts to get clinicians to some semblance of reasonable payment.”

Because these policy changes apply to the number of claims relating to health care services rendered on the same day and to any specific specialty, it’s unclear how they will impact Medicare beneficiaries. The American Parkinson Disease Association said patients with Parkinson’s disease are worried that it could impact their ability to get outpatient Botox injections that are critical for relieving pain.

McGuire estimates that the policy change will decrease her profits by 6%. The policy goes into effect on Jan. 1. She doesn’t know how much longer her practice will last.

“There are times where I ask myself if I should just close up shop and call it a day, and go find a job at Trader Joe’s or Starbucks, where I can have a reliable income,” she said. “If it wasn’t for the fact that medicine has always been a calling for me and the joy it brings me to take care of patients, I probably would have done that already. But I’m also getting to the point where I don’t think this is financially viable and a long-term solution.”

#5563. 5 Packing Tips for a Smooth Move

Moving can be a time-consuming process, but it doesn't need to be stressful. We have some tips to help you enjoy a smooth move from your old home to the new. With the right system in place, there is no need to be overwhelmed by the move.

Before you make the move, check out these 5 packing tips.

A common mistake people make when moving is to pack all of their belongings and move them, only to realize upon unpacking that many of the items should have been donated, sold, or thrown out. Before you pack, ruthlessly declutter your home. Packing things only to get rid of them at the new house is a waste of your time and money.

Some questions to ask yourself as you declutter before packing are:

As you pack and move, things are bound to get misplaced. To avoid the stress of a missing document or essential information, keep a folder (either physical, digital, or both) where you won't misplace it that is filled with essential paperwork. This might include:

Greg Dallaire - Green Bay Real Estate Expert says, "Be sure to set up any utilities in the new place to be turned on and ready when you arrive. Even if it means paying for utilities at two places for a brief overlap, it is often worth the convenience. In addition to basics like water and power, call ahead to make sure you will have internet, TV, and any other services you need."

This is also a great time to move additional services to the new address, like security, pest control, or house cleaning.

Even if you are moving all in one day from one Calgary home to another, don't count on being able to unpack everything you need on night one. Instead, pack a suitcase with a few days' worth of clothes and necessities for everyone in the house. This way, you can settle into your new home without scrambling to find a towel or toothbrush before spending your first night there.

The suitcase should include more than just your change of clothes and toiletries. Anything you might need for 2-3 days should be packed in it, including:

As you pack, or have your movers pack, label each box with not just the contents inside but the room it should be placed in at the new home. This way, whether you have professional movers, a team of friends and family, or just your own household, it will be easy to make sure each box lands in the proper place.

One of the easiest ways to do this is by color coding. Assign a color to each room and label accordingly. For example, let's say the kitchen is blue. All boxes that should be brought to the kitchen will be labeled with blue tape, and on move-in day you can hang a large blue paper in the kitchen. This simple system will make unpacking much smoother.

#5562. Fewer choices available to enrollees on ACA exchanges: RWJF

Fewer choices available to enrollees on ACA exchanges: RWJF" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

The number of regions where patients have limited choices for Affordable Care Act plans is on the rise, according to a new analysis.

The Robert Wood Johnson Foundation report found that for the 2027 plan year, there are more than 200 counties in which there is only one insurer available, and close to 1,000 where there are just two plans available for consumers to choose from.

This makes for an increase of 50% from the 2026 plan year, with more than a third of counties having limited options on the ACA's marketplaces for 2027.

Most states (39) will have at least one county where plan choices are limited for enrollees. For about half of these states, this is the norm and aligns with 2026, but for the rest, this marks a significant shift, the RWJF researchers wrote in the report.

"For the individual market as a whole, the decline in participation is sobering but not a fatal blow," per the report. "The presence of federal and some state subsidies provides an important backstop that will likely prevent a complete meltdown."

"Yet the prospect of a growing number of counties with little insurer participation is grim, and likely will not bode well for premium increases, morbidity or enrollment going forward," according to the report.

The foundation cites a recent analysis from Wakely that found the individual market declined by 16% in the first six months of 2026. The end of the enhanced premium tax credits, cost pressures and growing administrative burdens are likely to contribute to worsening trends in this space.

For instance, ACA marketplace exits from Cigna, CareSource and Medica are having a significant impact in Iowa and Indiana for the coming plan year, the researchers found. In the latter case, most Indiana counties have two or fewer plan choices.

However, there are some bright spots, RWJF researchers wrote. There are certain insurers participating in the exchanges who have beefed up their footprints, and there is a smattering of new entrants. Oscar Health, for example, is planning the largest growth, entering a new state and adding new counties in some of the states it already serves.

Some insurers, like Centene and UnitedHealthcare, are making strategic exits in some markets while entering others, for a neutral impact on their footprints overall.

Insurers like Antidote Health and Peak Health are also entering new regions—even if on a limited basis in some cases—which can help staunch the bleeding.

Blue Cross Blue Shield plans also often play a key role in limited markets, as in close to 80% of counties with a single insurer, that payer is a Blues plan. In addition, in 12% of counties, the single insurer is Elevance Health, which operates plans as Anthem Blue Cross Blue Shield.

"This suggests that were it not for the somewhat unique role of Blues plans as a backstop, the threat of a bare county might be higher," per the report. "Single-state Blues, in particular, are under social and political pressure to participate in much if not all of their state, and do not feel as free to exit unprofitable counties as are publicly traded insurers."

#5561. This simple habit is linked to a 33% lower risk of Alzheimer's

Reading for enjoyment may offer far more than entertainment. Whether someone prefers a classic Jane Austen novel or a Heartstopper graphic novel, research suggests that reading for pleasure is associated with better mental health, stronger empathy, and a lower risk of dementia.

Researchers at the University of Cambridge are working with The Queen's Reading Room, a charity established by Her Majesty The Queen, to raise awareness of these benefits across all age groups. Their collaboration is part of the National Year of Reading, an initiative encouraging more people to make reading part of their lives.

Cambridge psychiatry researchers Professor Barbara Sahakian and Dr. Christelle Langley began exploring the subject while writing their 2025 book, Brain Boost: Healthy Habits for a Happier Life. They discovered that reading for enjoyment was connected to a remarkably wide range of positive outcomes, yet the amount of research specifically examining these benefits was surprisingly limited.

In a review published in Psychological Medicine, Sahakian and Langley joined Vicki Perrin, CEO of The Queen's Reading Room, to examine the available evidence. Their findings suggest that the format and type of reading matter less than the enjoyment people get from it. They also highlight how reading together, whether through book clubs or parents sharing stories with children, can provide additional benefits.

Professor Sahakian said: "Reading is a great way to support our brain health, develop important cognitive skills and boost our well-being. It's something we ought to be encouraging from an early age, given the increasing evidence of its benefits, particularly to children, but really, it's never too late to start, and it can bring benefits throughout our lives and into old age."

Reading Early in Life Is Linked to Better Brain Development

Despite the growing evidence of its advantages, reading for enjoyment has become less common among young people. Surveys indicate that reading rates among children and teenagers have fallen to their lowest recorded levels, with particularly steep challenges among teenage boys and children from disadvantaged backgrounds.

Even children who are least enthusiastic about reading recognize that it can help them academically. Nearly half acknowledge that books and other reading materials can introduce them to unfamiliar words or teach them something new.

One of the most compelling studies examined more than 10,000 young people. Conducted by Sahakian, Langley, and their colleagues, the research found that children who started reading for pleasure at an early age tended to perform better in several important areas. These included attention, memory, and executive functioning, the mental abilities involved in planning, decision-making, and managing behavior.

Early readers also showed stronger academic performance, experienced fewer mental health problems, and were more likely to develop healthier daily routines. In particular, they tended to get more sleep and spend less time using screens.

Dr. Langley said: "Given how beneficial reading for pleasure is at a young age, we should be doing everything we can to introduce children and young people to reading. The important thing is to find something they'd really enjoy reading about - it might be a TV program or a game - and use this as a way in. Reading comics and graphic novels could also be a helpful introduction as they might be seen as less intimidating, maybe less boring, than novels."

The academic advantages may extend beyond language and literacy. Studies have also connected reading with stronger mathematical performance. Researchers suggest this relationship may arise because both activities rely on some of the same mental abilities, including language processing, memory, and executive function.

Just Five Minutes of Reading May Reduce Stress

The benefits of reading do not disappear after childhood. Among adults, surveys have associated reading for enjoyment with improved emotional well-being, greater relaxation, and reduced stress. Readers also tend to report more empathy, a deeper understanding of other people, and greater openness to viewpoints different from their own.

For many people, books are an especially appealing way to unwind. Reading ranks as the most popular approach to stress relief, with nearly two in five adults (38%) identifying it as their preferred way to relax.

A neuroscience study commissioned by The Queen's Reading Room in 2024 found that spending just five minutes reading fiction could lower stress by as much as 20%. The study also reported improvements in concentration and problem-solving abilities, along with a reduced sense of loneliness.

Books may even provide more comfort than some traditional relaxation habits. In one survey, more respondents said they turned to reading (35%) for comfort than to drinking wine (31%) or taking a hot bath (10%).

Reading Linked to Lower Dementia and Alzheimer's Risk

As people get older, the potential advantages of reading may become especially meaningful. Research has associated mentally stimulating leisure activities, including reading, with slower cognitive decline and a reduced likelihood of developing dementia.

One study followed nearly 5,500 adults aged 55 and older for five years. Participants who regularly took part in activities such as reading were significantly less likely to develop cognitive impairment during the study period.

Another investigation reported an even more striking association. People who read newspapers, magazines, and books had a 33% lower risk of Alzheimer's disease.

These findings suggest that keeping the mind engaged through reading may support cognitive health in later life. However, the researchers emphasize that most of the available studies identify associations rather than proving that reading itself prevents dementia.

How Reading May Change the Structure of the Brain

What could explain the many benefits associated with reading? Brain imaging research offers some intriguing clues.

Studies have identified differences in brain structure associated with reading, particularly in regions responsible for language, learning, emotional regulation, and executive control. These differences include greater brain volume and larger cortical areas in certain regions, as well as thicker cortex in areas important for language processing.

Researchers have also observed stronger connections within the brain's white matter, which helps different regions communicate and supports the processing of language.

Although much of this evidence is correlational, some research suggests that reading-related training can directly influence the brain's physical structure.

In one small study involving 11 children with dyslexia between the ages of 7 and 11, researchers tested an eight-week training program designed to strengthen reading abilities. The exercises involved mental imagery, articulation, and tracing letters, combinations of letters, and words.

Following the program, the children demonstrated significant improvements in reading skills. Brain scans also revealed increases in gray matter volume in important regions, providing evidence that reading interventions can be accompanied by measurable structural changes in the brain.

Why Reading Together May Offer Even Greater Benefits

Reading does not have to be a solitary activity. Researchers suggest that sharing books with other people can add a valuable social dimension, creating opportunities for connection and potentially improving both mental and physical well-being.

The Queen's Reading Room has made this idea a central part of its mission. Launched on social media in January 2021, the initiative originally provided a way for people to exchange book recommendations and stay connected during pandemic lockdowns.

It has since expanded into an international community reaching more than 12 million people across 184 countries. Through its flagship festival, neuroscience research, and other programs, the charity works to make reading a more prominent part of everyday life.

Its activities also extend to homeless shelters and domestic violence refuges, where shared reading is used as a therapeutic resource to help people during recovery.

The social connections created through reading groups may be particularly valuable for older adults, who can face increased isolation and reduced opportunities to participate in physically demanding activities.

Professor Sahakian said: "Shared reading groups and book clubs appear to provide additional benefits through social interaction. They can help people feel less isolated and more connected to others, which has been shown to reduce the risk of dementia.

"While these clubs can be fun and beneficial at any age, they're perfect for older people who may not be so mobile - they might not be able to go out as an exercise group or a cycling group, but a reading group is something most people can enjoy."

The researchers' overall message is that people can benefit from reading at any stage of life. Whether someone enjoys novels, newspapers, comics, or stories shared with friends, making time for reading may help support cognitive health, emotional well-being, and social connection.

Vicki Perrin, CEO of The Queen's Reading Room, added: "At The Queen's Reading Room, we have seen first-hand the transformative power of individual and shared reading to change lives. Books truly do make life better, and we're excited to do our bit to help everyone, everywhere, make more room for reading."

#5559. Catching up with the new CEO of UnitedHealthcare's Surest

Catching up with the new CEO of UnitedHealthcare's Surest" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Joe Clark is stepping into the CEO chair at UnitedHealthcare's Surest unit with an eye on affordability.

Clark was appointed to lead the division earlier this month, after serving as the chief financial officer for the insurer's employer and individual segment. In an interview with Fierce Healthcare, he said that the new role comes at "an exciting time" to be a part of a plan like Surest.

Under the model, Surest eliminates deductibles for a copayment-only approach, where members' costs are tied to the quality and value for their provider. Members connect to the Surest app or website to compare the cost between different providers.

"Affordability is a challenge every year, but especially right now, for employers," Clark said. "We've seen demand for Surest and other sort of alternative health plans just skyrocket over the last year. And being part of being able to deliver that and offer solutions to employers is incredibly exciting."

UnitedHealthcare first launched the unit in 2016 as Bind before rebranding as Surest in 2022 with an eye on growth. In a 2023 report, the company said that Surest members had 6% fewer emergency department visits and 13% fewer inpatient admissions compared to people enrolled in traditional commercial plans at the same company.

The plan also saw a 20% increase in visits to a physician and 9% increase in preventative physical exams compared to the members in traditional plans.

In a 2024 analysis, conducted by Aon, the company found that Surest enrollees generated $400 or more in cost claims savings per year. That study also identified improvements around spending and utilization across all age groups and accounting for several conditions.

Clark said that in a traditional health plan, only about 15% of people hit their deductible for the year, meaning they're ultimately not using their insurance during that time frame. Surest removes that problem by eliminating the deductible and puts the power in the consumers' hands to make choices for their own care.

He added that the Net Promoter Score for Surest is higher than its other commercial plan offerings. Consumers report satisfaction with the digital experience and the cost certainty that the plan presents, Clark said.

"It's very much like the Amazon shopping experience, but for healthcare, which hasn't happened before," Clark said.

Surest also aims to personalize the member experience by leaning on AI and other digital tools to present data on providers and costs that may be of use to the user, while leaving the ultimate decision in their hands.

"The consumer is in charge with their doctor in making those decisions," Clark said. "But we want to make sure that we are giving you, similar to what you would see with any shopping app, a personalized recommendation of what is a good fit."

Clark said that starting his career on the actuarial side of healthcare made plain how much of a challenge affordability can be, and that drew him to pursue his current path. Prior to UnitedHealthcare, he served as an associate partner at McKinsey and as an actuary at Cigna.

Through Surest, he believes he can help lead the charge toward a more modern healthcare system, he said.

As for the future of Surest, the first piece is continuing to make sure the team delivers on a personalized and simple-to-understand experience for consumers. The next level is building on that consumer-focused experience to add a provider layer, and work with them on the quality and value scores that are surfaced to members.

For example, a provider may consistently recommend a patient seek an MRI scan at a hospital rather than at a lower-cost lab. And Surest is gaining the "critical mass" of members where providers actively want to have these conversations, Clark said.

"I see that as sort of the next evolution beyond working with consumers and members: moving to providers as well," he said.

#5558. In a fertility advance, engineered molecular glue stabilizes chromosomes in aging eggs

We ranked the 25 most valuable publicly traded Chinese drugmakers

Megan covers the intersection of science and society. How is biomedical research funded? Who benefits? And how do new technologies reflect and shape our values? You can reach Megan on Signal at mmolteni.13.

Around the world, people are increasingly choosing to have babies later in life for reasons both social and economic. As they get older though, they face a mounting biological challenge: genetic errors caused by chromosomes failing to separate correctly. This phenomenon, known as aneuploidy, is the leading cause of age-related infertility, failed in-vitro fertilization (IVF) cycles, and miscarriage, and it increases dramatically around the age of 40. Studies have shown that between 50% and 80% of embryos from women in their 40s carry chromosomal abnormalities.

One of the main drivers of aneuploidy is the loss of a protein complex called cohesin, which acts like a molecular glue holding chromosomes together. In a new study, researchers at the Max Planck Institute for Multidisciplinary Sciences in Göttingen, Germany, engineered a novel protein system capable of restoring normal chromosome connections in aging mouse eggs. The study, published Thursday in Science, raises the possibility of one day developing such a system into a treatment that could reduce aneuploidy in human eggs used for IVF.

“There is still work ahead, but their proof of concept was highly successful,” said Rajiv McCoy, a biologist at Johns Hopkins University who was not involved in the work. McCoy’s lab is focused on pregnancy loss, the leading cause of which is aneuploidy. It is estimated that about half of all human conceptions are lost before birth, including the roughly 15% of known pregnancies that end in miscarriage. Technologies that could reduce the odds of miscarriage and expand women’s biological reproductive windows by addressing aneuploidy would have far-reaching consequences for the IVF industry and for society at large. “The stakes are very high,” McCoy said.

When a cell prepares to divide, its chromosomes replicate, forming two copies, or sister chromatids, that are all lined up and organized by a cellular winch system known as the spindle. Within the spindle, the sister chromatids are tethered to each other by cohesin — its ring-like structure traps DNA from both sisters inside it. In most cells, cohesin only has to do this work for a few hours before other enzymes cleave it apart, freeing the chromatids to separate into two new cells. But in oocytes, cohesin has to keep this bond going for decades.

That’s because female babies are born with all the oocytes they will ever have. And already at birth, those 1 to 2 million immature egg cells have begun to divide, and the cohesin’s job is only finished when fertilization occurs. That triggers the end of the division process called meiosis in which the egg cells eject half their genetic material so they can fuse with sperm to make an embryo.

Over all that time, the cohesin molecule doesn’t seem to be reloaded, said Melina Schuh, a director at the Max Planck Institute who led the new work.

For the last two decades, Schuh has been finding new ways of peering into egg cells to better understand how meiosis works and what happens when it goes awry. In 2015, her lab showed for the first time how the structures holding chromosomes together deteriorate in human eggs as they age. Not long after, Schuh began to wonder if they might be able to engineer a system of proteins that could step in and stabilize the chromosomes in older eggs. Over the last eight years, her team tested many different designs before settling on one that did everything they wanted it to.

Called TALhesins, the proteins are designed to attach to specific DNA regions near the centers of each chromosome, tethering them together. The research team also baked a deactivation switch into the TALhesin system —based on cohesin’s natural cleavage sites — so that it would automatically release the chromosomes only when fertilization occurs. In experiments with eggs from older mice, the team found that the TALhesin system reduced premature chromosome separation, increasing the proportion of eggs with properly connected chromatids from 47% to 74% — a level comparable to that found in young mice.

Schuh told STAT her lab has already taken the next step of adapting the TALhesin system to bind to chromosomes in human eggs. “We have initial signs that there is a positive effect on cohesion,” she said. “But what we have not done yet is to really test in human oocytes whether we can reduce errors by stabilizing the chromosomes.”

That’s a critical next step, said Eva Hoffman, a molecular geneticist at the University of Copenhagen, who was not involved in the work. After that, researchers would need to establish that this method for reducing aneuploidy doesn’t introduce other kinds of problems. “The clinical potential depends upon regulatory aspects including safety studies for embryonic development,” Hoffman said. Even with the long road ahead, she commended the German group for generating data that challenges the conventional view of aneuploidy as a condition impossible (or impractical) to intervene in. “Since cohesion is established during fetal life and has to be maintained for decades, its depletion over time was thought to be irreversible,” Hoffman said.

Efforts to address age-related ovarian infertility are long overdue. For older women struggling to get pregnant, currently the only solution that’s available to most patients is to try IVF over and over. (For women between 35 and 40, the odds of getting pregnant are about one in three IVF cycles; for women over 40 it drops to one in ten.) This is both expensive and inefficient, and online support groups are overflowing with heart-wrenching stories of women spending a fortune and years of their lives on failed fertility sagas.

Many clinics also offer a panoply of “add-ons” — experimental treatments with shaky scientific backing — to boost the odds of having a baby. Some clinics overseas have even begun to market mitochondrial replacement techniques (MRT), a controversial method for reducing the risk of mitochondrial disease transmission, as a potential solution for age-related ovarian infertility. A recent STAT investigation found that hundreds of women in their late 30s and 40s have traveled to clinics in the Ukraine, Albania, and other parts of the world seeking MRT to boost the odds of IVF, despite scant evidence that it can overcome issues of aneuploidy.

Schuh has co-founded a startup, Ovo Labs, in Munich and London that has licensed TALhesin from the Max Planck Institute and is trying to commercialize the technology. A key hurdle is that most eggs retrieved in IVF have already undergone the first meiotic division, so cohesin loss could have already caused chromosome errors that can no longer be fixed. While retrieving and treating immature eggs appears to prevent some of these earlier errors, this then requires maturation of eggs in lab dishes, which is not widely used and has its own drawbacks, including that many eggs fail to mature successfully. Shuh is hopeful they can establish a system where oocytes are removed and treated a bit earlier — during the first phase of meiosis — which would require less time and fewer steps to mature.

Ovo Labs has competition from a U.K.-based startup called U-Ploid, co-founded by Schuh’s Max Planck colleague and study co-author, Alexandre Webster. U-ploid’s approach is slightly different, designed to preserve a cell’s natural structures for keeping chromosomes together.

Its lead candidate, Lyvanta, is injected into immature eggs prior to IVF.

Last month, at the 2026 meeting of the American Society for Reproductive Medicine, U-Ploid reported results from a study using immature eggs donated by patients at six U.K. fertility clinics. The study found that 65.5% of eggs treated with Lyvanta matured without detectable chromosome errors, compared to 35.7% of untreated eggs in a control group. The effect appeared in donors both under and over the age of 35, however eggs in that study were not fertilized. Lyvanta has not yet been tested in patients or demonstrated the ability to improve pregnancy or live birth rates.
