#5557. Before Buying a Tiny Home on Amazon, Make Sure You Know the ABCs of ADUs

In recent years, social media has been flooded with videos of folks who’ve purchased a tiny home or accessory dwelling unit (ADU) on Amazon.

Touting to have dropped anywhere between $8,000 to $50,000, these homeowners shared the process of just buying a house with the click of a button, along with whatever else ended up in their carts.

But the reality is, Amazon actually prohibits the sale of habitable tiny homes and prefabricated dwellings. Its Seller Central policy explicitly banned complete prefab homes, tiny house kits marketed as living spaces, modular and container homes, and other factory-built housing units.

Despite that, you’re likely to still find listings for tiny homes on the platform, which makes it even more imperative that you learn the ABCs of ADUs.

To begin with, ADUs are additional small housing structures built on a property that already has a main home or main structure. Tiny homes are usually freestanding, compact units typically under 400 square feet—sometimes on foundations or other times on wheels like an RV.

But in both cases, the structures are economical and effective ways to achieve additional living space.

"As urban populations swell and sustainability becomes a central focus, the ability to build smaller, energy-efficient homes with reduced environmental impact will be key," says Paul Dashevsky, co-CEO of Maxable, a leader in ADU planning, building, and development.

But while tiny homes and ADUs may indeed be poised to make a positive impact toward solving the housing crisis, potential buyers need to know that you can't just plop one anywhere you please. Not to mention, tiny homes ordered online will probably also require hiring a contractor to help with assembly (adding to the overall cost).

With all that in mind, let's dig in to the details you must know prior to purchasing any ADU or tiny home. Because the last thing you want is to find yourself trying to return an entire house to sender.

While it can be exciting to imagine buying a "house" for $10,000 online, it's very important to not just look at the photos and think that's what will arrive. Read the fine print and all the reviews.

"Are you buying a complete tiny house that comes fully built, transported and rolled/craned into your backyard—or are you buying a bunch of parts that need to be assembled?" asks Dashevsy. "If assembly is required, make sure you first speak to a local contractor and determine the price of assembly."

Though some of the advertisements—like this two-story foldable container home—say they only require five people to assemble it in 30-minutes, are you really going to feel confident asking a couple friends over—with the promise of pizza and beer afterward—to get the job done?

The reality is that most people—unless they're cool with an adult-sized Lego project—will need a skilled contractor to assist with a tiny home or ADU build. Dashevsky suggests looking for a licensed general contractor with ADU experience. "You can find them through referrals or on sites like GreatBuildz, Angi, or Yelp," says Dashevsky.

As for the cost, it varies according to the type of tiny home or ADU.

"A brand new ADU built on your site will greatly depend on your region and the size of the ADU, but a good range is $80,000 to $400,000," says Dashevsky, though assembling a prefab ADU may run less predicated on its complexity.

Before you buy a prefab ADU or tiny home, you must make sure that the city or county you live in allows for such dwellings on your property.

You can start by doing an Internet search for this information. Look for your city’s planning or building department. Most will have a website, and you can probably glean some information there.

However, if you're seriously in the ready-to-buy stage, it's probably wise to visit one of these offices in person for a consultation. Make sure they allow the kind of tiny home or ADU you're considering on your property. Also confirm where you’re allowed to install it. And ask about any necessary permits, building codes, and occupancy requirements in your area.

"Essentially, you want to know every single guideline they have for this structure," says Dashevsky. "The last thing you want is a tiny home you have to sell or return because your city wont allow it."

Alternatively, you can hire a local architect who is experienced in ADUs—they should know all the city/county requirements for your location.

Unless you want to live in the dark with no water, you're going to need electrical and plumbing hookups for your tiny home or ADU. But some people who purchase a dwelling online neglect to consider those details in advance.

"A tiny home won’t do you much good if it isn’t connected to electrical power, water, and sewer at the very least," notes Dashevsky.

Speak with your local building department or utility providers to understand the process and costs to tie your tiny house in to municipal services. Or, if you have your own water well and septic tank, ask a contractor how much it will run to connect to these facilities.

For those who don't fully understand what this entails, connecting utilities to a tiny house or ADU is very similar to that for a normal house.

"You dig a trench from the location of the existing utilities—water, sewer, electrical gas—and run new pipes to the location of the new unit," says Dashevsky. "A general contractor can do this for you—this is not a DIY project— and it will probably cost around $10,000 to $20,000."

If your region is prone to weather events or natural disasters, you'll want to ensure that your tiny house has been tested to withstand extreme conditions.

"Is it rated to withstand snow, sleet, winds, earthquakes, hurricanes?" says Dashevsky. "There is no point spending a lot of money that gets wiped out in the first rainy season."

What exactly are you looking for when you're assessing a tiny home or ADU for purchase? Check to see if it says it's made of fire-resistant materials or has a fire rating (the best is a Class A or 1). Also see if it lists a wind rating—the Beaufort Wind Scale is most commonly used with levels ranging from 1 (light air) to 12 (hurricane winds). Finally, look for an earthquake resistance rating (0-9, like the Richter scale) or a Seismic Building Code. All of these will help give you an idea of the quality of the unit you're considering.

If you're having the ADU or tiny home built from scratch, it's a slightly different story as your contractor will be required to make sure it's up to code.

"ADUs are built under the same guiding building code—International Residential Code (IRC)—as principal houses and don't have any less requirements for seismic/hurricane/snow or structural bracing," says Jeremy Tetreault, of Four Brothers Design + Build in Washington, D.C. "They are treated with the same level of scrutiny and energy ratings, too, so you should have nothing to worry about from a standpoint of being less equipped to withstand natural events."

Getting insurance for your ADU or tiny home can sometimes be a hassle, so this is something to consider before buying an accessory unit.

Tiny homes—especially of the DIY or prefab variety—typically don't qualify for homeowners insurance policies. However, they may qualify for RV or mobile home insurance—especially if it's a tiny home on wheels (THOW)—as long as they meet building codes. The good news with this, however, is that you can often save 50% or more over regular homeowners insurance with a tiny home.

For people who have a tiny home on their property along with another home, or who build an ADU onto an existing home, it may be possible to insure the unit under the "other structures" portion of an existing homeowners policy.

The bottom line is you should speak with an insurance broker about what it will take to insure your ADU or tiny home since that will be an additional expense.

It's easy to get sucked into the idea that an ADU or a tiny home you can purchase online is a great deal! But it's important to be realistic about all the additional costs. We already mentioned the possibility of needing to hire a contractor to help with construction—and maybe a plumber and an electrician to hook up the utilities. But there are some other hidden costs of which potential buyers should also be aware.

To begin with, do you need to lay a foundation for your tiny home? If it's on wheels, then you can probably get away without one. But for people looking for a more permanent smaller housing situation, turning it into a tiny home on foundation (THOF) will give the structure more stability.

"Unless your tiny home is on wheels, it should sit on a concrete pad or foundation made of cement," says Dashevsky. "A general contractor can do this for you but expect a ballpark cost of about $5,000 to $15,000."

Also, if you purchase a home prebuilt but don't have room to roll it into the space where you plan to put it, you may need to pay for extra equipment. For example, if you have to "crane it in" then you need to factor in the price of hiring that service as well.

"The bottom line is that you really need to know all the costs involved, which are very likely to end up being close to double the Amazon 'price,'" says Dashevsky.

However, as long as you know what to expect, ordering up a tiny home or ADU can be a prime way to create an affordable housing solution.

Kimberly Dawn Neumann is a journalist based in New York City and the author of hundreds of articles on home-related topics for major publications, including Forbes, Real Simple, and Realtor.com. For more information, visit www.KDNeumann.com or IG @dancerscribe.

#5556. Scientists discover a hidden eye disease that slowly steals night vision

A newly identified genetic eye disease can gradually interfere with night vision and the ability to see objects at the edges of the visual field. The condition may be especially difficult to recognize because people can maintain good eyesight for much of their lives before noticeable problems develop.

An international research team, including scientists at the Scheie Eye Institute within the University of Pennsylvania's Perelman School of Medicine, traced the condition to a gene already associated with another form of vision loss. However, the two diseases affect eyesight in strikingly different ways. The previously known disorder primarily damages central vision, while the newly discovered condition affects peripheral vision and the ability to see in darkness.

Although the condition has not yet received an official name, researchers are calling it EFEMP1-associated late-onset retinal degeneration (L-ORD). It is linked to a specific genetic variant known as p.Arg140Trp in the EFEMP1 gene. This change causes an unusually thick accumulation of material between cells in the eye.

A Genetic Discovery That Began Decades Ago

The investigation traces back to 1998, when doctors documented an unusual pattern of vision loss in a family in the United States. As researchers uncovered new genetic evidence, they were able to connect those findings to families in Europe who showed similar symptoms.

The study, published in JAMA Ophthalmology, examined three unrelated families from different countries who carried the p.Arg140Trp variant. Their symptoms were compared with those of another family carrying a different change in the same gene, called p.Arg345Trp, which is associated with the previously recognized disease affecting central vision.

The international collaboration included researchers from Penn Medicine, the University of Edinburgh, the University of Basel, Charles University, and the University of Bonn.

At first, scientists suspected that the unusual symptoms in the original family might be caused by a different genetic disorder. Testing, however, failed to identify the variants responsible for that condition.

"The different disease expression in this family was thought to be similar to a condition caused by C1QTNF5 gene variants. However, none of the variants associated with that disease were found," said Artur V. Cideciyan, PhD, an ophthalmology researcher and co-director of the Center for Hereditary Retinal Degenerations. "Our collaborators then discovered a new variant in the EFEMP1 gene that normally causes a different disease where the macula, which is tied to central vision, is affected first."

How the New Eye Disease Affects Night Vision

The researchers found that the newly identified condition develops gradually in the outer regions of the retina. Located at the back of the eye, the retina detects incoming light and transforms it into signals that the brain uses to create visual images.

Unlike the previously known EFEMP1 disorder, which initially affects the macula and central vision, this newly identified disease begins in the peripheral retina. People may see normally for much of their lives before gradually noticing that their side vision is narrowing or that seeing in dim surroundings has become more difficult.

Problems may be particularly noticeable around dusk or at night, when the eyes must rely more heavily on specialized light-sensitive cells called rods.

One reason the disease is challenging to diagnose is that these cells may initially show no visible structural damage. The gradual progression of symptoms can make the condition even harder to recognize.

However, the researchers identified a potentially valuable early clue. In affected individuals, rod cells take unusually long to recover when the eyes move from bright surroundings into darkness. This abnormal response can be detected even when the retina still appears structurally normal.

"We can detect a major abnormality in the way rod photoreceptors recover in darkness with retinas that still look structurally intact," Cideciyan said. "This gives us a functional marker of disease at a stage when photoreceptor cells have not yet been lost."

The finding suggests that changes in how the retina functions may reveal the disease before the light-sensitive cells responsible for vision begin to disappear.

What the Discovery Could Mean for Age-Related Vision Loss

An important question remains unanswered: How many people carry this newly identified genetic variant?

Researchers suspect the condition is relatively uncommon, but they do not yet have enough information to determine its prevalence. Larger investigations will be necessary to establish how frequently the variant occurs and how many people may be affected.

Beyond identifying another inherited eye disorder, the findings could help scientists better understand why vision deteriorates with age. Studying rare genetic diseases can reveal biological processes that may also contribute to much more widespread retinal conditions.

"Aging is a risk factor for many medical conditions, including retinal diseases such as age-related macular degeneration, the most common retinal condition of aging," said Tomas S. Aleman, MD, a professor of ophthalmology and the other co-director of the Center for Hereditary Retinal Degenerations. "Lessons learned from these infrequent, late-onset genetic eye diseases offer glimpses at possible mechanisms of disease for much more frequent retinal problems."

By revealing how different changes in a single gene can produce distinct patterns of vision loss, the research adds to scientists' understanding of inherited retinal disease. It also highlights the potential importance of detecting changes in visual function before damage becomes apparent in the retina's structure.

The study received support from the University of Edinburgh Chancellor's Fellowship award, RS Macdonald Charitable Trust Seedcorn Award, the BrightFocus Foundation (M2024009N), the German Research Foundation (532367710), the Medical Research Council (MC_UU_00035/9, MC_UU_00007/10), the Swiss National Science Foundation (204285), the Ministry of Health of the Czech Republic (NW24-06-00083), Charles University in Prague (UNCE/24/MED/022 and SVV 2600631), and the Samuel G. Jacobson, MD, PhD, Memorial Fund.

#5555. Opinion: Montana’s ‘right to try’ law makes patients responsible for bearing costs — and risks

We ranked the 25 most valuable publicly traded Chinese drugmakers

Miner is a behavioral and social scientist at RAND. James is an associate policy researcher at RAND.

In July, Montana became the first state to license clinics to offer patients who are not terminally ill drugs and devices that the Food and Drug Administration has not approved. Supporters call state Senate bill 535 a first-in-the-nation expansion of the “right to try.” Critics say it lets patients, including medical tourists from other states, pay out of pocket for unproven therapies. They are both right, in different ways. While the expansion of access to experimental treatments may provide patients with hope, the risks that patients may pay high costs for ineffective and even unsafe treatments remain high.

The goal is to expand access to experimental therapies, with stem cell, anti-aging therapies, and biologics being likely use cases. But the law leaves major questions unanswered: How much will patients pay? Who will bear the cost if complications arise later? And, because these therapies are being used outside a rigorous research setting, how will anyone know whether they actually work?For patients, a primary concern is likely to be cost. SB535 makes patients financially responsible for the experimental treatment — with the price set by the company supplying the drug or device. The required patient agreement must describe “all the anticipated costs” of the treatment itself. But patients will likely face additional costs, including travel to Montana for those out of state, and follow-up care.

Patients are also, in theory, responsible to pay out of pocket for medical care related to any complications — they are not supposed to go through their insurance companies. But how will insurers determine if a medical problem stems from an experimental treatment? That’s left ambiguous by the law. Long-term medical effects will be particularly hard to trace, especially if a product hasn’t yet had robust safety testing and documentation of its long-term side effects. Thus, care for complications may fall on patients, or it may be paid by insurers who had no say in the use of an experimental treatment.

And how are people to judge whether a treatment is worth its price? For approved therapies, there’s trial data on survival rates, plus continued post-market study. These data help clarify the expected benefits for specific patients. SB535 does not require companies to conduct comparable analyses, nor are companies bound to set prices with any value framework in mind.

Proponents of SB535 argue that skipping costly trials will lower development costs and, eventually, prices. However, if companies wish to generate evidence for conventional FDA approval, they will need to go beyond the requirements in SB535. If they fail to collect detailed patient characteristics such as history of disease and patient demographics, it will be hard to determine how the drug might work in a larger patient population. Supporters say the data will resemble real-world evidence, but the validity of real-world evidence still depends on clear study methods and consistent data collection and reporting.

It’s also possible that SB535 could undermine the rigorous testing needed for FDA approval. That’s because SB535 does not require the same patient protections, data collection requirements, or oversight that the FDA requires. Some companies may forgo the clinical trial FDA pathway entirely, while others may find that direct access disincentivizes patients from enrolling in trials.

None of this means patients with few options for treatment should be dismissed or ignored. But they can make an informed decision about how much to pay for treatment only if the true costs and risks are visible. Montana currently has no systematic way to assess how patients interpret costs, what they actually incur and pay, or how those costs relate to short- and long-term outcomes.

If other states want to expand access to experimental treatment, there are other models they could look to, such as CMS’s Coverage with Evidence Development. It requires systematic collection and reporting of data on clinical effectiveness and short- and long-term harms.

States could also require companies to collect data on outcomes for 15 years, just like the FDA does for cell and gene therapies. These types of data can enable transparency and may help patients make informed decisions about potential treatments in consultation with their care team.

Montana can still move in that direction by requiring standardized cost disclosure before consent, a registry with defined long-term follow-up, and independent evaluation of financial and clinical outcomes.

Without those steps, we will not know whether state right to try laws can be a cost-effective way to generate evidence and access to emerging therapeutics. Patients who try may be left physically and financially vulnerable, with little knowledge gained from their risk.

Skye A. Miner is a behavioral and social scientist at RAND, a nonprofit, nonpartisan research institution. She specializes in the ethics of emerging technologies. Hannah O. James is an associate policy researcher at RAND who researches the value of U.S. health care spending and state-level health policies.

#5554. Weekly Rundown: Waystar integrates into Google Cloud’s Gemini for healthcare; Oracle debuts AI agents for clinical trials

Weekly Rundown: Waystar integrates into Google Cloud’s Gemini for healthcare; Oracle debuts AI agents for clinical trials" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Stay up to date on the latest in health tech, digital health and health AI news with this weekly brief. Read below for news from the week of Nov. 16 to 27.

Waystar said Tuesday it will integrate its AI-driven revenue cycle solutions into Google Cloud’s recently announced Gemini for healthcare solution.

The integration reflects an expanded partnership between Waystar and Google Cloud. Through it, users will have increased access to Waystar AltitudeAI innovations, advanced analytics and revenue cycle insights.

“By bringing Waystar's AI-powered revenue cycle capabilities into Gemini for healthcare, we're helping providers simplify some of the most complex operational and financial tasks in care delivery,” said Aashima Gupta, Google Cloud managing director of healthcare, in a statement. “Together, we are unifying data and workflows in a secure, governed workspace that drives better outcomes across the healthcare ecosystem.”

OpenAI is expanding ChatGPT’s health capabilities across various channels, it said Thursday.

The company’s Health feature is expanding to desktop app, Androids and its personal AI agents—dubbed dots.

ChatGPT Health is currently available to Free, Go, Plus, and Pro users in the U.S., while dots are available to Pro users.

Oracle launched a new agentic experience for life science organizations to improve clinical trial operations.

Oracle Life Science AI Agents is currently available for early adopters with a focus on portfolio monitoring, trial planning and conduct. The company plans to expand into clinical development domains, including data management, post-trial analytics and trial design.

Agents are designed to work with human oversight, executives say.

Oracle Health and Life Sciences EVP and General Manager Seema Verma said in a statement clinical development requires companies to “coordinate complex operational activity.”

“We are bringing AI-assisted intelligence into clinical trial operations to help organizations to monitor performance, identify emerging risks, and coordinate responses across the trial lifecycle,” Verma said. “By combining Oracle’s Life Sciences applications, AI-assisted capabilities, connected data services, on a secure, scalable cloud infrastructure, we are helping organizations coordinate clinical research workflows and operational decisions across their clinical trial environments.”

Agentic company Artera announced the roll out of an intake solution using AI Agents to collect, check and complete information throughout the patient visit.

Artera Intake has three core workflows, executives say: pre-visit intake, in-office and walk-in intake and complex form and consent digitization. The workflows are housed in a new Intake Hub, according to the Nov. 19 announcement.

Chief Product and Strategy Officer Zach Wood said in a statement what differentiates the solution from others is “where it starts.”

“Most intake solutions are built first, and providers have to change their workflows to fit them,” Wood said. “We start with the provider. We learn how their teams and patients actually move through intake, then build the agentic solution around that, together.”

Wood continued, “That starting point shapes everything that follows, and is designed to drive faster adoption, more completed intake and real value for practices.”

Amazon Connect Health announced Nov. 17 the launch of expanded patient access capabilities through the agentic solution.

As of the date of the announcement, four new capabilities are generally available to users: appointment management, prescription management, information assistance and password reset.

The company says the expansion builds on the foundation of Amazon Connect Health, which included patient verification, patient insights, ambient documentation and more.

One health system using the tool is Philadelphia-based Temple Health. AVP of Patient Access Joseph Alfonsi said in a statement the tool has handled patient verification on thousands of calls weekly since the system went live in June.

“Building on that success, we’re excited to expand agentic patient access capabilities for prescription management, portal password resets, and information assistance,” Alfonsi said. “Our patients shouldn’t have to wait until business hours—or wait on hold—to manage routine tasks. Now they can verify once and take care of everyday needs in a single call, any time of day, and our team can focus on the conversations where a human touch matters most.”

#5553. Pregnancy is the ‘perfect storm’ for eating disorders, but doctors keep missing them

We ranked the 25 most valuable publicly traded Chinese drugmakers

Reporting for this story was supported by the Pulitzer Center.

REISTERSTOWN, Md. — Katye Jorgensen had been fighting anorexia and bulimia for years when she got pregnant at 25. Weigh-ins at prenatal appointments filled her with dread and certain foods terrified her, but she powered through for her baby’s sake. Then she struggled to breastfeed her son and lose weight after giving birth, and her mental health deteriorated.

After her second pregnancy two years later, Jorgensen became obsessive about exercise and fixated on comments about how well she was “bouncing back.” At her husband’s urging, she started seeing a therapist and a dietitian. Eventually, they staged an intervention and she agreed to enter intensive treatment, which she said saved her life.

“I went to my postpartum appointment, I mentioned a lot of this, and even though I really liked those doctors, it still didn’t set off any red alarms for anybody,” said Jorgensen, who is now 37.

Jorgensen is one of many women who struggle with eating disorders before and after childbirth but slip through the cracks of the U.S. health care system. Research suggests about 4.3% of pregnant women and more than 9% of new mothers experience eating disorders such as anorexia nervosa, bulimia nervosa, or binge eating disorder, though research is limited and no one knows their exact toll.

Those rates are on par with national averages: an estimated 2.6% to 8.4% of women will experience an eating disorder over their lifetimes — that’s up to 14.6 million women and girls in the United States.

Eating disorders have been linked to health issues for pregnant women — including miscarriage, high blood pressure, anemia, and bleeding — and complications for their developing babies, including small head circumference, low birthweight, autism, and asthma. After birth, women with a history of eating disorders appear more likely to experience postpartum depression and anxiety and to report problems feeding their newborns.

The risks vary by eating disorder. Studies don’t prove that eating disorders directly cause these issues and not everyone with a perinatal eating disorder will experience them. Still, the evidence is enough to worry clinicians.

“If we don’t treat these disorders … there are risks involved there. This isn’t a neutral situation,” said Leah Graves, a registered dietitian and a clinical adviser at the National Eating Disorders Association.

Few screening tools have been validated for eating disorders in pregnancy, and none are widely used. Obstetricians typically receive very little training about these conditions, leaving them unequipped to identify or manage eating disorders. And even with a diagnosis, many pregnant women and new mothers don’t receive timely treatment due to spotty insurance coverage and a shortage of local specialists, according to research and interviews with more than a dozen eating disorder researchers, doctors, dietitians, therapists, policy advocates, and mothers.

“It’s been a huge gap,” said Elizabeth Claydon, an associate professor at West Virginia University who researches eating disorders. “People have had this; they’ve lived with eating disorders during pregnancy. We just haven’t caught them and been able to help.”

Eating disorders usually develop in adolescence or young adulthood, but they can also emerge around pregnancy, menopause, or other periods of profound physical and life change.

Several factors can raise the risks in pregnancy: the feeling of a lack of control, rapid physical and hormonal changes, negative body image, scrutiny of the pregnant person’s diet and weight for medical reasons, the need to consume extra calories to breastfeed, a new identity and family role, and societal pressure to return to pre-pregnancy weight and succeed at motherhood.

Many women struggle with body image issues or unhealthy thoughts or behaviors around food, weight, or exercise that don’t meet the criteria for a clinical diagnosis. Pregnancy can tip the scales into an active eating disorder.

Pregnancy can also hide symptoms that overlap with eating disorders, such as nausea, vomiting, appetite changes or pumping breast milk specifically to burn calories, said Christine Call, an assistant professor of psychiatry at the University of Pittsburgh.

But many women hide their symptoms, making it difficult for doctors, or even family members, to know when someone needs help.

There’s no single trajectory in the perinatal period. Some women with eating disorders fare better during pregnancy and sustain that recovery, while others relapse once their child is born. Other women, years into recovery, see their eating disorders come roaring back in pregnancy or postpartum. Some struggle throughout pregnancy, with no respite. And others develop an eating disorder for the first time in the perinatal period.

“There’s so much shame and guilt about eating and doing things right, taking care of yourself for your baby during this period,” Call said.

Jennifer Kreatsoulas was diagnosed with anorexia 15 years before her first pregnancy, but her eating disorder “came back with a vengeance” after her second child was born, alongside postpartum depression. She decided to seek treatment when she realized she was too weak to push a stroller while out on a Mother’s Day walk with her husband and 1-year-old daughter.

“It’s destructive, but I was really trying to cope, and my brain just switched back to what it knew how to do from all those years previous,” said Kreatsoulas, now 50 and living in Pennsylvania. She attributes her relapse to “hormones, lack of sleep, complete overwhelm, your identity becoming something that you don’t know — you lose yourself in it, just because that’s what’s demanded as a mother.”

In a recommendation buried in a 2019 opinion on obesity bias, the ethics committee of the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists suggests that OB-GYNs assess all their patients, pregnant or not, for eating disorders. And it recommends that all pregnant and postpartum patients be screened for anxiety and depression — as does the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force.

But ACOG’s clinical guidance on perinatal mental health doesn’t cover eating disorders, and the organization has no guidance on how to screen for or manage them during pregnancy and after birth.

“Providers don’t see it because we’re not looking for it,” said Danielle Prentice, a maternal-fetal medicine specialist at Oregon Health & Science University and a member of ACOG’s nutrition expert group.

Some states have expanded maternal mental health screening in recent years, but without a clinical standard on perinatal eating disorders, policymakers have had little to go on. In Massachusetts — where Lindsay Clancy’s high-profile murder trial drew public outrage over the inadequacy of postpartum mental health care in the U.S. — state officials recently said they would increase screening and support for depression, anxiety, bipolar spectrum disorder, obsessive-compulsive disorder, post-traumatic stress disorder, and postpartum psychosis.

Eating disorders were excluded because the state followed ACOG’s published guidance to decide which perinatal mental health conditions to include, according to a spokesperson for the Massachusetts Executive Office of Health and Human Services.

“Providers who have concerns about a patient’s eating behaviors, nutrition, body image, weight-related behaviors, or history of an eating disorder should use their clinical judgment and conduct or refer for further assessment as appropriate,” the spokesperson said via email.

Existing eating disorder screening tools may not be suitable for pregnant or postpartum patients. The most common one, known as the SCOFF (“Sick-Control-One Stone-Fat-Food”), has five questions, including: “Have you recently lost more than 14 pounds in a 3-month period?”

Researchers have also warned that eating disorder screening tools tend to be centered on white body ideals, suggesting they may miss women of color and feed into biases about who is at risk. Studies indicate Black women experience eating disorders, particularly binge eating, at rates similar to white women, but are less likely to be diagnosed or treated. Eating disorder experts say the “SWAG” stereotype — skinny, white, affluent girl — of eating disorder patients prevents clinicians from recognizing eating disorders in anyone who doesn’t fit that mold.

“People of color [and] trans people are not seen as having an eating disorder as an option, especially in pregnancy,” said Jessica Wilson, a registered dietitian in California.

Ideally, West Virginia University’s Claydon said, screening for eating disorders should become a standard part of perinatal health care. If the screener flags a potential eating disorder or worrisome symptoms, the patient could be referred to an expert for a final diagnosis.

Yet persuading obstetricians to adopt another screening tool could be a challenge. Screening at the six-week postpartum checkup can feel like a perfunctory exercise, though maternal mental health issues can emerge or linger much longer.

“They give you the questionnaire, which is really more like, ‘Do you want to hurt yourself or somebody else? No? OK, cool, bye.’ That’s it,” Jorgensen said.

Screening may identify a patient in need of support, but that doesn’t mean resources or specialists are available.

“Universal screening is only effective if there’s treatment,” said Marianna Thomeczek, a researcher at the University of Kansas who is developing a postpartum screening tool for Black women.

Women with an active or recent eating disorder can have complex medical needs during pregnancy, Prentice said. They may need supplementation to address nutritional deficiencies, preconception folic acid to support fetal development and prevent birth defects, and extra ultrasounds to monitor the baby’s growth, she said.

Pregnancy may also prompt women to seek eating disorder treatment, which typically calls for therapy paired with care from a doctor and dietitian, according to the American Psychiatric Association. It ranges from regular appointments to intensive day programs, residential treatment, or hospitalization, depending on how sick a patient is and her specific condition.

Health coverage can be a major barrier. Many private insurers cover visits with dietitians for patients with eating disorders, but dietitians say claims are often denied, and plans may limit the number of visits or require copays patients can’t afford, especially while preparing for a new baby. Specialized eating disorder dietitians may be out-of-network.

To get more intensive care, women often have to prove medical necessity, said Ashley Moser, a clinical education specialist at The Renfrew Center, one of the country’s oldest eating disorder treatment facilities. Pregnancy can help make the case, but it’s still difficult.

Access to care is even more difficult for low-income women who rely on Medicaid. Only 22 state Medicaid programs allow registered dietitian-nutritionists to bill independently for adult medical nutrition therapy. And while there are 384 eating disorder centers offering intensive treatment in the U.S., only about 25% accept Medicaid coverage, according to a study published earlier this year. Five states have no treatment centers at all.

There’s very little evidence about what works to prevent eating disorders or their relapse during pregnancy. Researchers in Massachusetts are currently testing whether peer group support and cognitive dissonance exercises can help, modeled on a longstanding program for teenage girls and young women called The Body Project. Early results, published this month, are promising, but bigger studies are needed to prove it actually works.

Pregnant women can also ask their doctors to adjust routine practices they find triggering. During Jorgensen’s third and final pregnancy, she pushed for blind weigh-ins and asked doctors not to relay her blood sugar levels unless there was a problem.

Overall, clinicians, researchers, and mothers said that as maternal mental health receives more national attention, perinatal eating disorders should as well. Partners and families should know the risks, they said, to help ensure women feel safe speaking up rather than suffering alone.

“We need to change the system, we need to change the policies, but women also need to know that they’re not alone in experiencing this,” Claydon said. “It’s not an unusual thing to occur during pregnancy, because it is that perfect storm.”

Gabriela Galvin is a freelance journalist in London who covers health and social policy. In 2025, she was awarded a European Press Prize.

#5552. A common blood pressure drug has a surprising effect on calorie-burning brown fat

A widely used blood pressure medication may have an unexpected benefit beyond its ability to control hypertension. Scientists have found that losartan can activate brown fat, a specialized type of body fat that burns energy, and improve metabolic activity in mice. The discovery suggests that an existing medication could potentially be repurposed to stimulate brown fat and support metabolic health.

Losartan belongs to a class of medications called angiotensin receptor blockers (ARB), which have an established safety profile. In a new study published in Nature, researchers found that the drug increased brown fat activity through a biological mechanism separate from its blood pressure effects. This raises the possibility of developing treatments that activate brown fat without lowering blood pressure.

The findings also revealed a surprising connection between brown fat and mental health. After examining data from more than 100,000 patients, researchers discovered that people with detectable brown fat had lower rates of several medical conditions, including anxiety and depression. This is the first time the research team has reported associations between brown fat and psychiatric health, adding to earlier evidence linking the tissue to better cardiovascular and metabolic health.

The research was led by Paul Cohen at Rockefeller University's Laboratory of Molecular Metabolism, working with Heiko Schöder and Daniel Lafontaine from Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (MSKCC). It expands on research published in 2021, when Cohen's team analyzed approximately 50,000 patients and found that those with more brown fat had substantially lower odds of developing cardiometabolic conditions such as coronary artery disease and type II diabetes.

"We only looked for a few diagnostic codes in that study, mainly focusing on cardiovascular disease since that's what this tissue has historically been associated with," says Cohen. "The scope of this new analysis is far more expansive. We doubled our number of patients and considered more than 500 codes, which allowed us to unearth many new insights."

AI Analysis Reveals New Benefits of Brown Fat

To investigate brown fat's relationship with human health, the researchers examined PET/CT scans from more than 100,000 patients who had undergone imaging as part of their cancer monitoring. They focused on scans showing brown adipose tissue, which can be found in six regions of the body, including the neck, armpits, and areas around organs such as the heart and kidneys.

The team used an approach known as reverse translation, which begins with observations in patients and then investigates the biological processes responsible for them. Cohen's laboratory has previously used this strategy to uncover important details about brown fat and its effects on health.

Nicolás Gómez-Banoy, the study's first author and an endocrinologist and instructor in clinical investigation in Cohen's laboratory, used a machine learning system developed by researchers at MSKCC to measure brown fat activity. The technology allowed him to assess both the total activity in each patient and the activity within each of the six anatomical regions.

The analysis showed that brown fat's location could be just as important as its presence. Activity in particular regions appeared to have stronger associations with certain health conditions, suggesting that brown fat may influence the body differently depending on where it is found.

"For example, the axillary, or armpit, area was linked to a decreased risk of high blood pressure compared to other regions," he says. "But overall, patients with brown fat have better glycemic parameters, lipid profiles, and echocardiographic indices, as well as lower inflammatory markers."

These findings indicate that people with brown fat tend to have healthier blood sugar levels, blood fat profiles, measures of heart function, and indicators of inflammation.

Common Blood Pressure Drug Activates Brown Fat

As the researchers investigated medications associated with brown fat activity, they noticed an intriguing pattern. Patients taking angiotensin receptor blockers were more likely to have detectable brown fat on their scans, suggesting that these widely prescribed medications might influence the tissue.

To explore that possibility, the team conducted laboratory experiments using cultured brown fat cells. They found that losartan directly increased the cells' metabolic activity, providing evidence that the drug could stimulate brown fat rather than simply being associated with its presence.

Even more interestingly, the researchers discovered that losartan activated brown fat through molecular pathways different from those responsible for lowering blood pressure. That distinction could be especially valuable for developing future medications that target metabolism without interfering with normal blood pressure regulation.

"The fact that its different effects are mediated by different molecular pathways is advantageous, since it means we could potentially isolate them in future therapies," says Gómez-Banoy. "That way you would be able to stimulate brown fat in people with normal blood pressure."

Additional experiments in healthy mice strengthened the findings. Animals given losartan showed increased energy expenditure, consumed more oxygen, and produced more carbon dioxide, all signs of heightened metabolic activity. Despite these changes, their body weight remained stable.

Brown Fat's Surprising Connection to Mental Health

Beyond its metabolic effects, brown fat may have a previously unrecognized relationship with psychological well-being. The patient analysis revealed that individuals with detectable brown fat had lower rates of anxiety and depression, extending the tissue's potential health associations beyond the cardiovascular system.

"We know that metabolically healthy people tend to have lower incidence of psychiatric diseases, so it could be that having brown fat makes you more metabolically healthy, and this correlates with fewer psychiatric issues," says Gómez-Banoy.

The researchers also found an intriguing relationship involving selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, or SSRIs, medications commonly prescribed to treat depression. These drugs appeared to suppress brown fat activity, suggesting another possible connection between psychiatric treatments and metabolic regulation.

However, the findings do not suggest that brown fat is beneficial in every respect. The analysis also identified higher rates of osteoporosis and certain skin diseases among people with brown fat, raising questions about possible trade-offs that require further investigation.

The discoveries have opened several avenues for future research. Scientists hope to examine the genetics of people with particularly high brown fat activity, investigate why the tissue is associated with lower rates of anxiety and depression, and determine whether its apparent benefits can be harnessed safely.

Losartan may also be only one of several existing medications worth investigating. The extensive patient analysis identified additional drugs associated with brown fat activity, offering researchers a range of potential candidates for future studies.

"There were plenty of other medications associated with brown fat activity in our large cohort," Cohen notes. "This is just a start."

#5551. Rural communities face heavier chronic disease burden, increasing pressure on PCPs: athenaInstitute

Rural communities face heavier chronic disease burden, increasing pressure on PCPs: athenaInstitute" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Millennials living in rural areas have 42% more documented chronic conditions on average compared to those in other environments, a new report from athenaInstitute found.

And, millennials in rural communities are 47% more likely to have at least two chronic conditions. This heavier chronic disease burden extends to other generations as well, analysts note.

Half of Baby Boomers (50.4%) in rural areas have three or more documented conditions, which the report says is “on par” with non-rural individuals in the Silent and Greatest generations.

The 2026 Rural Ambulatory Care Report (PDF) analyzed athenahealth network data from 12.3 million rural patients between 2021 and 2025, along with more than 30,000 clinicians and 1,861 rural practices across the U.S. It examined factors such as appointment activity, workforce composition, payments, and more.

Athenahealth CMO and athenaInstitute co-chair Nele Jessel, M.D., said in a statement the findings show that while rural practices are not “standing still in the face of enormous challenges,” there are “limits to how much more they can absorb as patient needs continue to grow.”

“They are adapting how they deliver care and finding ways to keep patients connected to the care they need,” Jessel said. “With renewed focus on rural healthcare, there is a real opportunity to build on what is working by investing in the workforce, technology and models of care that can help these practices continue serving the communities that depend on them.”

Primary care physicians in rural areas have to wear multiple hats, as specialty care needs at practices are higher in rural communities.

The report found that primary care handles 68.7% of visits involving anxiety or depression diagnoses versus 55.1% in non-rural areas. Moreover, 25% of rural patients with documented anxiety or depression had a substance use disorder—up from 19.8% in non-rural communities.

Data shows rural and non-rural healthcare practices collected roughly the same share of what they were owed by insurers in 2025, but analysts note a difference in patient balances.

Rural practices collected about $70 of every $100 owed, while non-rural practices collected about $78—which analysts say is about a 10% gap.

Another potential source of financial vulnerability for rural practices is Medicaid. Medicaid covered 27.5% of rural visits, which analysts note leaves these practices more exposed to eligibility changes set to begin in 2027.

#5549. Mortgage Rates Dip, Offering Moderate Relief to Buyers Ahead of Thanksgiving as Fed Rate Hike Looms

Mortgage rates have pulled back this week as AI investment trade creates volatility in financial markets and Treasury yields fall back below 5%.

The average rate on 30-year fixed home loans dropped to 7.21% for the week ending Nov. 25, down 7 basis points from 7.28% recorded the week before, according to Freddie Mac. For perspective, rates averaged 6.26% one year ago.

“Mortgage rates moved back down this week, offering modest relief for prospective homebuyers heading into the Thanksgiving holiday,” says Sam Khater, Freddie Mac's chief economist.

It is all but guaranteed that the Federal Reserve will raise its benchmark rate to curb inflation at the next Federal Open Market Committee meeting on Dec. 8.

The looming hike, combined with the persistence of the war in Iran, pushed the 10-year Treasury yield back toward 4.816% this week, putting mortgage rates on an upward trajectory once again.

The AI investment trade has created volatility in financial markets as investors try to value companies, including the Anthropic IPO, which gave the company a valuation greater than the value of every home currently listed for sale.

AI-generated wealth is already shaping consumer housing behavior, with San Francisco Bay Area buyers and those in other tech hubs leaning toward higher down payments.

Markets are currently pricing a 97.6% chance of a 25-basis-point increase next month, according to the CME FedWatch tool.

Meanwhile, pending home sales fell to a record low in October, and existing-home sales hit their lowest level since 2010, as the surge in mortgage rates through mid-October took its toll on buyers and sellers.

For buyers who remain active in the market, current conditions offer some meaningful advantages, including less competition from other shoppers, inventory climbing 8.6% year over year, and sellers increasingly willing to negotiate on price.

This week, the median listing price fell 2.4% from a year ago to $400,000, according to the latest Realtor.com weekly housing market update.

"The challenge is that until inflation cools enough to put mortgage rates on a durable downward path, affordability will remain the dominant constraint on the market," says Realtor.com® senior economist Anthony Smith.

Your credit score plays a role when you apply for a mortgage. A credit score will determine whether you qualify for a mortgage and the interest rate you'll receive. The higher the credit score, the lower the interest rate you'll qualify for.

The credit score you need will vary depending on the type of loan. A score of 620 is a "fair" rating. However, people applying for a Federal Housing Administration loan might be able to get approved with a credit score of 500, which is considered a low score.

Homebuyers with credit scores of 740 or higher are typically considered to be in very good standing and can usually qualify for better rates, which can reduce monthly payments.

Tristan Navera is a senior reporter on housing policy, covering trends and solutions in the housing market from Washington, DC. He was previously a senior reporter at Bloomberg Law, and before that covered real estate for the Washington Business Journal. Earlier in his career, he spent a decade reporting on business and real estate in Dayton and Columbus, OH. A Cincinnati native, he holds a journalism degree from Ohio University.

#5547. For better mental health, how often you exercise may matter more than how hard

How often you exercise may matter more for your mental health than how hard you push yourself during a workout. A large study of Norwegian college students found that those who exercised less frequently were more likely to experience depression and anxiety one year later. The findings suggest that maintaining a consistent exercise routine could be particularly important for supporting mental well-being.

The research, published in the open access journal PLOS One, was conducted by Michael Grasdalsmoen of Western Norway University of Applied Sciences and his colleagues. Their results point to the potential benefits of exercising regularly rather than focusing primarily on longer or more demanding workouts.

Why Exercise Habits Matter for Mental Health

Depression, anxiety, and other common mental health conditions are among the leading causes of disability in young adults worldwide. The college years can be an especially challenging period as students adjust to new academic, social, and personal responsibilities. Identifying everyday behaviors that may help protect mental health is therefore an important research priority.

Although previous research has linked regular physical activity to better psychological well-being, many young adults remain physically inactive. Scientists have also had relatively limited evidence about how exercise habits relate to the development of mental health conditions over time, particularly when those conditions are evaluated using standardized diagnostic tools.

To investigate this relationship, Grasdalsmoen and his team followed 10,460 full-time students enrolled in higher education in Norway. Participants ranged in age from 18 to 35.

At the beginning of the study, students completed questionnaires describing their exercise habits, including how frequently they worked out, how strenuous their activities were, how long they exercised, and how many total hours they were active each week. One year later, they completed a self-administered diagnostic assessment designed to identify common mental health disorders.

Exercise Frequency May Matter More Than Intensity

The researchers found that students who reported lower levels of physical activity were more likely to meet diagnostic criteria for anxiety or depression one year later. However, not every aspect of exercise showed the same relationship with mental health.

Exercise frequency emerged as a particularly consistent factor. How often students exercised was more reliably associated with their later mental health than the intensity of their workouts or the amount of time they spent exercising.

The researchers also identified differences between men and women. Among women, lower exercise intensity was associated with a greater likelihood of anxiety and depression. Among men, spending fewer total hours exercising each week showed a stronger association with these conditions.

Overall, the likelihood of common mental health disorders decreased as weekly exercise increased, with this pattern continuing up to approximately 10 hours of physical activity per week.

The results also support the World Health Organization's recommendation that adults complete at least 150 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous physical activity each week.

Regular Exercise Could Help Support Student Mental Health

Taken together, the findings suggest that exercising consistently may be especially valuable for reducing the likelihood of anxiety and depression among college students. Rather than concentrating exclusively on workout intensity or duration, maintaining a regular routine could be an important part of supporting mental health.

However, the researchers emphasize that their observational study cannot establish a direct cause-and-effect relationship. Although students who exercised more regularly tended to have better mental health outcomes, the results do not prove that exercise itself prevented depression or anxiety.

Even with this limitation, promoting accessible opportunities for physical activity could be a useful part of broader efforts to improve student well-being. Such efforts may be especially relevant for students who are beginning to experience mental health difficulties or symptoms that have not yet reached the threshold for a clinical diagnosis.

The authors add: "Our findings show that students who engage in regular physical exercise are at lower risk of developing common mental disorders over time. These findings highlight the importance of making physical activity an accessible and natural part of student life."

"Mental health among students is a growing public health concern. Our findings suggest that supporting students to be physically active may contribute to better mental health and should be recognized as an important part of a healthy learning environment."

Funding: The SHoT study was financially supported by the Norwegian Ministry of Education and Research (2017) and the Norwegian Ministry of Health and Care Services (2016). Neither funding organization participated in designing the research, collecting or analyzing data, deciding whether to publish the findings, or preparing the manuscript.

Research is limited, but we do know a few things: About 4.3% of pregnant women and more than 9% of new mothers experience eating disorders. Women with a history of eating disorders appear more likely to experience postpartum depression and anxiety and to report problems feeding their newborns. And obstetricians typically receive very little training about these conditions or how to use the few screening tools we have validated for eating disorders in pregnancy.

Read more about the gap in this research.

In the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services’ recent update to how Medicare pays physicians, the agency cut the payment rate for certain services provided on the same day by 20% when the services are provided by the same physician or practice.

A bit wonky, I know, but it’s part of the agency’s broader shift away from specialist care and the fee-for-service model, and one of many reimbursement challenges that specialists are contending with.

What does this mean? Opponents say the policy change will force patients to return for separate appointments and increase out-of-pocket costs and wait times. People with Parkinson’s disease, for example, could struggle  to get outpatient Botox injections that are critical for relieving pain. Read more.

We asked STAT staffers to share some of their favorite stories — the pieces they loved reading, or ones they’re still thinking about. Here’s what they said:

I’m grateful for this dispatch from a big conference of people who want to live forever, or at least create a lot of shareholder value before they die. I’m guilty of gawking at the loudest voices in the longevity movement and occasionally dismissing them as men who say alarming things while being weird with their fluids. Sarah Todd, being a good journalist, meets them where they are (the Bay Area, obviously) and finds that whether they’re pitching full-body scans or plotting to reenact ” Never Let Me Go,” most longevity enthusiasts are just like the rest of us: scared to death of inevitably dying. — Damian Garde, STAT reporter at large, live and feature journalism

“Thankful” is not exactly the best word for how I feel about Megan’s story about scientist Brian Donovan; it’s actually pretty depressing. But it’s stayed with me since April because it so well captured the broad impact of federal grant cancellations, the specific challenges interdisciplinary academic researchers face, and the important work that gets left behind as a result. — Andrew Joseph, STAT Europe correspondent

Great journalism doesn’t only uncover secret injustices or corruption. It also reveals the scourges that are hiding in plain sight. Alcohol is so embedded in our culture and consciousness that we may not realize how harmful it has been and could be. This amazing series doesn’t exist to ban drinks from our family Thanksgivings. But it does a great public service of explaining the scope of alcohol addiction, the influence of the industry, and the failures that got us to this point. — Bob Herman, STAT business of health care reporter

Not a story per se, but I loved getting to debrief the Elizabeth Holmes documentary with my fellow STAT reporters. — Margaret Manto, STAT Washington correspondent

I’m especially thankful for Tara Bannow’s tour-de-force investigation of HaloMD. This was especially gutsy reporting because it didn’t stop at the doors of HaloMD. It dug deeper into the lives and motivations of the people leading the company. The reporting led the way in scrutinizing how profiteers have taken advantage of a well-intended policy to ban surprise bills. It was followed by many other outlets and again showed why STAT’s agenda-setting coverage is so vital. — Casey Ross, STAT chief investigative reporter, data and technology

It’s easy to feel pessimistic about what technology is doing to our brains and those of future generations. Which is why I’m grateful for this story from Isa Cueto, which explores creative ways people are working to reclaim kids’ attention spans from compulsive social media scrolling. Rich with rigorous science and insights gleaned from time spent with real teenagers, it offers a welcome antidote to the notion that the attention crisis is a foregone facet of modern life. — Megan Molteni, STAT science writer

We think of human anatomy — organs, muscles, nerves, bones — as a conquered science. Medical students master its intricacies, layer by layer. We can scan the body, palpate it, examine its cells. But anatomy is not history. Subramaniam Krishnan, a cardiac electrophysiologist in California, reminded me that the architecture of our bodies still contains mysteries. Krishnan discovered a pouch within the atrial septum of one of the most studied organs in medical history. He described his finding in his First Opinion essay, “I discovered a new structure in the heart — just by looking closely.” Scientific insight, he wrote, is often limited by “our own assumptions about where to stop looking.” Krishnan nudges us to remember that the frontiers of medicine don’t lie only in AI or genomics — and that curiosity and observation can still spark discovery. — Kathy Burge, STAT contributing editor

In a world of hot takes and outrage for the algo, a thoughtful, beautifully nuanced essay on a simple question: What, exactly, is “religious” about refusing vaccination? In the same vein, our piece on why vaccine skepticism is rational. — Gary Marshall, STAT SEO editor

I’m thankful not only for the incredible investigations and explainers about health insurers by my colleague Bob Herman, but also for the memes he crafts for his weekly newsletter. Some of my favorites are here, here, and here (scroll to the bottom). — Elaine Chen, STAT national biotech reporter

This year, I’m grateful for this poignant essay by Torie Bosch, editor of First Opinion, on how medical aid in dying could have offered her mother a more comfortable death — or, perhaps, averted her suicide. It takes incredible courage to open up about such a painful and personal moment, and a great deal of wisdom to extract larger lessons from the experience. Those are qualities we could use more of in this world. — Jonathan Wosen, STAT West Coast biotech and life science reporter

It’s hard to know how to talk about something as sensitive and upsetting as suicide, and that goes double when it comes to the complicated question of whether assisted suicide should be available to people suffering from mental illness. But I am so thankful for the grace, compassion, and nuance that STAT’s First Opinion editor Torie Bosch brought to the subject in her stunning personal essay. — Sarah Todd, STAT reporter, commercial determinants of health

As a health care journalist, writing about your own health is a deeply vulnerable experience. I’m thankful that STAT’s editors encouraged me to be upfront about how my own experiences inform my approach toward writing about declining trust in science. I’m also grateful to all of our readers who reached out in support after this essay was published; it truly is a privilege to write about such an important topic for such an engaged and sincere audience. — Nick Florko, STAT trust in science reporter

#5543. Keto diet slashes liver fat by 67% in just 4 months

A ketogenic diet may offer significant health benefits beyond weight loss, according to a new clinical trial that compared three popular approaches to eating. Researchers found that people following a very low-carbohydrate, high-fat diet experienced substantially greater reductions in liver fat than those eating Mediterranean or low-fat diets, even though all three groups lost similar amounts of weight.

The results were especially striking for people with prediabetes. After just four to five months on a ketogenic (or "Keto") diet, approximately half of the participants no longer met the diagnostic criteria for the condition. The findings, published in the journal Cell Metabolism, suggest that the types of foods people eat can influence metabolic health in ways that extend beyond the number of pounds they lose.

"We know weight loss can improve metabolic health in people who are obese," says Samuel Klein, the study's corresponding author at Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis, Missouri. "Our data suggest that if you have high liver fat content and prediabetes, reducing carbohydrate intake can have important therapeutic effects on metabolism beyond just weight loss alone."

Comparing Keto, Mediterranean, and Low-Fat Diets

An estimated 40% of American adults have obesity, a condition associated with increased risks of type 2 diabetes, fatty liver disease, and other health problems. Doctors frequently recommend dietary changes to help patients lose weight and improve their metabolic health, which refers to how effectively the body manages energy, blood sugar, and fats.

Three commonly recommended approaches are low-carbohydrate diets, low-fat diets, and Mediterranean diets. Although each can support weight loss, researchers have been uncertain whether one offers additional metabolic advantages when the amount of weight lost is roughly the same.

These eating patterns differ substantially in their nutritional makeup. Low-carbohydrate approaches, including Atkins and ketogenic diets, restrict carbohydrate consumption, while low-fat diets may obtain as much as 70% of their calories from carbohydrates. The Mediterranean diet emphasizes plant foods such as vegetables, nuts, and olive oil, along with moderate amounts of fish and dairy. Ketogenic diets, meanwhile, can include considerable amounts of fat from animal products, including saturated fat.

To compare their effects, Klein and his colleagues recruited 42 adults with obesity, prediabetes, and fatty liver disease. Prediabetes occurs when blood sugar levels rise above the normal range but have not yet reached the threshold for type 2 diabetes. Fatty liver disease involves excess fat accumulating inside liver cells, which can interfere with the body's ability to regulate metabolism.

A Controlled Clinical Trial With Similar Weight Loss

Participants were randomly assigned to follow one of three diets: ketogenic, Mediterranean, or a low-fat diet emphasizing plant-based foods. To ensure that participants followed their assigned eating plans, the research team supplied all their meals and arranged weekly consultations with a dietitian.

The diets had sharply different proportions of carbohydrates and fat. In the ketogenic group, carbohydrates accounted for just 4% of daily calories, while fat supplied 73%. The Mediterranean group received 50% of its calories from carbohydrates and 35% from fat. The plant-forward group consumed 70% of its calories from carbohydrates and 15% from fat.

Researchers adjusted calorie intake individually so that participants across all three groups lost approximately 10% of their starting body weight. Reaching this target took about four to five months.

By the end of the intervention, every group had experienced meaningful reductions in body fat and improvements in insulin sensitivity. Insulin is the hormone that helps move sugar from the bloodstream into cells, where it can be used for energy. Greater insulin sensitivity makes it easier for the body to maintain healthy blood sugar levels.

However, the similarities between the groups largely ended there.

The ketogenic diet produced the largest improvements in several important indicators of liver function and metabolic health.

Participants following keto experienced an average 67% reduction in liver fat, compared with a 45% reduction in both the Mediterranean and low-fat groups. Because the groups lost comparable amounts of weight, the difference suggests that carbohydrate restriction may influence liver fat through mechanisms beyond weight loss alone.

To investigate these effects, the researchers collected blood samples repeatedly over a 24-hour period, allowing them to observe changes in hormones involved in energy metabolism.

The ketogenic group showed the greatest increase in glucagon, a hormone that helps regulate the body's energy supply and promotes the reduction of fat stored in the liver. Participants on keto also experienced the largest decrease in insulin levels, another change that can help reduce liver fat accumulation.

One result was particularly unexpected. Despite getting nearly three-quarters of their calories from fat, the keto participants did not show an increase in blood fat or cholesterol levels during the study.

"The most surprising finding was that participants in the ketogenic diet group didn't experience an increase in blood fat or cholesterol levels despite consuming the most fat," says Max Petersen, the study's first author at Washington University School of Medicine.

Half of Keto Participants No Longer Had Prediabetes

The benefits extended beyond liver fat. After the weight-loss intervention, approximately 50% of participants assigned to the ketogenic diet no longer met the criteria for prediabetes. By comparison, that milestone was reached by 29% of those on the Mediterranean diet and just 7% of those following the low-fat, plant-forward diet.

These differences are notable because prediabetes signals an elevated risk of developing type 2 diabetes. Bringing blood sugar levels below the prediabetes threshold is an important improvement, although it does not necessarily mean the condition has been permanently reversed.

The findings also highlight a potentially important distinction in weight management: losing weight and improving metabolic health are closely connected, but they are not necessarily the same thing. The composition of a diet may affect how the body handles blood sugar, stores fat, and responds to hormones, even when weight loss is similar.

Researchers emphasize the growing importance of understanding these effects as powerful new obesity treatments become more widely available. GLP-1 medications, which act on hormone pathways involved in appetite and blood sugar regulation, have transformed the treatment of obesity by helping many patients achieve substantial weight loss.

"GLP-1-based medications have revolutionized the therapy of obesity. We now have a very effective pharmacotherapy for achieving significant weight loss," Petersen says. "But in addition, our study shows that the specific composition of the diet can give you added benefits."

Although the trial was relatively small and lasted only four to five months, its carefully controlled design offers evidence that dietary composition can play an important role in metabolic health. Longer studies involving more participants will be needed to determine whether the benefits persist and how different diets compare over time.

The research was supported by the National Institutes of Health and the Foundation for Barnes-Jewish Hospital.

Materials provided by Cell Press. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#5542. Infamous ‘Hoarders’ Mansion in North Carolina Sells for $3.85 Million After Jaw-Dropping Restoration

A stunning 1929 English Tudor home in Greensboro, NC, that gained notoriety after it appeared in "Hoarders" closed last week for $3.85 million after two years on the market.

The home was built during the Gilded Age for prominent local businessman Julian Price, and designed by New York architect Charles C. Hartmann.

The 8,616-square-foot home, found at 301 Fisher Park Circle in Greensboro, has over 30 rooms, including eight bedrooms, six full bathrooms, and two half bathrooms.

The Julian Price Home was put on the National Register of Historic Place in 1980, it gained attention in 2017, when it was featured on an episode of A&E’s "Hoarders".

The home was owned, at the time, by interior designer Sandra Cowart. She had lived in the home since 1975, and kept the home in pristine condition for years, even giving tours and renting out rooms, according to a 2017 article from the Chicago Tribune.

After 2005, she became closed off, became a compulsive collector, and her home was ultimately foreclosed on. The home was purchased out of foreclosure by Eric and Michael Fuko-Rizzo for $415,000, a fraction of the property’s value.

The couple transformed the home back to its former glory with their deep knowledge and love of old homes and architecture.

“They were great people to re-do it, Eric and Michael. Michael’s energy and knowledge of loving old places is honestly over the top,” listing agent Kay Chesnutt, of Berkshire Hathaway Home Services, told Realtor.com. “Not many people would even consider redoing something or saving something like that.”

In addition to its numerous bedrooms, the home has an elaborate butlers' pantry, library, great room, and breakfast room. For sunny North Carolina days, there  is also a sunroom and a screened porch. All of the details were restored with intention and care for the home’s history.

“It’s like walking into a magical part of history. The beauty of the details and how they were restored—or, if they had to remove something, they’d replicate it,” Chesnutt described the restoration process. “It is something that should be saved for Greensboro. Anybody that goes into it says ‘Wow,’ because the pictures don’t even do it justice.

After the restoration, the Fuko-Rizzos opened the home up as an inn. At times, the home would be rented out in its entirety by families or host community events. It even received visits from stars like Carrie Underwood and Leanne Morgan, according to Chesnutt.

“Unwind in our drawing room with a book and glass of wine while observing the detail of the original molded plaster ceiling and fireplace surround,” the inn’s website reads. “However you plan your visit, it is certain that the charm, elegance and restored original details of this 1929 Tudor mansion will captivate and leave you and your guests with lasting memories.”

The Fuko-Rizzos listed the home for sale again in August of 2024, for an initial price of $5.25 million.

The property’s operation as an inn is one of the reasons that such a stunning home would remain on the market for two years, Chesnutt said. As the listing agent, she and the owners would have to coordinate showings around room availability.

“We couldn’t show it when there were people that were registered and paying guests. Their rooms were locked, so we only showed it when times were open, and it was empty and clean and always immaculate,” said Chesnutt.

After over two years, the home closed on November 19 for $3.85 million. The new owners are a local couple.

“It just suited them,” said Chesnutt. “And I think they’ll be good care takers.”

Chesnutt could not disclose whether the the new owners plan to keep the property open as an inn or make it a family home, but the property is no longer active on Airbnb. Either way, the Julian Price Home has a long life ahead of it due to good bones and quality craftsmanship.

“It has a wonderful feeling, and even on the darkest days, it’s very light,” said Chesnutt. “And the quality that was done then, we couldn’t reproduce today.”
